n: Barren Jews in captivity, or Church of the Gentiles, to which alone many of the expressions can be applied. (Calmet) --- The Gentiles were before unfruitful, as the Jews will be till towards the latter times. (Worthington)
Stakes, to receive so great a family. All the Israelites did not return, and it does not appear that many embraced their religion, as they have done that of Christ.
Left. To the north and south. Jerusalem increased. But what was it compared with the Christian establishment!
Widowhood. Thy former excesses shall be forgotten. (Calmet)

Thee. Hebrew, "Bohalaic (Haydock) shall be your Baalim," or husband, who was styled Lord, 1 Peter iii. 6. Perhaps he may allude to the two wives, the synagogue and the Church, or to the idols, which should be adored no more.
Youth. This enhances her fault. God is pleased to overlook it, in the captives (chap. l. 1.) and Gentiles.

Earth. Giving him the rainbow for a sign. My covenant with the Church is equally irrevocable: she is founded on a rock, Matthew xvi. 18. (Calmet) --- Christ will no more abandon her than he will drown the world. Some mountains shall be moved out of their place, but she shall not. (Worthington)
Sapphires. Hebrew, "antimony," a mineral shining like silver, 4 Kings ix. 30.
Bulwarks. Hebrew, windows of crystal; (Ezechiel xxvii. 1[].; Calmet) Protestants, "of agate." (Haydock) --- All this is allegorical, like the redemption of the new Jerusalem, Apocalypse. xxi.
Lord, Christ, Jeremias xxxi. 33., and John vi. 45.
Thee. The Cutheans rendered the Jews suspected, 1 Esdras iv. 2., and vi. 1
To thee, in the inheritance. This was verified in the Church. We have no accout of many being converted before.
Destroy. I can give peace or war. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "but I have created thee not for utter destruction." (Haydock)

f: The First Apology, Chapter LIII

For all the Gentiles were "desolate" of the true God, serving the works of their hands; but the Jews and Samaritans, having the word of God delivered to them by the prophets, and always expecting the Christ, did not recognise Him when He came, except some few, of whom the Spirit of prophecy by Isaiah had predicted that they should be saved.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 40: ON “REJOICE, O BARREN ONE”

WHAT DOES THE PROPHET MEAN WHEN HE SAYS, “REJOICE, O BARREN ONE WHO DOES NOT BEAR; BREAK FORTH AND CRY ALOUD, YOU WHO DO NOT LABOR, BECAUSE THE CHILDREN OF THE DESOLATE ARE MORE THAN THOSE OF HER WHO HAS A HUSBAND." — Since the children of earthly Jerusalem have fallen away from God, joy cannot be ascribed to her, but rather sorrow. Therefore, as a criticism to this Jerusalem, the prophet says that that higher Jerusalem should rejoice, the one the Apostle calls “our mother” (Gal. 4:26): because without groaning and pains she has far more children than this Jerusalem, which in tears gives birth carnally, namely, the Jews, whereas the other gives birth to Christians spiritually through faith. He calls her “desolate” because she is the life that Adam, the first man, abandoned when he followed death. So when people are reborn, they return to the life they had deserted. This life is Christ, because he says, “I am the life” (Jn. 14:6). And God the Father is also life, because the Lord says, “As the Father has life, so he has given the Son to have life” (Jn. 5:26). Without doubt the Holy Spirit is life as well, since the Lord says, “He will receive from what is mine” (Jn. 16:15). Whoever receives from life is necessarily life. Therefore the three are one life. This is the life by faith in whom we are reborn. She is our mother, as we read in Genesis, because she, namely, Life, is the mother of all the living (Gen. 3:20). And who are the living, if not those who believe?
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 15: ON “REJOICE, O BARREN ONE”

WHAT IS IT THAT THE PROPHET SAYS: REJOICE, BARREN WOMAN, YOU WHO DO NOT GIVE BIRTH; BREAK FORTH AND CRY OUT, YOU WHO DO NOT LABOR IN CHILDBIRTH, BECAUSE THE CHILDREN OF THE DESOLATE ARE MORE NUMEROUS THAN THOSE OF HER WHO HAS A HUSBAND? — In this passage we understand two mothers: the heavenly and the earthly, that is, the free Jerusalem, of which the Apostle says that she is our mother, and this Jerusalem which he says is in slavery with her children, that is, the Jews. For the prophet, proclaiming the coming of the Lord and seriously calling out in joyful voice for the time of grace, exhorts the heavenly Jerusalem, called “desolate” because she did not yet have dwelling in her the children generated through faith, to rejoice. For the time had come when she should have the children foretold long ago, and many more than those of this Jerusalem, because Christians have surpassed the number of Jews. She is therefore called barren because she is a virgin, who does not bring forth a son through physical union and embrace, but spiritually through faith alone. Therefore she is not said to be in labor; for one who is in labor suffers pains. This one cries out instead in the joy of human salvation. But earthly Jerusalem is said to have a husband because she gave birth carnally. For the city is presented as a kind of mother, just as that heavenly dwelling to which we are called is called our mother.
Commentary on Galatians

For it is written: Rejoice, barren one, you who do not bear; break forth and cry out, you who do not travail: for many more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband (Isa. 54:1.)

The synagogue had the Law as her husband; and, according also to the prophecy of Hannah, she was once fruitful in children (1 Sam. 1). But the barren Church, without Christ as husband, without any address of the Bridegroom's word, lay long in the desert. But after the synagogue received the bill of divorce into her hands, and turned all her husband's ornaments into the ornament of an idol, then the husband, his former girdle rotting, wove another belt for his loins, another loincloth out of the Gentiles; and she, as soon as she was joined to her husband, conceived and gave birth. And in Isaac the Lord cries out through the prophet: "Is a nation born all at once?" (Isa. 66:8): when in a single day, in the Acts of the Apostles, three thousand and five thousand men believed (Acts 3 ff.). Nor do I think it necessary for us to speak of the Christian multitude and of the fewness of the Jews, since the banners of the cross shine forth in the whole world, and a Jew scarcely appears in the cities, rare and conspicuous.
Commentary on Isaiah

I know that I have often said, Eustochium, that the Apostles and Evangelists, wherever they set down testimonies from the Old Instrument, were accustomed, if there is no difference between the Hebrew and the Septuagint, to use either their own words or those of the Seventy Translators; but if the sense is one thing in the Hebrew and another in the old edition, they follow the Hebrew rather than the Seventy Translators. In short, just as we have shown that they set down many things from the Hebrew which are not found in the Seventy, so let our rivals show some testimonies taken from the Seventy which are not in the books of the Hebrews, and the dispute is finished. We have said this because the present passage, though it is one in sense, differs in words. With its explanation the fifteenth book on Isaiah begins.
Commentary on Isaiah

Praise, O barren one, who do not bear; sing out praise and neigh, you who were not in labor: for more are the sons of the deserted one than of her who had a husband, says the Lord. LXX: Rejoice, O barren one, who do not bear: break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor: for more are the sons of the deserted one than of her who has a husband. For the Lord has said. Symmachus translated this passage thus: Rejoice, O barren one, who have not borne. Be glad in exultation, and neigh, you who have not been in labor: For more are the sons of the scattered one than of her who was under a husband. From him Theodotion and Aquila do not differ, apart from a few words. After the nativity of the Savior, and the course of His life and mighty works, the passion of the cross, and the glory of the resurrection, when, laying down His soul, He saw a long-lived seed, and in His knowledge He, the righteous one, justified very many, and divided the spoils of the strong, and prayed for the transgressors, giving room for repentance, the Prophet passes to the calling of the nations, and describes in full discourse those who were to believe in Him. This passage the apostle Paul too refers, under the name of Sarah and Isaac, to the Church (Gal 4:27ff.): that the former people, from Mount Sinai and Hagar, is in bondage with her children, but the later one is free, of whom Isaiah says: Rejoice, O barren one, who do not bear: break forth and cry out, you who are not in labor: for more are the sons of the deserted one than of her who has a husband; and immediately: But we, he says, brethren, are sons of the promise according to Isaac. But as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the spirit, so it is now also. But what does the Scripture say? Cast out the bondwoman and her son. For the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman. But we, brethren, are not sons of the bondwoman, but of the free: with which freedom Christ has endowed us (Gal 4:27ff.). If, then, the vessel of election, taking from Isaiah the testimony which we now have in hand, referred it to the sons of the promise, and to the Church gathered from the nations, or from both peoples, which had been deserted and abandoned among the Jews, which had not had God as her husband, nor had received the Law or the Prophets, we are compelled by that very reasoning to follow the footsteps of our predecessor, and to call her the deserted one of whom we read above (cf. Isa 35): Rejoice, O deserted one, and the rest like these. Of her too it is written in Jeremiah, in the person of God: She who bore seven has been made empty, and her soul has fainted. Her sun has set while it was yet midday (Jer 15:9). And in the volume of Samuel: The barren has borne seven, and she who had many sons has been weakened (1 Sam 2:5). And in the Psalms: Who makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of sons (Ps 112 [113]:9). Now the synagogue is said to have borne seven sons because of the mystery of the week and of the sabbath, to which the former people had been bound. Or else, for seven, many are to be understood, according to an ambiguity of the Hebrew speech, by which both sabbath and many are signified; of this more has been said in the book of Hebrew Questions which we wrote on Genesis. She, then, as long as she had God, the divine word, for her husband and was joined to the Law, bore very many sons to God; but when she received the bill of divorce, and would not answer her husband when he called, she heard: You are your mother's daughter, who have forsaken your husband (Ezek 16:45). And again: You have not called me as Lord, nor as father and guide of your virginity (Jer 3:4): therefore she is lamented in this same Prophet: How has the faithful city become a harlot, Zion, full of judgment: in which righteousness slept in her, but now robbers (Isa 1:21). But this too is to be noted, that when he says: More are the sons of the deserted one than of her who has a husband, the synagogue is not wholly excluded from childbearing, but the multitude of the nations is preferred to her. For she too, in the Apostles and through the Apostles, first bore a people from the Jews. Hence the two chief of the Apostles divided between them the hosts of those who believed in Christ, of the Circumcision and of the Gentiles, so that from both peoples they might build up Jerusalem, formerly deserted and poor. And that the Hebrew has put neighing for gladness signifies the greatness of joy, in the likeness of a horse neighing for victory; of which more is written in Job (Job 39). This passage and the rest that follow the Jews and our own judaizers refer to Jerusalem, which they say is to be restored in a kingdom of a thousand years, and they say she is the same who formerly had a husband and afterward ceased to have one, and that after the divorce she will have many more sons than she had before under a husband. Yet the comparison is plainly set out of two women: of her who had a husband and was put away, and of her who was always deserted and without a husband. Nor is it to be wondered at in the Jews, whose eyes and ears are closed, if they do not see the open truth. Of the Christians I do not know what to say, who, though the Apostle says, which things are allegorical, and refers Sarah and Hagar to the two Testaments, the old and the new, give their hands to the Jews out of desire for earthly pleasures in the thousand years.
Commentary on Isaiah

Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles: do not spare: make your cords long, and make your stakes firm. For you shall penetrate to the right and to the left, and your seed shall inherit the nations, and shall inhabit the deserted cities. LXX: Enlarge the place of your tabernacle, and fix the skins of your curtains, do not spare. Lengthen your cords, and strengthen your stakes; yet more to the right, and to the left spread out, and your seed shall possess the nations, and you shall make the deserted cities to be inhabited. To her to whom he had said: Praise, O barren one, who do not bear; break the bonds, by which you were formerly held bound, and cry out in confession of the Lord, you who had no children, it is now commanded, in the likeness of the tabernacle of Moses which he once had (Exod 36) in the desert, that she enlarge her tent and stretch out the skins; and make her cords longer, and drive deep and strengthen the stakes by which every tent is shaped, lest it be scattered by the blasts of the winds. And let her penetrate to the right and to the left, and by no means imitate the narrowness of the Jewish tabernacle, which enclosed a hundred cubits of length and fifty of breadth, nor be shut in by the smallness of the Temple, which had sixty cubits in length and twenty in breadth; but let her not cease to take up room to the right and to the left (Exod 27). And lest we think this is said, according to the frivolous contention of the Hebrews, of Zion, which is to be restored by the Lord to its ancient state, he sets out more plainly what lay hidden: And your seed shall inherit the nations. Of this we read in the Gospel also: He who sows went out to sow (Matt 13:3); and again: Did you not sow good seed in your field (ibid., 27)? This seed will also make the deserted cities to be inhabited, so that Churches of the nations rise up throughout the whole world. Or certainly the seed is to be called that of the Apostles and the remnant of the Jewish people, of which it is said in this same Prophet: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9). And the Apostle: A remnant, he says, has been saved (Rom 11:5). This concerns the greatness of the Churches, which, in place of the one land of Judea, and that a very narrow one, will spread their bounds through the whole world. Let us come to the spiritual understanding. He who is in a tabernacle does not possess a firm and perpetual dwelling; but he always changes places, and hastens on to what lies beyond, saying in the psalm: I will pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle (Ps 41 [42]:5), forgetting the things that are past and stretching himself forward to what is to come, until he attains the prize of the heavenly calling. Of this tabernacle we read in another place also: How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of powers! my soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord (Ps 83 [84]:1). And afterward he adds: Blessed are they who dwell in your house; for ages of ages they shall praise you (ibid., 6). For the end of the tabernacles is the possession of an eternal house, which does not change its foundations, nor is moved from one place into another. For those who are planted in the house of the Lord have first flowered in His courts, so that they may come from flowers to fruit, and may be able to say: But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God (Ps 51 [52]:10). In short, the holy man, hastening to pass beyond the tabernacles and longing to see the house of God, says that he has one wish, never to go out of the house of God: One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life (Ps 26 [27]:4). The tabernacle, then, must be enlarged, and the curtains and skins stretched out, and the cords of manifold and varied discourses drawn out further, and the stakes made firm by reason on the right and on the left, so that the seed of the word, that is, of the doctrine of God, may be able to possess the nations, and to make habitable the cities which he received who had doubled the mina. Now the right and the left in the holy Scriptures are taken in a good sense when we understand them both according to the spirit and according to the letter, through the arms of righteousness on the right and on the left (2 Cor 6), so that the humbler understanding may hold to the ordering of life and the examples of our forebears, and the spiritual and sublime one may carry us over from present things to things to come. This is what the Lord also said to the Pharisees when they questioned Him: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's (Matt 22:21): that we should both be subject to the powers of this world, which not unjustly bear the sword for vengeance on those who have done evil, and this is understood as the left; and that we should render to God the things that are God's, so as to fear no one else but Him who has power over both soul and body, and this is taken as the right (Matt 10). Finally, it is said of the wisdom of God, to which nothing precious can be compared, that in her right hand she has length of life and very many years, but in her left riches and glory; so that those riches are to be understood which consist in knowledge in the present and in good works, and the glory which he receives through whose works God is glorified among the nations; while length of life and very many years signify eternal life, which, disregarding present things, hastens toward what is to come.
Commentary on Isaiah

Do not fear, for you shall not be confounded, nor shall you blush: for you shall not be ashamed, because you shall forget the confusion of your youth, and shall no more remember the reproach of your widowhood. For He who made you shall rule over you, the Lord of hosts is His name: and your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, shall be called the God of all the earth. LXX: Do not fear, because you have been confounded: nor be confounded, because you have been reproached: for you shall forget the eternal confusion, and of the reproach of your widowhood you shall not be mindful: for the Lord who made you, the Lord Sabaoth is His name: and He who delivered you, the God of Israel, shall be called of all the earth. A question arises: if it is said to the Church gathered from the nations: Rejoice, O barren one, who do not bear; and: More are the sons of the deserted one than of her who has a husband, meaning that she who afterward bore more sons had not had a husband, and that she who formerly had a husband was turned to barrenness, how is it now said to her who had no husband: You shall no more remember your widowhood, and you shall forget the confusion of your youth? From this the Jews wish it to be understood that all that is said is said to Jerusalem, which, deserted by God, is to be restored by Him again. They will easily be repelled when they are reminded that it is said in the person of the Lord in Zechariah: And I took to myself two rods: the one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord: and I fed the flock (Zech 11:7). Of this we have spoken more fully in its place, and now it will be spoken of in part. The two rods are the two peoples, of the nations and of the Jews; of these the first to be called was the throng of the Gentiles, which received the natural law fixed in their hearts, about which Paul, writing to the Romans, argues most forcefully (Rom 1); and nothing is more beautiful than this rod, that every creature should be called equally to the worship of its Creator. But the second, that is, the rod of the people of the Jews, was called Cord: which, after the offense of the nations, is called the portion of the Lord, and Israel the cord of His inheritance (Deut 32). Finally, after Israel was called in Abraham, the Lord says: I took my rod which was called Beauty, and I cut it off, to make void my covenant which I struck with all the nations (Zech 11:10). Therefore at the coming of Christ it is said to the rod that had been cut off: Do not fear, nor blush, nor flood your face with shame. For you shall by no means be confounded any longer, as you had been confounded before, nor shall you be mindful of the confusion of your youth, and you shall not remember your widowhood, through which you were abandoned by God: for your maker Himself shall rule over you, whose name is the Almighty, who reigns not in the one nation of Judea but in the whole world. Finally, there follows: He who had made you has Himself redeemed you with His blood, and He shall be called the God of all the earth: that is to say, of all who dwell on the earth. From this it is plainly evident that this is by no means said to Jerusalem, which never ruled over the whole world, but to the Church of Christ, whose inheritance is the possession of the world.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:2.54:4-5

We have been justified in Christ, and not from works of righteousness that we have done but according to his mercy. But this is also what the supremely wise Paul has written. For we have been set free from the darkness, deceit and wickedness, which have been inherited from our ancestors.… [Therefore,] do not fear that you will be put to shame. For just as a parent looks after children, the Lord will look after those who fear him. Your sins will be as far removed from you as the east is from the west. How necessary is it, then, that you not stumble again but reject those same sins in fear. Remember the grace of our justifying God, and do not bear malice or demand justice from those who sin against you.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:2.54:4-5

He makes clear how he makes the shame of widowhood disappear, saying that it is "the Lord who makes you, the Lord of hosts is his name." He is making you rather than creating you, transferring us into another type of citizenship and beautiful life. For we are being transformed in Christ into the newness of the holy and evangelical life, ascending to his own beautiful form through the Spirit so that others see us as different from the rest [of humanity].
Commentary on Isaiah

For the Lord has called you as a woman forsaken and mourning in spirit: and as a wife cast off from her youth, says your God. For a moment, for a little while, I forsook you: and with great mercies I will gather you. In a moment of indignation I hid my face from you for a little while: and with everlasting mercy I have had pity on you, says your redeemer, the Lord. LXX: Not as a woman forsaken and faint-hearted has the Lord called you, nor as a woman who is hated from her youth, says your God. For a little time I left you: and with great mercy I will have pity on you. In a little wrath I turned away my face from you: and with everlasting mercy I will have pity on you: says the Lord who delivered you. Here the friends of the Jews debase the forsaken woman and the wife cast off from her youth, whom the Lord forsook for a moment and for a little while, saying that she is Jerusalem; and that He, hiding His face for a little while, took her up again in everlasting mercies and changed her past grief into joy. This is according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy he says that He did not call her as a forsaken woman and faint-hearted, nor as a wife who had been held in hatred from her youth; but that He left her for a little while and turned away His face for this reason, that He might have pity on her forever. If, then, the Jews and our judaizers say that Israel was forsaken for a little while, so that at the coming of Christ God might have pity on it, and interpret 'a little' by comparison with the whole of eternity, why do they not grant us too to call that a little time during which the nations were forsaken, so that they, cast off in the middle period, who in their youth had been God's, might afterward in their old age obtain eternal mercy? Especially since, in the time of Israel's calling, the throng of the Gentiles was never shut out, but a door of return always lay open to them through the proselytes; so that, as we seem to have been shut out for a little while by their calling, so by their perpetual exclusion a return to God is granted to us. But we have spoken of a perpetual exclusion if they do not repent. Otherwise the apostle Paul says: God has shut up all things under sin, that He may have mercy on all (Gal 3:22). What we have interpreted of the Church gathered from both peoples, and the Jews take of Jerusalem, those who follow tropology alone, and in the most difficult places flee the questions that arise by an excursion of free disputation, refer to the sinful soul, which has been cast off by God, not out of hatred but by dispensation, so that, pressed by the weight of evils, she may return to her former husband, and, having lost her substance, may not despair of the father's clemency (Luke 15). Is it not great mercy to run to meet the returning son, to hold out the ring and the robe and a kiss, and, after the likeness of another parable, to say to the envious brother: Friend, if I am good, why is your eye evil (Matt 20:15)?
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:2.54:8

"And by my eternal mercy I will have mercy on you." For the season of anger is short and brief in comparison with the measure of the boundless loving-kindness given to us from God. He rescued us out of the power of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of the Son of his love in light. It is appropriate to think greatly of the mercy that is through Christ, who cleanses us from every stain and takes away the accusation of justice. He restores us to a relationship with him through holinesss and gives the garlands of the glory of sonship to those whom he establishes in the kingdom of heaven.
Commentary on Isaiah

As in the days of Noah, so is this to me, to whom I swore that I would no more bring the waters of Noah upon the earth: so I have sworn not to be angry with you and not to rebuke you. For the mountains shall be moved, and the hills shall tremble: but my mercy shall not depart from you, and the covenant of my peace shall not be moved, says the Lord who has compassion on you. LXX: From the water which was under Noah this is to me: as I swore to him at that time that I would by no means any more be angry with the earth over you, nor in threatening you remove the mountains: nor shall your hills be removed. So neither shall my mercy fail, nor shall the covenant of my peace be taken away, says the Lord who is merciful to you. So that the congregation of the saints may believe the mercy of the Lord to be everlasting, and that we were forsaken for a moment and briefly for this reason, that they might be joined in friendship with God by an eternal covenant, he sets forth the examples of the forebears, saying: As, when the whole world was sinning, after all the earth had corrupted the way of the Lord, the flood was brought in, and together with all the authors of sins all sins were blotted out, and in one man, Noah, the human race was preserved; to whom I swore that a flood would by no means be brought on the lands, and my pledge has been kept until now and will never be made void (Gen 8 and 9): so I swear to my Church, which I have redeemed for myself with my blood, that I will by no means be angry with those on whom I have had pity, nor will my clemency be changed by any harshness of rebuke. For the mountains and hills will more easily be moved than my sentence will be changed. In accordance with which He also says in the Gospel: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away (Matt 24:35). And this, he says, is my mercy: that the covenant of peace, by which the world has been reconciled to me, is kept not by the merit of those to whom it was given, but by my clemency. According to the Seventy the sense is confused, and everything is so disordered that what is being said can hardly be understood: not that I do not know what a most prudent man has said on this passage, but that it does not satisfy my mind. For he posits a tropological flood, which he interprets of the baptism of the Savior, gathering very many examples, such as this: The Lord makes the flood to be inhabited (Ps 28 [29]:10). And again: The Lord is sweet to those who wait for Him in the day of tribulation: and knowing those who fear Him, in the flood of the journey He makes an end (Nah 1:7, LXX): namely, that He blotted out all sins in baptism, saying in another place: I am, I am He who blots out your iniquities (Isa 43:25). For all had turned aside, together they had become unprofitable (Ps 13 [14]:3). There was none who did mercy or truth, nor was there knowledge of God upon the earth. Cursing and lying and murder and adultery and theft had seized everything, and they had mingled blood with blood. Whence He speaks through the Prophet: Woe is me! for the devout man has perished from the earth. There is none who does right among men; all are judged in my blood. Each afflicts his neighbor with affliction, and they prepare their hands for evil (Mic 7:2, LXX); and the rest like these. Among them is this: No one is clean from filth, not even if his life upon the earth be of one day (Job 14:4). Hence he holds that the Lord made the flood, who according to the apostle Peter was put to death in the flesh and made alive in the spirit (1 Pet 3), and preached to the spirits set in prison, when the patience of God waited in the days of Noah, bringing the flood upon the ungodly; after whose pattern water cleanses us, not washing away the filth of the flesh, but as the questioning of a good conscience toward God. And the mountains and hills which are not moved, and in a flood of this kind had been shaken, he wants to be understood as the saints, once the everlasting covenant has been received, who in the former flood had been moved and had left their firmness. He says that the mountains are also the demons and the adverse powers, who saw the daughters of men, that they were fair, and, wounded by the dart of love, took for themselves wives of all whom they chose, and lost their former strength; and they will by no means be in this flood (Gen 6). This is what he may have said; its explanation I leave to the reader's judgment.
Commentary on Isaiah

Poor little one, torn by the tempest, without consolation. Behold, I will lay your stones in order: and I will found you on sapphires: and I will make your battlements of jasper, and your gates of carved stones, and all your borders of desirable stones: All your sons taught by the Lord, and a multitude of peace for your sons, and in righteousness you shall be founded. LXX: Lowly and unstable, without consolation. Behold, I prepare for you the carbuncle as your stone, and sapphire as your foundations: and I will make your battlements jasper, and your gates stones of crystal, and your walls choice stones: and all your sons disciples of God, and great peace shall be for your sons, and in righteousness you shall be built. Where we have said: I will lay your stones in order, in the Hebrew is written BAPHPHUCH (בפך), which all except the Seventy have translated alike: I will lay your stones in stibium, in the likeness of an adorned woman who paints her eyes with stibium, so as to signify the beauty of the city. And where we, following the Seventy, have said jasper, the Hebrew has written CHODCHOD (כדכד), which Symmachus alone translated χαλκηδόνιον. For crystal also, in whose place ECDA (אקדה) is read among the Hebrews, Symmachus and Theodotion put of carving, that is, γλυφῆς, and Aquila τρυπανισμοῦ: a word that conveys the sense of bored and engraved gems. We have spoken of the difference of translation; let us come to the sense. He is still speaking to the Church, formerly lowly and poor, which had neither the Law nor the Prophets nor the word of God; torn by the tempest or unstable, which had endured many whirlwinds of the world and wavered among the various errors of idols; which had no comforter, and in vain spent all her substance on physicians: that He Himself will come, He Himself will descend, and build on earth the heavenly Jerusalem, which in the Apocalypse of John is called the bride and wife of the Lamb, having light like a precious stone, like jasper and crystal, and a great wall, and twelve gates inscribed with the names of the tribes of Israel, of which three were on the East, and three on the North, and three on the South, and three on the West (Rev 21); and the wall rested on twelve foundations, its whole building of jasper stone, and the several foundations of the walls had each its own stone: the first jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald, the fifth sardonyx, the sixth sardius, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh jacinth, the twelfth amethyst. Reading this, we cry out and say: O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how inscrutable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counselor (Rom 11:33, 34)? And again: Who is wise, and he will understand these things; understanding, and he will know them (Hos 14:10)? Let them answer, the lovers of the letter alone, which kills, who in the thousand years make ready exquisite foods for gluttony and luxury, whose God is the belly and whose glory is in their shame (Phil 3); who after the second coming of the Savior in glory hope for marriages, and little children of a hundred years, and the outrage of circumcision, and the blood of victims, and a perpetual sabbath; who say with Israel, in a perverse way: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall reign: let them answer what this heavenly Jerusalem is to which it is now said: Behold, I will lay your stones in order; or according to the Seventy: Behold, I prepare for you the carbuncle, your stone: so that the whole city is full of carbuncles, and has sapphire foundations, and battlements of jasper or chalcedony, and gates of crystal or carved in relief, and a wall of precious stones round about; and all her sons have no men as teachers, but God, and are called disciples of God; and there is in her perpetual peace and the building up of righteousness. From this it is clear that under the occasion of righteousness, which is the name of a virtue, we ought to seek the other virtues too for the building up of the Church, and not follow Jewish ravings. For let them explain what it is that is said of wisdom in Proverbs: She is more precious than all the most precious stones (Prov 3:15). For if Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1), it is foolish for Christ to be compared to senseless stones. And again we read of the judgments of God: The judgments of the Lord are right, justified in themselves, desirable above gold and very precious stone (Ps 18 [19]:10, 11). From this it is plain that the stone compared with the other stones is the one of which it is said above in this same Prophet, in the person of God: Behold, I will lay in the foundations of Zion a corner stone, a chosen stone, precious: and he who believes in it shall not be confounded (Isa 28:16). This stone the builders rejected (Ps 117 [118]), namely the Scribes and Pharisees and the chief men of the Jews, and it has become the head of the corner (Matt 21). Of it the Apostle Peter also says in his discourse: To us therefore who believe in the corner stone, precious and chosen, there is honor; but to unbelievers it is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense (1 Pet 2:7, 8). And he too speaks to the chief priests in the Acts of the Apostles: This is the chosen stone, precious, which you despised and rejected (Acts 4:11); which has become the head of the corner, and holds together the two peoples, of the nations and of Israel; which built the city whose builder and maker is God: of which the Apostle also writes to the Corinthians: You are God's building. And: As a wise architect I have laid the foundation, and another builds upon it. But let each one see how he builds. For no one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, Jesus Christ (1 Cor 3:9, 10). And if anyone builds on this foundation gold and precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, each one's work will be made manifest. Of this foundation he speaks in another Epistle also: Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the corner stone (Eph 2:20); and again: In whom you are all being built as living stones into a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices (1 Pet 2:5). Of these stones it is said mystically: Holy stones are rolled upon the earth (Zech 9:16), with which Christ builds the Church upon the rock, saying in the Gospel: Upon this rock I will build my Church (Matt 16:18). He who has deserved to enter this city says joyfully to the Lord: As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of powers, in the city of our God: God has founded it forever (Ps 47 [48]:9). Concerning the founder of this city it is said in another place also: He shall build my city, and shall bring back the captivity of my people (Isa 45:13). As for the nature of the twelve stones and gems, this is not the time to speak, since very many both of the Greeks and of the Latins have written of it. Of these I will name only two: the bishop Epiphanius, a man of holy and venerable memory, who has left us a notable volume of his genius and learning, which he entitled περὶ λίθων; and Pliny the Second, at once orator and philosopher among the Latins, who in his most beautiful work of natural history filled the thirty-seventh book, which is also the last, with a treatment of stones and gems. These twelve stones are written in order in Exodus and in Ezekiel, that is, ἐν τῷ λογείῳ of the high priest, and in the crown and diadem of the prince of Tyre. Let us speak first of Exodus: four rows of stones were woven in (Exod 28). The first row had the sardius, topaz, emerald; the second row, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper; the third row, ligure, agate, amethyst; the fourth row, chrysolite, beryl, onyx, set in gold; and they were inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel. In which it is to be noted that the second row of stones is also set down in the present Scripture: carbuncle, sapphire and jasper. For we do not yet hold what is perfect, nor have we come to the first things, because now we see through a mirror in an enigma. Further, in Ezekiel we find it written thus: You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God. You were clothed with every first stone: sardius, topaz and emerald, carbuncle and sapphire and jasper, silver also, and gold and ligure, and agate and amethyst, and chrysolite and beryl and onyx; and with gold you filled your treasuries and your storehouses within you. From the day you were created, I set you with the Cherubim on my holy mountain; you were in the midst of the fiery stones, spotless in your days, from the time you were created until your iniquities were found in you (Ezek 28:12ff.). For who is so foolish and of so senseless a mind as to think that the prince of Tyre, whoever he believes him to be, set in the paradise of God, and created among the Cherubim, and dwelling among the fiery stones (which we understand without doubt as the Angels and heavenly Powers), was one adorned with earthly stones and having the likeness and the seal? Of the nature of all the stones, then, and of each one in part, this is not the time to speak; for not everything is always to be said. Now let us discourse only of the carbuncle, the sapphire and the jasper. The carbuncle which is prepared, or laid in order, seems to me the fiery word of doctrine, which, putting to flight the error of darkness, illuminates the hearts of believers. This is the one which one of the Seraphim took, grasped with tongs, to purify the lips of Isaiah (Isa 6); which is born, according to the faith of Genesis, in the land of Havilah, where there is the best gold (Gen 2), and the carbuncle stone and the leek-green. Further, the sapphire, which is placed in the foundations, has the likeness of heaven and of the air above us: and it is such that it can say that line of Aristophanes with Socrates: Ἀεροβατῶ καὶ περιφρονῶ τὸν ἥλιον; which we can turn into the Latin tongue: I tread the air and look down upon the sun (See Suidas under περιφρονεῖν). Or with the apostle Paul: But our conversation is in heaven (Phil 3:20). The Scripture of Ezekiel also records that the place where the throne of God is has the likeness of sapphire, and that the glory of the Lord consists in this color, which bears the image of what is above the heavens. And the battlements of the Lord's city, that is, the ramparts of the walls, are strengthened with jasper: those who can destroy and refute every height that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God, and subject falsehood to truth (Ezek 1; 1 Cor 15). He, then, who is most strong in disputing and strengthened by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, he is a battlement of the Church. There are many kinds of jasper: one has the likeness of emerald, which is found at the springs of the river Thermodon, and is called Grammatias, by which they assert that all phantoms are put to flight. Another is greener than the sea, and tinged as if with flowers; they report that this is born on Mount Ida in Phrygia and in its deepest caves. Another, again, is found among the Iberians and the Hyrcanians and by the Caspian Sea, and especially by the lake Neusis. There is also another jasper like snow and the foam of the sea waves, and mildly reddish as though with blood mixed in. We have said this so that we may recognize all the spiritual graces in the battlements of the Church; he who has them puts vain fears to flight, and can say with the bride: My kinsman is white and ruddy (Song 5:10). And the gates of this city are of crystal stone, which is carved in various ways; than this stone nothing is purer. In short, in the most violent frosts of the Alps, and in caves inaccessible to the sun, waters are said to congeal into crystal: to the touch it is stone, to the sight water. By this it is shown that those who are at the doors of the Church ought to be stained by no filth, but to be of the purest faith, and to say with the prophet: From your commandments I have understanding (Ps 118 [119]:104), and to hear this: Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:2.54:11-13

"I will place you as a carbon stone." It is fitting to want to signify Jesus through this stone that was set, the Scriptures say, as the foundation of Zion. If anyone trusts in this foundation, he will not be ashamed. He calls him a foundation stone among them. And he is also mentioned by the holy prophets. For he says through the voice of Amos, "Look, I am setting a diamond in the middle of my people Israel." And through the voice of Zechariah, "Behold, I will bring my servant the sunrise." "I have placed a stone before the face of Jesus; on the one stone there are seven eyes." For the all-seeing one is Christ who is able to survey all things everywhere. For the carbon is placed to be a stone and a fixed foundation of the holy city. On it are the stones of sapphire, which perhaps signify the ranks of the apostles who are set. For they were very close to Christ, and when they followed him they became foundations in the earthly realm.
AGAINST CELSUS 7:30

It seems to me also that that fancy of Plato, that those stones that we call precious stones which derive their luster from a reflection, as it were, of the stones in that better land, is taken from the words of Isaiah in describing the city of God: "I will make your battlements of jasper, your stones shall be crystal and your borders of precious stones."
Commentary on Isaiah

And the walls of the city, or the borders and περίβολος, are built of choice stones, by which we can understand the remaining stones, and that all her sons are taught, or are disciples of God: a testimony the Lord uses in the Gospel of John, saying: No one can come to me unless my Father who sent me draws him, and everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me (John 6:44, 45). And shortly after: It is written in the prophets: They shall all be taught by God. He also speaks through Jeremiah: Putting my laws in their minds, and I will write them on their heart; and they shall no more teach each his neighbor and his brother, saying: Know the Lord. For all shall know me, from the least to the greatest. For I will be merciful to their iniquities, and their sins I will not remember (Jer 31:33, 34). And the teaching of the disciples of God has a multitude of peace, which was left to them by the Lord; and the building of the most beautiful city is completed in righteousness, so that He is the God not of one nation but of the whole world, calling to His faith slaves and free, Greeks and Barbarians, rich and poor, noble and lowly, men and women, little children and old men, and all things in the world which seem to be contrary (John 14). We have gone beyond the measure of brevity, which is useful in all that has to be said, since we seek the city of God not, with the Hebrews and our Half-Jews, on earth, but in the heavens: the city which, set on Christ the mountain, cannot be hidden.
Commentary on Isaiah

Withdraw far from calumny, for you shall not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near you. LXX: Withdraw from the unjust man, and you shall not fear, and trembling shall not come near you. A most beautiful order. He had consoled the poor and lowly one, promising her spiritual graces. Now he teaches what she ought to do if she does not wish to dread the assaults of her adversaries. And the sense is: You do not wish to fear your enemies? Do what I say: Withdraw far from calumny, or from iniquity, for all iniquity and plunder is born of calumny; and you shall not fear, and trembling and terror shall not come near you, so that you fear not men but God, saying with Moses: I am trembling and fearful (Deut 9:19); and with one of Job's friends: Horror and trembling came upon me, and shook my bones greatly (Job 4:14); and with the prophet: At the voice of my prayer trembling entered into my bones (Hab 3:16); and: Upon whom does the Lord rest, but upon the humble and quiet, and him who trembles at His words (Isa 66:2)? But the trembling of the ungodly is another, which is born of the fear of punishment; of it is written: Trembling seized the ungodly (Ps 47 [48]:7).
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, the sojourner shall come who was not with me; he who was once a stranger to you shall be joined to you. LXX: Behold, proselytes shall come to you through me, and they shall be your settlers, and shall flee to you for refuge. These things too the Jews think are said to Jerusalem: that many of the nations will be proselytes and will take up the law of Moses and its ceremonies. We, according to the interpretation we have begun, refer this to the Church, which has been gathered through the apostles from both peoples, which has neither spot nor wrinkle, which is free, and the mother of all believers (Eph 5; Gal 4). To gather these proselytes and strangers the Lord sent His disciples, saying: Teach all nations (Matt 28:19), so that they might flee to the Gospel and take up the new Law, and that those who were once dwellers in idolatry might become settlers of the Church. Of them it is said in the psalms: The Lord makes the blind wise. Or, as is read in the Latin codices: The Lord gives light to the blind, the Lord loves strangers (Ps 145 [146]:8, 9): so that after the blind have received the light of truth, and the foolish have learned wisdom, then, passing over to the Church, they may be loved by the Lord, and hear through the prophet: I will call not my people, my people (Hos 2:24); and when this people enters the Temple of God, jealousy seizes the unlearned people.
Commentary on Isaiah

Further, according to the Seventy this seems to me the sense: I, your Creator, have not made you as the devil, that worst of smiths, forges vessels of iniquity with an unclean spirit and brings them forth to perdition; and he ought to know that vessels of this kind do not have a prosperous course, but are broken in mid-career. What the vessels are he shows in the following words: And every voice that shall rise against you in judgment, you shall overcome them all. The vessels of iniquity have a voice, and this voice rises against the Church when the heretics set their mouth on high and their tongue passes through the earth. And what follows, And they shall be liable to you in it, we have marked beforehand with an obelus, because it seems to have been added not so much by the Seventy as by bad copyists. And when the Church has overcome every voice that rises against her, then those who serve and obey the Lord will have an inheritance, an eternal possession; of which it is said in Jeremiah in other words: There is a reward for your works (Jer 31:16). And the dwellers of the Church will be righteous to the Lord. For everyone who does righteousness is born of God; and to them the Lord says: Be holy, for I am holy (Lev 20:26).
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, I have created the smith who blows the coals in the fire, and brings forth a vessel for his work: and I have created the slayer to destroy. Every vessel that is fashioned against you shall not prosper: and every tongue that resists you in judgment you shall judge. This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord: and their righteousness is with me, says the Lord. LXX: Behold, I have created you, not as a coppersmith blowing the coals in the fire and bringing forth a vessel for work. But I have created you not for perdition, to destroy: every vessel that is made against you shall not prosper: and every voice shall rise against you in judgment: you shall overcome them all ÷ and they shall be liable to you in it ⁚ There is an inheritance for those who serve the Lord, and you shall be righteous to me, says the Lord. Let us speak first according to the Hebrew: If you wish not to fear, and that dread be far from you, do what the preceding discourse has related; for I am He through whom you are to have proselytes. I am He who created the smith who blows the coals in the fire, that is, the devil, the craftsman of all evils, not by necessity of nature but by the choice of his mind; who has kindled fires and will bring forth vessels against you, such as were Simon and Elymas the magicians, who resisted the apostles Peter and Paul (Acts 13). I have created the slayer of those who are going to be unbelievers: not that I am the cause of their perdition, but that the adversary is created for battle, so as to be perdition to the vanquished and a cause of rewards to the victors.
Commentary on Isaiah

And all who have been fashioned against you by the blowing smith shall not prosper, but shall feel both present punishments and those to come. And what before seemed hidden is said more plainly in what follows: And every tongue that resists you in judgment you shall judge, destroying the wisdom of the wise and rejecting the prudence of the prudent. And all the leaders of the heretics, and the teachers of the Jews, and the philosophers of the world, whom that smith had forged, you will condemn by your judgment; as the Queen of Sheba also condemned the unbelievers, and the Ninevites; and on the contrary Sodom will be justified by comparison with a worse Jerusalem (Matt 12). After this he adds what the rewards to come are, lest they think the contest is in vain and ends with the present death. This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord, that is, the kingdom of heaven, and life everlasting, and the repayment of labors, the things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love Him (1 Cor 2). And if for those who love Him, then also for those who serve Him, who have no other Lord but God. And this is the righteousness of those who are with God, says the Lord: that present tribulation should be compensated by future joy.

n: Waters, which in that country are very scarce. --- Milk. Septuagint, "fat." (Calmet) --- In the western Churches, wine and honey were given to the new baptized, chap. vii. 15. (St. Jerome) --- Christ invites all to come to him, John iv. 14,. and vii. 37. The establishment of the Church is described under the figure of the return from Babylon. (Calmet) --- Grace is offered to all. But only those are justified who thirst, and do their best, Matthew v. 6. (Worthington)
David. I will be equally faithful to you, Psalm lxxxviii. 29. Septuagint, "the holy things of David faithful," Acts xiii. 34. The resurrection of Christ fully accomplished the promise made to David.
Him. David, who continually proclaimed the divine mercies, (Psalm xvii. 1.) or rather Christ; though Grotius alone would refer it to Jeremias. (Calmet)
Not with approbation. (Haydock) --- The Gentiles are converted.
Near. He will shortly (Calmet) turn to the Gentiles, John xii. 35., and Acts xiii. 46. (Haydock)
Way. This is a necessary preliminary to God's service. (Worthington)
My ways. I am not vindictive, but require a sincere conversion. (Calmet) --- We cannot serve both God and the world. We must therefore adhere to the former. (Worthington)
Sent it. I will assuredly bring you from Babylon; and the rain shall sooner return upwards than I will break my promise.
Peace, by strangers, chap. xlix. 22. --- Hands, for joy. (Calmet) --- Ipsa sonant arbusta Deus Deus ille, Menacla. (Virgil, Eclogues v.)
Myrtle-tree. Instead of the wicked, the just shall be seen. (Chaldean) --- Away. The conversion and sanctity of the Gentiles shall be a trophy to the Lord. (Menochius)

f: Letter 37, 15

He then who is wise is free, bought with the price of the heavenly oracles, with that gold, that silver of the Divine Word; bought with the price of blood (for it is no small thing to acknowledge one's Redeemer;) bought with the price of Grace: he who heard and understood the words, Ho every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money, come ye, buy and drink and eat.
Commentary on Isaiah

All you who thirst, come to the waters, and you who have no money, hasten, buy and eat: come, buy without silver and without any exchange wine and milk. Why do you weigh out silver not for bread, and your labor not for fullness? LXX: You who thirst, go to the water, and as many as have no money, go, buy, and eat, and walk, and buy without money and without price wine and fat. Why do you buy with money, and your labor not for fullness? The Hebrew word OI (הוי), of which I had said above, in the prophecy against Ariel (cf. Isa 29), that it was ambiguous, and signified either the interjection of one calling or woe, set here at the beginning of the passage, is read not with the feeling of one lamenting but of one calling. Since, then, he had said that every vessel fashioned against the Church is to be broken, and that every voice and tongue that had armed itself against the knowledge of God is to be overcome, he summons the believers to the river of God, which is filled with waters, and whose stream gladdens the city of God, that they may drink waters from the fountains of the Savior, who says to the Samaritan woman: If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, Give me to drink, you would have asked Him, and He would have given you water. The water that I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into life eternal (John 4:10, 14). Of these waters He cried out in the Temple: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who drinks of the water that I shall give him, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water (John 7:37, 38), signifying the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed were to receive, and of whom the Prophet sounded forth in mystical speech: My soul has thirsted for the living God (Ps 41 [42]:2); and again: With you is the fountain of life (Ps 35 [36]:10). He Himself spoke of Himself: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold waters (Jer 2:13). These waters the clouds sprinkle, to which the truth of God reaches, as it is written: And the clouds sprinkle righteousness (Isa 45:8, LXX). And the thirsty are commanded by no means to drink the muddy waters of Sihor and the swelling floods of the Assyrians, but to go to the waters of Siloam, which go with silence; and not to fear poverty of speech if perhaps they have no silver (Isa 45; Jer 2), but to hear the Apostle saying: By grace you have been saved (Eph 2:8); and the Lord saying to the disciples: Freely you have received, freely give (Matt 10:8). And in a wonderful manner they buy waters without money; and they do not drink them, but eat them. For He is both water and the bread which came down from heaven (John 6). Therefore what is read in some copies, Buy and drink, was changed by unskilled copyists, who thought it more consistent if the waters were drunk rather than eaten. But there is also a most wicked money, or silver, which the Scripture rejects, saying: Money that is given with deceit shall be reckoned as a potsherd (Prov 26:23, LXX); and in another place: Your silver is reprobate (Jer 6:30). And there is a silver which is compared to the utterances of God: The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances: silver tried in the fire of earth, purified sevenfold (Ps 11 [12]:7). Spurning, then, that silver and those moneys with which we cannot buy the waters of the Lord, let us go to Him who, holding the cup of the Sacrament, said to the disciples: Take and drink; this is my blood, which shall be shed for you for the remission of sins (Matt 26:27, 28). This wine Wisdom too mixed in her bowl, summoning to drink all the foolish of the world and those who do not have the wisdom of the world; and so that we may buy not only wine but also milk, which signifies the innocence of little children: a custom and type which is kept to this day in the Churches of the West, that wine and milk are given to those reborn in Christ. Of this milk Paul also said: I gave you milk to drink, not solid food (1 Cor 3:2). And Peter: As newborn little children, desire the rational milk (1 Pet 2:2). Hence Moses too, understanding the wine and the milk of the passion of Christ, testifies in mystical speech: His eyes are lovely with wine, and his teeth white with milk (Gen 49:12). For milk in the present passage the Seventy translated fat; of which holy David says in the psalm: Let my soul be filled as with fat and fatness (Ps 62 [63]:6); and in another place: He fed them with the fat of wheat, and with honey from the rock He satisfied them (Ps 80 [81]:17). These fats denote nothing other than the mystical flesh, to which the Lord exhorted the disciples, saying: Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in you (John 6:54). Hence also He was betrayed in Gethsemane, which means valley of fat, or most fertile.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:2.55:1-2

How can they purchase, yet receive gifts without paying? Well, because we accept the payment in faith from Christ, and we pay for none of these things with short-term or perishable goods. For it says, "I said to my Lord, 'You are my Lord since you have no need of goods from me.' " By way of gifts and honor to Christ we offer to Christ the confession of faith in him. So without money and payment comes this drink and bountiful gift of spiritual charisms. For what could we offer and what price could we pay for such a drink? For those drinking the living water are those enriched with grace through the Holy Spirit through participation in him and purchasing this through faith, since they are sharers of the wine and suet, that is, of the holy body and the blood of Christ.
Commentary on Isaiah

And at the same time he rebukes those who follow worldly wisdom and the perverse and feigned doctrines of the heretics, and the traditions of the Pharisees, and all knowledge falsely so called which is lifted up against God, and who at great prices and with unceasing labor weigh out silver for a discipline in which there is no bread, and sweat for foods in which there is no fullness. From this it is shown that the wisdom to be pursued is the one which lies not in the leaves and flower of words but in the marrow and fruits of meanings; which does not fly past the ear but refreshes the mind. To learn it we do not cross the seas, nor do we need great expense, but the word is near, in our mouth and in our heart.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hear, you who hear me, and eat what is good, and your soul shall delight in fatness. Incline your ear, and come to me: hear, and your soul shall live. And I will strike with you an everlasting covenant: the faithful mercies of David. LXX: Hear me, and eat good things, and your soul shall delight in good things. Attend with your ears, and follow my ways: and hear me, and your soul shall live in good things. And I will establish for you an eternal testament, the faithful holy things of David. Lest anyone think that the hearing to which the divine word exhorts those who are to hear is of the flesh and not of the mind, it promises them good things not of the flesh but of the soul. For if, he says, you hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land (Isa 1:19). Or the good: He who says, I am the good shepherd (John 10:11). And your soul shall delight in good things and in fatness. Therefore the good things promised to the soul are not riches, and health of body, and the dignities of the world, which even the philosophers call indifferent, that is, neither good nor evil, and which vary according to the quality of those who use them; but those are to be believed good to which God exhorts us: Turn aside from evil, and do good (Ps 36 [37]:27). But if honesty and the virtues are called the good things of the soul, then evils too are to be taken to be not poverty, and infirmity of body, and low birth, but all the vices, which are truly evil. In short, Abraham did not have good things because he was rich, but because he used his riches well (Gen 13). And Lazarus, who afterward rested in his bosom, did not endure evils because he suffered the torments of diseases together with want; rather, through what were thought evils in the world, he obtained true goods. Hence too that rich man clad in purple received his good things in his lifetime, which were good to him who thought them good (Luke 16); and of Lazarus it is not said, conversely: He received his evil things in his lifetime; but: he received evil things in his lifetime, which seemed evil not to him who suffered them but to others. An example of both is given us by blessed Job, who was overcome neither by the goods nor by the evils of the world, but bore all things with equal firmness of mind (Job 2). Wherefore Solomon prays to God: Give me neither riches nor poverty. But appoint for me what is necessary and sufficient for my living, lest, being full, I become a liar and say: Who sees me? or, being in want, I steal and forswear the name of the Lord (Prov 30:8, 9). And if he prays for this, to have neither riches nor poverty but only the necessaries of living, of which the Apostle also says: Having food and clothing, with these we are content (1 Tim 6), it is clear that riches and want, health and sickness, pleasure and torments, are neither good nor evil, but become good and evil according to the difference of those who bear them. Therefore it is not, as the χιλιαστὰς would have it, abundance of wealth, and dainty foods, and fatness of body, pheasants and stuffed turtledoves, mead, unmixed wine, the beauty of wives, swarms of children, that the Lord promises to the soul, but those delights to which He summons us mystically, saying: Delight, or take your delight in the Lord, and He will give you the petitions of your heart (Ps 36 [37]:4); and elsewhere: I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (Ps 26 [27]:13); and in another psalm: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me His holy name; who fills your desire with good things (Ps 102 [103]:1 and 5).
Commentary on Isaiah

Finally he adds: Hear me, and your soul shall live (Isa 55:3). The promise of all good things is life everlasting. If you are willing to hear, and your soul lives forever, I will strike with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David. Of these the same Psalmist sang: The mercies of the Lord I will sing forever. From generation to generation I will proclaim your truth (Ps 88 [89]:1, 2). And so that we may know what these mercies are, he shows in the following words: Once I have sworn by my holy one: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever, and his throne as the sun in my sight, and as the full moon forever, and a faithful witness in heaven. He is called faithful for this reason, that He has fulfilled His promises. For these the Seventy translated the faithful holy things of David (Acts 13:34), which can be taken as firm and strong; as is this: All His commandments are faithful, confirmed for ever and ever (Ps 110 [111]:8). And in another place: God is faithful, and there is no iniquity in Him (Deut 32:4). And the apostle Paul: If we deny Him, he says, He remains faithful: He cannot deny Himself (2 Tim 2:13). And in another place, writing to Timothy: A faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance (1 Tim 1:15). And this covenant which the Lord promises will not be brief and for one time, as was that of the people of the Jews, but will remain forever, so that the true David may come, and in the Gospel may be fulfilled what was promised in the person of God: I have found David my servant; with holy mercy I have anointed him (Ps 88 [89]:21); whose hand He set in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers. Him, according to Ezekiel, when David had already been asleep for many ages, He calls His servant and shepherd, saying: I will raise up for you one shepherd, my servant David (Ezek 34:23).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:2.55:1-5

For the law was not a perpetual and immoveable law, but it remained in force only as long as the time of its imposition. As the most wise Paul said, "For the former and ancient command has a gap whose filling is to be sought in the second, that is, the new has many things quite different from the old." …That second one is the eternal covenant, and that he fulfilled it for those approaching him by faith is confirmed when it immediately adds, "the holy trustworthy things of David." This concerns the announcements about the Savior of us all, Christ, which are declared to be given to those who are attentive among the nations, or it means the divine and sacred prophecies of Christ, who was born from the seed of David according to his humanity. These are called "holy," for they make perfect those in whom they dwell, just as the fear of God is called "pure" because it is purifying and the gospel word is called "life" because it gives life.… This is the power through Christ of these prophecies.…
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the nations. Behold, you shall call a nation which you did not know: and nations which have not known you shall run to you, because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, because He has glorified you. LXX: Behold, I have given him as a testimony among the nations, a prince and commander to the nations: nations which did not know you shall call upon you: and peoples who were ignorant of you shall flee to you for refuge: because of the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, who has glorified you. He had summoned the people of the Jews to believe, to incline their ear and receive the everlasting covenant which the Lord had promised to David, and to Abraham and his seed, saying: In your seed the nations shall be blessed (Gen 22:18). The apostle Paul, explaining this: He did not say, he says, in seeds, but, in seed, which is Christ (Gal 3:16). And because He knew that, while they did not believe, the peoples of the nations would believe, He passes over to the nations, and says that He has sent His Son as a witness or testimony of all the nations, to announce His precepts and commandments to the peoples; who says of Himself: This Gospel must be preached in the whole world, for a testimony to all the nations (Matt 24:14). Finally, He refutes the proud Pilate with this word: For this I was born, to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37). Of Him the apostle Paul writes to Timothy: One mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself a redemption for all, a testimony in its proper times: in which I have been appointed a herald and an Apostle (1 Tim 2:5). All that is said, then, is to be referred to Him who was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the shearer did not open His mouth. Of Him it is said above: We saw Him, and He had neither form nor comeliness (Isa 53:2); and: He Himself bore our sins, and suffers for us. To Him have fled, or run, those who before did not know Him, saying: Our God is refuge and strength (Ps 45 [46]:1); and again: Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation (Ps 89 [90]:1). Of their faith we read above also: Those to whom it was not preached concerning Him shall see: and those who had not heard shall understand. He is the witness of all that the Father promised and bestowed on the world, whose mystery Paul gathers up in a brief word to the Ephesians: The God, he says, of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory (Eph 1:17); of whom it is written now as well: Because of the Lord your God, and the Holy One of Israel, who has glorified you, and that with the glory which He had before the world was made. Of it the Prophet also testifies: The glory of God shall appear (Heb 1), He who is the brightness of glory and the form of His substance, when every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of the Father (Phil 2). He answered the Son, when He asked for the glory which He had had before: I have both glorified it, and will glorify it. Of which the apostle John also says: We saw, he says, His glory, the glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth (John 12:28; 1:14). Therefore, when he speaks of Him who in the beginning was with God, God the Word, He is called the Father of glory; but when of Him who says in the Gospel, Why do you persecute me, a man who speaks the truth to you (John 8:40)? He is called the God of our Lord Jesus Christ. Not that there is one and another (which is the very bad error of many), but because one and the same Son of God speaks now with the feelings of the glory of His divinity, now with those of our nature, which He deigned to take up.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:2.55:1-5

For those who had never seen Christ on account of residing in gloom and darkness called on him, that is, they acknowledged Jesus as God and fled to him calling him their hope and shelter and means of salvation and called on him as God … for although according to the measure of humanity Christ was thought to be ignoble, he went back to that which was appropriate to him and divine and the highest glory—but not without his flesh.
Commentary on Isaiah

Seek the Lord while He can be found: call upon Him while He is near. Let the ungodly man forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and He will have mercy on him, and to our God: for He is abundant in forgiving. LXX: Seek the Lord: and when you have found Him, call upon Him. And after He has drawn near to you, let the ungodly man forsake his ways and the unrighteous man his thoughts and return to the Lord: and he shall obtain mercy: for He will abundantly forgive your sins. Since, then, as we have already said before, you would not receive the everlasting covenant and the faithful mercies of David, which, when you were unwilling to take them up, the throng of the Gentiles took up, I the Prophet warn you, my own people, and solemnly charge you: while there is time, do penance. Turn to Him who now speaks to you through the Prophets, who afterward will speak in person. Seek Him while He can be found, while you are in the body, while room for repentance is given; and seek Him not by place but by faith. How God is to be sought is said more fully in another place: Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek Him in simplicity of heart: for He is found by those who do not tempt Him, and appears to those who are not unbelieving toward Him (Wis 1:1, 2). Hence we too, knowing the word spoken of sinners, Those who withdraw far from you shall perish, let us say to the Lord: Whither shall I go from your spirit, and whither shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there: if I descend into hell, you are present (Ps 138 [139]:7, 8). And let us call upon Him while He is near, lest through our vices and sins He withdraw far away. For He draws near to those who draw near to Him, and joyfully runs to meet the son returning after a long time. Wherefore the holy man sings in the psalm: But for me it is good to cleave to God (Ps 72 [73]:28). And Moses alone drew near to the Lord (Exod 20). And through Jeremiah God says: I am a God who draws near, and not from afar (Jer 23:23): drawing near to those who draw near to me by faith, and withdrawing far from those who depart far from me by unbelief. Because of this it is said to believers: Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. And lest we should think this could suffice, he at once adds: Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (Jas 4:8). Of him it had been said above: Your adversary the devil, like a lion, going about, seeks whom he may devour. Resist him, strong in faith (1 Pet 5:8, 9).
Confessions 10.20

How then am I to seek for you, Lord? When I seek for you, my God, my quest is for the happy life. I will seek you that "my soul may live," for my body derives life from my soul, and my soul derives life from you.… Is not the happy life that which all desire, which indeed no one fails to desire?
ON THE TRINITY 15:2.2

And yet the prophet Isaiah testifies, that the Lord God can be found when He is sought, when he says: "Seek ye the Lord; and as soon as ye have found Him, call upon Him: and when He has drawn near to you, let the wicked man forsake his ways, and the unrighteous man his thoughts." If, then, when sought, He can be found, why is it said, "Seek ye His face evermore?" Is He perhaps to be sought even when found? For things incomprehensible must so be investigated, as that no one may think he has found nothing, when he has been able to find how incomprehensible that is which he was seeking. Why then does he so seek, if he comprehends that which he seeks to be incomprehensible, unless because he may not give over seeking so long as he makes progress in the inquiry itself into things incomprehensible, and becomes ever better and better while seeking so great a good, which is both sought in order to be found, and found in order to be sought? For it is both sought in order that it may be found more sweetly, and found in order that it may be sought more eagerly.
Commentary on Isaiah

Nor is it enough to seek the Lord, and to find Him while it is the time of repentance, and to call upon Him while He is near, unless the ungodly man forsakes his former ways and the old thoughts by which he had turned aside from the Lord. For then we shall return to the Lord, who will have mercy on us, and to the most clement father, who is abundant in mercies and ready to forgive, when we have forsaken our former thoughts and ways, so that afterward we may deserve to hear: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered (Ps 31 [32]:1).
Homily on Acts 50

Do not want to be more merciful than God, or rather, if you wish it, you will not be able, not even in the least degree. How should you? As far as the heaven is from the earth, Scripture says, so far are My counsels from your counsels: and again, If ye, He says, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more your heavenly Father? But in fact this talk is mere pretext and subterfuge. Let us not prevaricate with God's commandments.
Commentary on Isaiah

For my thoughts are not your thoughts: nor are your ways my ways, says the Lord. For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts. LXX: For my thoughts are not as your thoughts: nor are your ways as my ways, says the Lord. But as far as heaven is distant from the earth, so far is my way distant from your ways, and your thoughts from my thought. Do not think, he says, that what I promise is difficult, and let it not seem incredible to you that the ungodly and the unrighteous can be saved, whether the people of the Jews or all those among the nations who did not know God: consider this, that there is a great difference between my counsels and yours, and as great a diversity of will as of nature (Prov 19). For many are the thoughts in the heart of a man, but the counsel of the Lord abides forever. You, as men, often repenting of a promise, have overturned your old will with a new will. For the Lord scatters the counsels of the nations, and rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and makes void the wills of princes (Ps 32 [33]); but the thoughts of His heart are from generation to generation, and whatever He has decreed cannot be changed.
Commentary on Isaiah

Do you wish to know the difference between my counsel and yours? As far as heaven is distant in place from the earth, and the dwelling of the Angels is one thing and that of men another, so far are my thoughts separated from your counsels. For of my thoughts it is said: His judgments are inscrutable, and His ways past finding out (Rom 11:33). But of yours: They devised a counsel which they could not establish (Ps 20 [21]:12). And in another place: Whatever counsel you have entered upon shall be scattered, and whatever you have spoken shall not remain among you (Isa 8:10). Things that are clear need no interpretation; therefore they are touched on briefly rather than discussed.
Commentary on Isaiah

And as the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and will not return thither again; but they soak the earth, and water it, and make it spring up, and give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall do whatever I willed, and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it.
