What has been added in the Alexandrian copies at the beginning of this chapter, And still my praise shall be in you always, and at the end, and your bones shall spring up like grass, and shall grow fat, and they shall possess by inheritance unto generation and generations, is not found in the Hebrew, nor even in the corrected and true copies of the Seventy; hence it must be marked beforehand with an obelus. When the darkness, he says, of your breast has been dissolved by the rising of the light, and noonday has arisen in place of a palpable night, then you will always have God dwelling in you, to fill your soul with splendors. Of these we read in the psalm: With you is the principality in the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints; from the womb before the daystar I have begotten you (Ps 109 [110]:3). Or: you will be satisfied with all that your soul desires, because you yourself have satisfied the hungry soul, and you will be able to say: Bless the Lord, O my soul, who fills your desire with good things (Ps 102 [103]:5); and your bones will be delivered from destruction and from everlasting fire. Or: they will grow fat, so as to recover their former stoutness, having been wasted by the famine of the word of the Lord. This indeed we can understand according to the letter of the resurrection of the bodies which are to fall, and also of the virtues of the soul, which the saint signifies when he says in the psalm: All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you? (Ps 34 [35]:10). Of these it is also written in Proverbs: A good report makes the bones fat (Prov 15:30). And to those to whom rewards are promised: There shall be health for your body, and healing for your bones (Prov 16:24). Of these again it is written: The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them shall be broken (Ps 33 [34]:21). On the contrary, he who is a sinner, and has lost the strength and virtue of the soul, laments and says: Our bones are scattered beside hell (Ps 140 [141]:7). For we cannot believe that the bones of sinners are not in hell but beside hell. And a good report makes the bones fat (Prov 15:30), which has nothing to do with the fattening of the body. It follows: And you shall be, or it shall be, that is, either you or your soul, like a watered garden; of which it is written: A fountain went forth and watered the whole face of paradise (Gen 2:6), where in the Hebrew garden is read. This fountain we can call no other than him to whom it is said, With you is the fountain of life (Ps 35 [36]:10), who unceasingly waters his Church and the hearts of all believers.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:4.58:11

Those who were of Israel by blood are written as a type when God sent down manna from heaven. For this figure can be thought of as the bread of angels and as heavenly bread. For there are those in whose minds the divine light shines brightly and who work hard and irreproachably to know the holy Scriptures—we say that these people are filled and brimming with the heavenly nourishment of God.… Now whoever receives knowledge and is filled by his divine mysteries, that person's bones have flesh put on them. For the oracle here is constructed in fleshly terms. Their soul became like a lush garden, that is, luxuriant and tree-filled and with many types of flowers abounding and providing all sorts of fruit. For gardens that lack water are exceedingly ugly, being dry and barren of all fruit.… For just the hardiest among trees has the most beautiful fruit, so also fairest and finest virtues exist in God's sight among the souls of the saints.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the deserts of ages shall be built up in you; you shall raise up the foundations of generation and generation; and there shall be called in you the builder of hedges, turning the paths into rest. LXX: And the places desert from of old shall be built up for you, and your foundations shall be everlasting for generations and generations; and you shall be called the builder of the wall, and you shall make the paths in the midst to rest. Not only, he says, will your light rise in the darkness, and your darkness be like noonday, and the Lord give you rest always, and you be like a watered garden, and the rest, but there shall be built up in you the things that had been desert for a long time; and the foundations of your dwellings will be laid to endure through many generations; so that either you yourself will be called the builder of hedges and walls, or one will arise in you who will be the builder of hedges and will turn the paths into rest, or, according to the Seventy, will make the tracks in the midst to rest. The Jews, and the friends only of the letter that kills, refer these things to the restoration of the cities of Palestine; and they contend either that they were done under Zerubbabel and Ezra and Nehemiah, or that they will be in the last time: that for the restoration of Jerusalem and of the cities round about, very deep foundations are to be laid, and walls built so high that none of the enemy can enter, and the entry of all foes into them is barred. But we, following the order of the explanation we have begun, say that the things that had been desert among the Jews are built up in the Church, not for a short time but for ever, and that its foundations are to be raised up from both peoples, that is, in two generations. Hence the Apostle said: As a wise architect I have laid the foundation; another builds upon it; but let each one see what he builds upon it (1 Cor 3:10); and in another place: We are God's husbandry, God's building; and again: Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets (Eph 2:20); and that she, or he who was born in her, is to be called the builder of hedges. Of him we read in the psalm: A man was born in her, and the Most High himself has founded her (Ps 86 [87]:5). These hedges and walls (for this is what φραγμοῦς signifies in the Greek tongue) Scripture records as being set around a field and vineyards: You brought a vine out of Egypt; you cast out the nations and planted it; and a little after: Why have you broken down its wall, and all who pass by the way gather its vintage? (Ps 79 [80]:9 and 13). And in this same Prophet: A vineyard was made for the beloved; describing it in beautiful language, he adds: I built a tower and surrounded it with a wall (Eccl 2:4). Whoever breaks it down, according to Ecclesiastes, a serpent will bite him. It was surrounded for this purpose, that the approach of all beasts into the vineyard of God might be barred. This is the crooked serpent who deceived Eve in paradise; because she had broken down the precepts of God, she was therefore open to his bites, and heard from the Lord: You shall watch for his head, and he shall watch for your heel (Gen 3:15). In the place where we, lest we seem to innovate in anything, interpreted according to the Seventy, because the testimony is widely known, and you shall be called the builder of hedges, in the Hebrew is read and there shall be called in you GODER PHERES גדר פרץ, which Aquila interpreted περιφράκτης διακοπῆς, which we can render according to the sense as one who sets himself against the raging anger of God. Indeed, Symmachus translated setting a wall against the one who strikes (1 Sam 7), such as were Moses and Aaron and Samuel, who withstood the anger of the Lord and, as though by building a wall, set a limit to his indignation. This is also said to Jeremiah: that he should not run to meet the Lord, nor wish to resist his anger, and so shut off his indignation by prayers as by a kind of wall (Jer 7); and to Moses, as though the Lord were being held back by him: Let me go, he says, and I will strike this people (Exod 32:10). A builder, then, of walls, ramparts and hedges of this kind will turn the paths into rest, so that the wrath of God may by no means rage, but the Lord may be appeased toward them, and all the paths of indignation may come to rest.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:4.58:12

The prophetic word comes to us through two further metaphors, and the beautiful form of hidden ideas is displayed. For it is about a deserted town and its defenseless state that a form of words is molded. It declares, your deserts will be lived in perpetually, that is, you will not be naked of good thoughts indwelling your heart, nor will you be defenseless or unguarded and insecure. For Christ will be your enduring foundation and support, and like a city you will have countless people dwelling there. For the souls of the saints are full of holy words and thoughts. And many will come to it as the level of perfection, running up and down, declaring it to be full of good things. And you will be called a builder of walls.… You must know that there are evil and contrary powers invading the vulnerable soul, giving rise to awful desires and in a despotic way carrying off whatever they want and strolling round the barren garden. But they will stop this interference when a wall is erected, that is, the divine fear set up within [the soul].
Commentary on Isaiah

If you turn away your foot from the sabbath, from doing your own will on my holy day, and call the sabbath delightful, and the holy of the Lord glorious, and glorify him while you do not make your own ways, and your own will is not found to speak a word. LXX: If you turn away your foot on the sabbaths, so as not to do your own wills on the holy day; and you shall call the sabbaths delightful, holy to the Lord; you shall not lift your foot to work, nor speak a word ÷ in anger from your mouth ⁚. To the one to whom he had said above, Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen: loose the bond of impiety, undo the bundles that weigh down, and the rest, he now too promises rewards, if he is willing to do the things that follow (Exod 20): namely, that he restrain his foot on the sabbaths, and not do his own wills, nor stain the holy day of the Lord with his wills. It is commanded in the Law that on the sabbaths we should do no servile work, kindle no fire, sit in one place, and do only those works that belong to the salvation of the soul. If we take this according to the letter, it cannot be fulfilled at all. For who can do this: sitting the whole day and night on the sabbath, not go away from one place, or rather not even move slightly, since if he did he would be a transgressor of the law? From one commandment, then, which is impossible according to the letter, we are compelled to understand the rest spiritually as well: that we should not do servile work and lose the freedom of the soul, for he who commits sin is the slave of sin (John 8); that we should not carry a burden on the sabbath, such as he carried who says: My iniquities have gone up over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me (Ps 37 [38]:5); that the iniquity which sits upon the talent of lead should have no power in us; that the pleasure and lust of the body should not set us on fire (Zech 5), for all adulterers, their hearts are like an oven (Hos 7); and the fiery darts of the devil are there to shoot in the dark at the upright of heart (Ps 10 [11]). We are commanded too that, having taken hold of the plow, we should not look behind us; that, having climbed to the height of the roofs, we should by no means wish to come down to take the garments of the world (Luke 9); but that we should hear with Moses, But you, stand here with me (Exod 34:2); and sit with the Lord, weary on the way of this world, at the well of the Samaritan woman, thirsting for the conversion and salvation of those who stray (John 4); that we should hear the Apostle warning, Be firm and immovable (1 Cor 15:58), lest we suffer what Judas the traitor suffered, who lost the place of his ministry and became a transgressor; and let us always remember that sentence: If the spirit of him who has power rises up against you, do not leave your place (Eccl 10:4). He who rests thus on the sabbath washes his hands among the innocent, and does not move his feet to do his own wills: he keeps the delightful sabbaths of the Lord. This sabbath rest, according to the Epistle written to the Hebrews, is promised to us in the heavens, and glory is prepared (Heb 4): so long as we do not make our own ways on the sabbath, nor is our own will found, to speak a word; that is, that we sin neither in deed nor in word. Otherwise, if these things are forbidden only on the sabbath, then on the other six days freedom to sin is granted us. And since it is foolish to believe this, it remains that the sabbath, which means rest, must be sanctified by the faithful at all times, while they do the wills not of the flesh but of the soul. What is added according to the Seventy, in anger from your mouth, is not found in the Hebrew. To this sabbath, to be celebrated with all festivity, the Savior calls us in the Gospel, saying: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28); for this is what ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς signifies: that, laying down the burdens of sins, we may keep sabbath in Christ and say: He has set my feet upon a rock (Ps 39 [40]:3), and may avoid what the saint says he almost suffered: But my feet were almost moved (Ps 72 [73]:2).
Commentary on Isaiah

Then you shall delight upon the Lord, and I will lift you up above the heights of the earth, and I will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken. LXX: And you shall be confident upon the Lord, and he will lift you up above the good things of the earth, and he will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken. When you have called the sabbaths delightful, and have not moved your foot on the sabbath to do servile work, nor spoken a word, that is, have always kept silent and fulfilled what is commanded, Keep your tongue from evil, and let your lips speak no deceit (Ps 33 [34]:14), then you will delight in the Lord, and will see fulfilled in yourself: Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart (Ps 36 [37]:4). Or: you will have confidence in the Lord, according to what is written: He who trusts in the Lord is blessed; and in Jeremiah: Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his hope (Jer 17:7); and elsewhere: It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man (Ps 117 [118]:8). And the Lord will lift you up and raise you above the heights and good things of the earth. For the land of the meek and the land of the living is not below but above. Thus it is said to Lot as he fled from the valley of Sodom and Gomorrah: Save yourself on the mountain (Gen 19); and after he had reached it, the sun rose for him in Zoar. Of this land the Lord said: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land (Matt 5:4); and many other things which we have often used, among which is this: Honor your father and your mother, and you shall be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God will give you (Exod 20:12). According to the letter this cannot stand at all; for many honor their parents and die soon, and other men, parricides, live a long time. But so that we may know more surely that this land is in the heights, let us briefly recall the thirty-sixth psalm, in which it is written: The meek shall possess the land, and shall feast in the abundance of peace. After this it adds: Wait for the Lord and keep his ways, and he will lift you up to possess the land (Ps 36 [37]:11); of which it is sung in another place: The righteous shall possess the land, and shall dwell upon it for ever and ever (ibid., 34). This too is impossible: for if the earth shall pass away, this one certainly which we inhabit, how shall the righteous dwell upon it for ever and ever? From this we learn that there is a land which is set in the heights. After this it adds: And I will feed you, or the Lord will feed you, with the inheritance of Jacob your father. For as he who has the faith of Abraham is called a son of Abraham, so he who supplants vices and sins is called a son of Jacob; and whose virtue anyone imitates, his son he is also called. The good things of the land set in the heights, with which the son of Jacob is satisfied, must be taken as those which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man (1 Cor 2). Of them it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews: For those who say these things show that they seek a homeland; and if indeed they were seeking that from which they had come out, they had time to return to it. But now they desire a better homeland, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 11:14ff.). From this we learn that the fable of the thousand years, in which marriages are promised again, and foods, and the conduct of an earthly life, is to be rejected. For if in the resurrection they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the Angels, because they are sons of the resurrection (Matt 22); and the Apostle speaks of the belly and foods: Food for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both the one and the other (1 Cor 6:13): how shall we seek again, in an incorrupt, spiritual and immortal body, the vices of our former mortal and corrupt flesh? And we say this not as denying the substance of the glorified body, but as taking away entirely the former works in those who are like the Angels. Otherwise, even in this body of ours we imitate the angelic virtues by fasts and continence and perpetual chastity and charity, and yet we do not lose the substance of our bodies. That we may believe all these things to be future, let us know that they have been promised by God, whose mouth has spoken; so that, as in the hands we understand work, and in the feet walking, and in the belly generation, and in the ears and eyes hearing and sight, so in the mouth we may understand the speech of God.
Register of Epistles, Book 1, Epistle 5

I used to strive daily to win my way outside the world, outside the flesh; to drive all phantasms of the body from the eyes of my soul, and to see incorporeally supernal joys; and not only with my voice but in the core of my heart I used to say, "My heart hath said unto Thee, I have sought Thy face, Thy face, Lord, will I seek." Moreover desiring nothing, fearing nothing, in this world, I seemed to myself to stand on a certain summit of things, so that I almost believed to be fulfilled in me what I had learnt of the Lord's promise through the prophet, "I will lift thee up upon the high places of the earth." For he is lifted up upon the high places of the earth who treads under foot through looking down upon them in his mind even the very things of the present world which seem lofty and glorious. But, having been suddenly dashed from this summit of things by the whirlwind of this trial, I have fallen into fears and tremors, since, even though I have no fears for myself, I am greatly afraid for those who have been committed to me. On every side I am tossed by the waves of business, and sunk by storms, so that I may truly say, "I am come into the depth of the sea, and the storm hath overwhelmed me." After business I long to return to my heart; but, driven therefrom by vain tumults of thoughts, I am unable to return.

n: Iniquities. The history of Susanna shews that the captives were not all free from sin, which alone prevented their liberation, Lamentations iii. 44. (Calmet) [Daniel xiii.] --- God is willing and able to save. He punishes for sin, to cause us to repent, ver. 20. (Worthington)
Justice. They arraign unjustly. None call upon the just God, but trust in idols. --- Iniquity. They kill themselves, while they strive to injure others, Psalm vii. 15., and Micheas ii. 1.
Basilisk, or viper. (Calmet) --- The young ones "burst through the viper's sides." (Pliny, [Natural History?] x. 62.) --- So the works of the wicked are useless or destructive.
Peace, or prosperity. They quarrel with all, and ruin themselves, Psalm xiii.
Therefore. The wicked Jews nevertheless confess that their sins prove their destruction.
Dead. The Jews will not recognize Christ, notwithstanding the prophecies and miracles.
Judgment, that God would avenge us, (ver. 9.) and regard our fasts, chap. lviii. 3.
In. Where truth is disregarded, there can be no justice.

Himself, to arrest his arm, stretched out to chastise his son; or to second him. There is nothing in man to stop God's vengeance. He therefore pardons out of his own goodness, chap. lix. 2., and lxiii. 4. (Calmet) --- He became man to redeem us, as no pure mortal could do it. (Worthington)
Justice. None can blame his conduct.
On. Hebrew, "is standard-bearer." (Aquila) (St. Jerome) --- Cyrus, the figurative redeemer, proceeds rapidly.

To Sion. Septuagint, "from Sion, and will turn away iniquity from Jacob. (21.) And this," &c. (Haydock) --- St. Paul hence proves that the Jews will at last be converted, Romans xi. 26. The return of the captives prefigured this event. (Calmet)

Covenant. Note here a clear promise of perpetual orthodoxy to the Church of Christ. (Challoner) --- She hath still the spirit of truth. (Worthington) (Matthew xxviii. 20.) --- None will apply this to the synagogue, which is visibly in the dark, and abandoned. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, the hand of the Lord is not shortened, that it cannot save, nor is his ear made heavy, that it cannot hear; but your iniquities have divided between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he would not hear. LXX: Is the hand of the Lord not able to save, or is his ear made heavy, that it cannot hear? But your sins separate between you and God, and because of your sins he has turned his face away from you, so as not to have mercy. The things which I have now said I will do, You shall be confident in the Lord, and he will lift you up to the good things of the land, and will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father, I could have fulfilled before as well. For my hand is not shortened and drawn in, so that I cannot stretch it out to set my people free; nor do I have deaf ears, so that I cannot hear. From this it is shown that the ears of the Lord, which hear the righteous and do not hear sinners, are by no means like our ears, which hear equally the voice uttered, whether of righteousness or of unrighteousness.
Treatise III. On the Lapsed 21
Let us consider our sins, and reviewing the secrets of our action and mind, let us weigh the merits of our conscience.
Treatise V. An Address to Demetrianus 11

The Lord can prohibit adversities, but the merits of sinners cause him to give no aid.… Therefore, let your sins and offences be numbered; let the wounds of your conscience be considered; and let each one cease to complain about God and about us, if he understands that he deserves what he suffers.
HOMILIES ON EPHESIANS 5

What the middle wall of partition is, he interprets by saying, "the enmity having abolished in His flesh, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances." Some indeed affirm that he means the wall of the Jews against the Greeks, because it did not allow the Jews to hold intercourse with the Greeks. To me, however, this does not seem to be the meaning, but rather that he calls "the enmity in the flesh," a middle wall, in that it is a common barrier, cutting us off alike from God. As the Prophet says, "Your iniquities separate between you and Me;" for that enmity which He had both against Jews and Gentiles was, as it were, a middle wall. And this, whilst the law existed, was not only not abolished, but rather was strengthened; "for the law," saith the Apostle, "worketh wrath."
HOMILIES CONCERNING THE STATUES 6:14

It is the greatest punishment to commit sin, though we may remain unpunished; as on the other hand, it is the greatest honour and repose to live virtuously, though we may be punished. For sins separate us from God; as He Himself speaks; "Have not your sins separated between you and Me?" But punishments lead us back to God. As one saith, "Give peace; for Thou hast recompensed us for all things." Suppose any one hath a wound; which is the most deserving of fear, gangrene, or the surgeon's knife? the steel, or the devouring progress of the ulcer? Sin is a gangrene, punishment is the surgeon's knife. As then, he who hath a gangrene, although he is not lanced, hath to sustain the malady, and is then in the worse condition, when he is not lanced; so also the sinner, though he be not punished, is the most wretched of men; and is then especially wretched, when he hath no punishment, and is suffering no distress.
LETTER TO THE FALLEN THEODORE 1:8

For He Himself never turns away from us, but it is we who put ourselves far off: for "I am a God" we read "at hand and not a God afar off." And again, when He was rebuking them by the mouth of this prophet He said "Do not your sins separate between you and me?" Inasmuch then as this is the cause which puts us far from God, let us remove this obnoxious barrier, which prevents any near approach being made.

But now hear how this has actually occurred in real instances. Amongst the Corinthians some man of mark committed a sin such as was not named even among the Gentiles. This man was a believer and belonged to the household of Christ; and some say that he was actually a member of the priesthood. What then? Did Paul cut him off from the communion of those who were in the way of salvation. By no means: for he himself it is who rebukes the Corinthians countless times, backwards and forwards, because they did not bring the man to a state of repentance: but, desiring to prove to us that there is no sin which cannot be healed, he said again concerning the man who had transgressed more grievously than the Gentiles: "Deliver such an one to Satan for destruction of the flesh that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus Christ."
Commentary on Isaiah

But the sins, he says, of yours, like a wall set up in the midst, divide you and God. Hence the Savior too in his passion made both one (Eph 2), and, dissolving the middle wall of partition, destroyed the enmity in his own flesh, so that those whom the wall of sins had divided the blood of Christ might join together. He opened the gate of paradise, which had been shut for a long time (Gen 3), and quenched the fiery sword with his own blood, so that the thief might hear: Today you shall be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). What follows, And because of your sins he has turned his face away from you, so that he would not hear, or so as not to have mercy, shows this: that he could not bear the stench of their sins and their iniquities, but turned away his face, so as not to see their foulness and be compelled at once to strike. Hence the sinner, longing to see the face of the Lord, says in the psalm: How long, Lord, will you forget me to the end? How long will you turn your face away from me? (Ps 12 [13]:1). And elsewhere: Show your face, and we shall be saved (Ps 79 [80]:4).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:4.59:4-5

Scripture is accustomed to call hatred "toil." For the word has more than one meaning. Hatred wastes and withers up the hearts of those who receive it. Thus says the psalmist about someone or about Israel as a whole, "He conceived toil and bore iniquity."
Commentary on Isaiah

For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken falsehood, and your tongue utters iniquity. There is none who calls for righteousness, nor is there any who judges truly; but they trust in nothing and speak vanities. LXX: For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with sins. Your lips are defiled with iniquity, and your tongue meditates unrighteousness. No one speaks righteous things, nor is there righteous judgment. They trust in vain things and speak empty things, iniquities and sins. What he named above in general, he now sets out in its parts. And we must note that he by no means charges them with the idolatry in which they were held in the times of Isaiah, but with the shedding of blood, of which he had already spoken before: The righteous man perishes, and there is none who considers it. And righteous men are taken away, and no one understands in his heart. For the righteous man has been taken away from the face of iniquity; his burial shall be in peace, and he shall be taken from the midst (Isa 57:1, 2). And although they themselves did not lay hands on the Lord the Savior, yet by crying with one voice of impiety, His blood be on us and on our children (Matt 27:25), they are guilty of his death and have defiled hands. Of them the same Prophet testifies, saying: If you lift up your hands to me, I will not hear. Your hands are full of blood (Isa 1:15).
Commentary on Isaiah

Their lips too and their tongue speak iniquity and falsehood, so that instead of Christ they promise themselves the Antichrist; and there is no one among the people who calls for righteousness and judges truth, or, as it is in the Hebrew, faith, that is, who believes in Christ; but they trust in nothing and speak vanities. Hence the Apostle commands that we should not give heed to Jewish fables and the commandments of men who turn away from the truth (Titus 1). For truly they trust in nothing and follow vanities; in which the Lord's prophecy is fulfilled: I have come in the name of my Father, and you have not received me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive (John 5:43).
Commentary on Isaiah

They have conceived toil and brought forth iniquity; they have broken the eggs of asps and woven the webs of the spider. He who eats of their eggs shall die, and what has been warmed shall break out into a basilisk. Their webs shall not serve for a garment, nor shall they be covered with their works. LXX: For they are in labor with pain and beget iniquity. They have broken the eggs of asps and woven the web of the spider. And he who wishes to eat of their eggs, breaking one, will find it rotten, and in it a basilisk. Their web shall not serve for a garment, nor shall they be covered with their works. Those who await the coming of the Antichrist, and cannot say, From your fear, Lord, we have conceived, and been in labor, and brought forth; we have wrought the spirit of your salvation upon the earth (Isa 26:18), rightly conceive pain and bring forth iniquity, so that the one whom they seek with much labor they may receive in iniquity. Of their father it is written: He conceived pain and brought forth iniquity (Ps 7:15).
AGAINST EUNOMIUS 2:7

Of such a kind as this, perhaps, is that of which the prophet says, touching the ungodly, "They weave a spider's web." For as in the cobweb there is the appearance of something woven, but no substantiality in the appearance,—for he who touches it touches nothing substantial, as the spider's threads break with the touch of a finger,—just such is the unsubstantial texture of idle phrases. "Not dividing His own essence by begetting and being at once begetter and begotten." Ought we to give his words the name of argument, or to call them rather a swelling of humours secreted by some dropsical inflation? … Who is so distracted, who is so demented, as to make the statement against which Eunomius thinks he is doing battle? For the Church believes that the true Father is truly Father of His own Son, as the Apostle says, not of a Son alien from Him.
Commentary on Isaiah

Some explain this place thus: The eggs of asps they have split, or broken: that is, they abandoned all the biting words of the Prophets, and wove for themselves the smooth speeches of the false prophets; and whoever eats of them will be struck by the serpent, and will understand that the words of falsehood have profited him nothing.
Commentary on Isaiah

These break and burst the eggs of asps, so as to take their poisons into their own minds; to them it is said in the Gospel: Serpents, brood of vipers (Matt 3:7). And he fittingly set down the eggs of asps and serpents, which are said to produce eggs first. And because they not only retain the poisons of malice in their hearts, but also meditate on the law of the Lord day and night, muttering old wives' fables, therefore it is said: And they weave the webs of the spider, with which they catch flies and gnats and small creatures; but if anything strong comes against them, it flies through as though through empty air. He who eats, he says, of their eggs shall die, that is, he who yields to their counsels, as Abel yielded to Cain when he said, Let us go out into the field (Gen 4:8), will at once be killed; or, as the Seventy translated: He who wishes to eat of their eggs, crushing one, will find it rotten, and in it a basilisk. For he who, deceived at first sight, thinks them the eggs of hens and other birds, which are harmless to eat, if he breaks one before he eats, will at once perceive a most foul stench and stink, and in what has been warmed he will find a basilisk; or, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, an asp. Aquila put a viper, for which in the Hebrew is read EPHEE (אפעה). He, then, who, hearing the Jewish traditions, wishes to prepare himself for the feasts of the thousand years, and, entangled in the delights of the promises, to stretch out his hand to the egg: if before he eats, that is, before he yields to deadly words, he is willing first to consider what is said, and to examine each word and handle its reasoning, he will at once find that in them the Antichrist is being prepared. According to the Hebrew, then, he who eats of their eggs shall die. But he who, according to the Seventy, is willing to break them first, and to look more carefully and see what lies hidden, will find a most foul stench, and the serpent, the prince of all, the devil, lying hidden in their traditions.
Commentary on Isaiah

And because he had said above, They weave the webs of the spider, he explains that the weaving of these webs does no good. Their labor, he says, and all their doctrine does not make the garment of Christ, nor a cloak by which the nakedness of the soul may be covered; but they sweat with fruitless labor, as this same Prophet says: This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. And in vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines and precepts of men (Isa 29:13); following these, they neglect the law of God. And so that we may know that works are signified by the web, he added: Nor shall they be covered with their works.
Commentary on Isaiah

Their works are useless works, and the work of iniquity is in their hands. Their feet run to evil, and they hasten to shed innocent blood. Their thoughts are useless thoughts; desolation and destruction are in their ways. The way of peace they have not known, and there is no judgment in their steps. Their paths have become crooked to them; everyone who treads in them does not know peace. LXX: For their works are works of iniquity, and their feet run to malice; swift to shed harmless blood; and their thoughts are the thoughts of fools. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known, and there is no judgment in their ways. For their paths are perverse, which they pass along, and they do not know peace. Therefore they are not covered with their works, because their works are works of iniquity, which the Apostle calls unfruitful, that is, having no fruits (Eph 5).
Commentary on Isaiah

What follows, Their thoughts are the thoughts of fools; destruction and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known, and, above, Their feet are swift to shed blood, the Apostle set down in Romans (ch. 3). Many, not knowing this, think it was taken from the thirteenth psalm, in which the verses were added in the common edition and are not found in the Hebrew; about this we spoke more fully at the beginning of this volume.
Commentary on Isaiah

And their feet run to evil and hasten to shed harmless blood (Prov 1). For they had this custom in the slaying of the Prophets too. To them Stephen said: For which of the Prophets did your fathers not persecute? (Acts 7:52). And the Lord in the Gospel: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the Prophets and stone those who are sent to you (Matt 23:37); and again: All the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth shall come upon you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple and the altar (ibid., 35). Hence it is said to them above as well: For your hands are defiled with blood, and your tongue speaks iniquity (Isa 59:3). And through this practice of cruelty and blasphemy they came to the slaying of the Lord, just as Judas too came by the way of avarice to murder, or rather to sacrilege joined with avarice.
Commentary on Isaiah

Rightly did they not know the way of peace, who refused to receive its author. For he is our peace, who says to the Apostles: My peace I give you, my peace I leave you (John 14:27); and to Jerusalem: If you knew the things that are for your peace; for the days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall surround you with a rampart, and besiege you, and dash your children to the ground (Luke 19:42, 43). And those who have not received peace consequently have no judgment in their ways either: namely him of whom it was said above, Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved whom my soul has loved; he shall bring forth judgment to the nations (Isa 42:1). It follows: Their ways are perverse, not by nature, but by their own will. For whatever is perverted and bent is twisted from straight into crooked. The whole doctrine of the Pharisees is a subversion of the truth; whoever walks by it not only does not find peace, but does not even know it, so as to know what he ought to seek.
Commentary on Isaiah

Because of this judgment is far removed from us, and righteousness will not overtake us. We waited for light, and behold, darkness; for brightness, and we have walked in darkness. We have groped for the wall like the blind, and we have felt about as if without eyes; we have stumbled at noon as in darkness; in dark places as dead men. We shall all roar like bears, and like doves we shall moan in meditation. We waited for judgment, and there shall be none; for salvation, and it is far removed from us. LXX: Therefore judgment has departed from them, and righteousness does not overtake them. While they waited for light, darkness came upon them. Waiting for it, they shall walk in darkness; they shall grope for the wall like the blind, and shall feel about as though having no eyes. They shall fall at noon as at midnight; like dying men they shall groan; like a bear and like a dove they shall walk together. We waited for judgment, and there is none; salvation has departed far from us. After the accusation of the people of the Jews, the Prophet answers in their person what they ought to say as penitents, if indeed they wish to recover health after their wounds. And I wonder why the Seventy framed the speech as though the Prophet were speaking about them, and not they themselves answering the Prophet's words, when in what follows, overcome by the truth, they did this very thing, saying: We waited for judgment, and there is none; salvation has departed far from us. For our iniquity is great in your sight, and our sins have withstood us, and the rest. In the present time, then, all things are fulfilled. Judgment, which has been announced to the nations, is far removed from the Jews; and righteousness, which has been laid hold of by the nations, will not overtake them. They waited for the light, saying, Send forth your light and your truth (Ps 42 [43]:3), which had been promised them through the Prophets, and they have been seized by the darkness of error. They waited for brightness, and they walked in darkness.
Commentary on Isaiah

So they grope at the holy Scriptures like the blind feeling for a wall, seeking in them only the words and the leaves, not the sense and the fruit which is held in the letters. Then he adds and says: We have stumbled, or we shall fall at noon as in darkness; in dark places, as dead men. For while the sun of righteousness flashes its brightness over the whole world, they linger in darkness, namely as men dead in sin.
Commentary on Isaiah

We shall all roar, he says, like bears, and like doves we shall moan in meditation; so that they are at once cruel and wretched: fierce and savage toward the lowly and those subject to them, fearful and trembling toward those who are stronger, whom they dread as doves dread hawks. We read in another place too: Like a she-bear robbed of her cubs; and in Daniel the bloody kingdom, in which there are three rows of teeth, is compared to a most ferocious she-bear (2 Sam 17:8; Dan 7). And like doves we shall moan in meditation, without sense and understanding of the Scriptures, meditating only on the words, which they chant by heart. But just as the doves of which it is written, Ephraim is like a dove that has no sense (Hos 7:11), and as in the Gospel the simplicity of doves is set against the malice of serpents (Matt 10), so in the present place simplicity without prudence, which is close to folly, is shown in the mere meditation of words. They will wait for judgment, and there will be none; for salvation, understood, they will wait, and there will be none, because it has gone far away to the nations. Here it must be noted that everything is said in the future tense, so as to indicate what the Jews are now enduring.
1 CLEMENT 3:4

For this reason righteousness and peace are far from you, since each has abandoned the fear of God and grown blind in his faith and ceased to walk by the rules of his precepts or to behave in a way worthy of Christ. Rather does each follow the lusts of his evil heart by reviving that wicked and unholy rivalry, by which, indeed, "death came into the world."
Commentary on Isaiah

Our iniquities are multiplied before you, and our sins have answered against us; for our crimes are with us, and we have known our iniquities: to sin and to lie against the Lord; and we have turned away so as not to go behind our Lord, so as to speak calumny; and we have conceived transgression, and have spoken from the heart words of falsehood. And judgment is turned backward, and righteousness has stood far off, for truth has fallen in the street, and equity could not enter. And truth has been given over to forgetfulness, and he who departed from evil lay open to be a prey. LXX: For our iniquity is great in your sight, and our sins have withstood us. For our iniquities are in us, and we have known our unrighteousnesses. We have acted impiously, and we have lied, and we have departed from our God. We have spoken unjust things and been disobedient. We have been in labor with and meditated from our hearts unjust words. And we have departed from judgment, and righteousness has stood far off, for truth has been consumed in their ways, and they could not pass by the straight road. And truth has been taken away, and they turned aside their mind so as not to understand. He gives the reasons why they roared like bears and meditated like doves, and waited for a judgment that was not there, and for a salvation that passed over to the nations: because multiplied, they say, are our iniquities in your sight, from which you had turned away your face for a long time, so as not to see them, so as not to strike. And our sins have answered against us, so that we have received what we deserved. And our crimes are with us, and we have known our iniquities, which, while we committed them for a long time, we thought to be righteousness.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what are the iniquities? To sin and to lie against God; or, as Aquila translated according to the Hebrew, to deny God: which refers to the Savior. And we have forsaken, they say, our God, saying: We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from (John 9:29); so as to speak calumny: If this man were from God, he would not break the sabbath (ibid., 16); and: By Beelzebub the prince of demons he casts out demons (Luke 11:15). And transgression, which in Greek is called more expressively ἀπόστασις, when someone denies God and is convicted of prevarication. We have conceived and spoken from the heart words of falsehood, despising the law of God and following the traditions of men, which they call δευτερώσεις, and which we feigned in our heart:
Commentary on Isaiah

And judgment is turned backward, and righteousness has stood far off. For what share has righteousness with iniquity? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Righteousness has taken its stand among the nations and has departed from us, because truth has fallen in the street. For wide and spacious is the way that leads to death (Matt 7), because they would not enter the narrow way in which truth abides.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord saw, and it appeared evil in his eyes, that there is no judgment; and he saw that there is no man, and he was at a loss, because there is none to meet him. And his own arm will save for him, and his righteousness itself has strengthened him. He has put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation upon his head. He has put on the garments of vengeance, and is covered as with a cloak of zeal. As for vengeance, as for the repayment of indignation to his foes, and recompense to his enemies, he will repay recompense to the islands. LXX: The Lord saw, and it did not please him, because there was no judgment. And he saw, and there was no man. And he considered, and there was none to defend. And he avenged them with his arm, and upheld with mercy. And he put on righteousness as a breastplate, and set the helmet of salvation on his head. And he was wrapped in the garment of vengeance, and in a cloak, as one repaying vengeance, reproach to his adversaries. Up to this point the prophetic discourse has been woven in the person of the people; now the prophet speaks in his own person. When they said these things, the Lord saw that they made a show of repentance with the mouth and did not practice it in the heart, and it did not please him. For he sought in them the truth of judgment, which had been transferred to the nations, and did not find it. He longed for some righteous man who could meet him in his anger, and did not find one; he who had said above as well: I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was none to hear (Isa 50:2). And because, while they persisted in their crime, not even one righteous man was found, but all had turned aside, together they had become useless, and there is none who does good, there is not even one (Ps 13 [14]), he strengthened him with his arm and righteousness, or mercy, so that those who wish to be converted from error may be preserved not by their own merit but by the clemency of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

And truth has been given over to forgetfulness, of which it is written: Truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven (Ps 84 [85]:12). Here we must observe that truth is named often, so that the person of Christ might be shown; forsaking him, they followed falsehood. And he who departed from evil lay open to be a prey. Although this seems obscure, it can be explained thus: when we were fashioning falsehood from our own heart and forsaking the law of God, righteousness stood far off, and truth fell in the streets, and equity could not enter in to us, and the Son of God, who is the truth, was given over to forgetfulness; so much so that whoever wished to depart from the traditions of the Jews at once lay open to plots and persecutions, so that they cast out of the synagogues the man blind from birth who had received his sight (John 9). And after the resurrection of the Lord the Savior they persecuted and stripped all who believed in him, to whom the Churches from the whole world of the nations sent ministrations, for them to distribute through the hands of the Apostles.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then he put on the breastplate of righteousness, and the helmet of salvation, and the garments of vengeance, and was wrapped in the cloak of zeal; and thus armed he went forth to war, to render vengeance to his enemies, doubtless meaning the Jews who persevered in their blasphemies, and recompense to his foes, when the Roman army surrounded them; and in their victory the Lord is shown to have fought. Paul used this testimony when writing to the Ephesians, wishing us to put on the armor of Christ, by which we may resist the fiery darts of the devil (Eph 6). And what is not found in the Seventy Translators, He will repay recompense to the islands, signifies the cities of Judea, which the Roman army laid waste. For above too (Isa 20) the Lord speaks through the Prophet to the inhabitants of the island, that is, of Jerusalem.
Commentary on Isaiah

And those from the West shall fear the name of the Lord, and those from the rising of the sun his glory, when he comes like a violent river which the spirit of the Lord drives on; and the redeemer shall come to Zion, and to those who return from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord. This is my covenant with them, says the Lord: My spirit which is in you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of the seed of your seed, says the Lord, from now and for ever. LXX: And those from the West shall fear the name of the Lord, and those from the rising of the sun the glorious name. For the wrath of the Lord shall come like a violent river, ÷ it shall come with fury ⁚ and he who delivers shall come from Zion. And he shall turn away impieties from Jacob, and this shall be my testament to them, says the Lord. My spirit which is in you, and my words which I have given in your mouth, shall not fail from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, says the Lord, from now and for ever. After the Lord has put on the breastplate of righteousness, and the helmet of salvation, and the garments of vengeance, and the cloak of zeal for the fight, and has come to the contest and to vengeance, to repay his foes and render to his enemies, and to overthrow their islands, that is, their cities and villages, then the foreigners who are to come from the West and the East to rest in the bosom of Abraham (Matt 8), of whom it was also said above (cf. Isa 49:12), Behold, these shall come from afar, some from the West, and others from the North, and others from the land of the Persians, will fear the Lord with that fear which is the beginning of wisdom (Sir 1). Of this we read in many places, of which let us set down a few: Blessed is the man who fears the Lord (Ps 111 [112]:1); and: There is no want for those who fear him (Ps 33 [34]:10); and: The fear of the Lord is discipline and wisdom (Prov 15:33); and: Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord (Ps 33 [34]:12); and: Blessed is the man who fears the Lord (Ps 127 [128]:4); and: The fear of the Lord adds days (Prov 10:27). That, once Israel has been rejected, the crowd of the nations takes its place, the prophet Malachi teaches more fully, in whom it is said to the Jews: I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands (Mal 1:10, 11); and again of the multitude of the nations: For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations. The author of this blessedness is he who will come like a violent river which the spirit of the Lord drives on; or, as Aquila translated, like a narrow river, the spirit of the Lord its seal; or Theodotion, like an assailing river, the spirit of the Lord is sealed. In this testimony, then, as the Seventy translated it, like a violent river the wrath of the Lord shall come with fury, the last part is not found in the Hebrew. For wrath and fury are not to be set among the promises of God, since in the other things that follow there is the blessedness of things to come, and the threat and punishment of sinners. According to Aquila and Theodotion, the spirit of the Lord which is sealed in Christ confirms the example which is read in John the Evangelist: For him God the Father has sealed (John 6:27); of whom it has already been said before: A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from its root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord has filled him (Isa 11:1ff.). Hence we too say: The light of your countenance, Lord, is sealed upon us (Ps 4:7). And in Ezekiel the foreheads of the men who groan are sealed with the impression of THAV, the Hebrew letter which is the last among them (Ezek 9). But if we wish to know how the Holy Spirit is a violent river, let us read again the Acts of the Apostles, in which it is written: And when they were gathered together, suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them tongues parted as of fire, and it sat upon each of them; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:2, 3).
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 44: HOW THE PROMISE TO ABRAHAM WAS FULFILLED IN CHRIST

How could it be shown from the testimony of the prophets, already received among the Gentiles in the New Testament, that the promise which God made to Abraham has been fulfilled through the coming of Christ? — It is written in the prophet Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56:7). But perhaps the Jews will say: The house of God, that is, the synagogue, is open to all. Nor do we object; yet in such a way that, as always, the circumcised join themselves to the Law. For their Law is that by which they were commanded, after the manner of Abraham, to be circumcised. Therefore, nothing new can seem to be signified by this example of the prophet; since anyone coming from any nation has never been forbidden from the beginning of Judaism to join himself to the Law. Nothing new spoken by the prophet can be thought, indeed it would be unessential, if the Gentiles have always been admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are never found to have been forbidden. And this is true, because those who submit themselves to the Law are never found not to have been received. If, therefore, these things are so, it seems needless that the prophet admonished about what, once handed down, has always been observed. And could anyone so dull be found as to say that the prophet spoke something unnecessary and empty? I do not know for whom it would be safe even to hear this and not oppose it. For since the Jewish people, on account of the sins which they committed against God, seeking help from idols, were often rebuked by the prophets but refused to enter upon the path of repentance so as to return to God, God, in reproach of them, indicated that He would open His house to all nations to pray, so that, the Jews being cast off, He would show that He would place others in their place. For if the nations have always been admitted to the Law, as was said above, how could the prophet say that this would happen in the future, unless he meant something different from what had been previously commanded? He could not speak of a thing which was done daily as though it were going to come. Therefore it is clear that this tends to the ruin of the Jews, to whom the prophet shows that, with them removed, others were to be called and were to receive the house of God’s grace, which had been promised to the Jews. What that promise is, the prophet Isaiah teaches, saying: “There shall come out of Zion one who shall deliver and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob; and this shall be my covenant with them” (Isa. 59:20–21). Therefore this covenant is the removal of sins. This is the New Covenant, which was promised through Jeremiah, who says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will accomplish for the house of Israel and the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I arranged for their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not continue in my covenant, and I neglected them, says the Lord” (Jer. 31:31–32). This is their transgression, when they made the image of a calf; then they corrupted His covenant. Therefore also the tablets on which the Law had been given were shattered under the mountain (Exod. 32:4, 19), because they deserved to receive more severe precepts. But because God is mild and merciful, He promised through the prophets that He would change the Law, so as to give another Covenant, which would differ from that which He had given before: that not only what was burdensome might be changed, but also those things which were given in figure, that is, the sabbath and circumcision; so that, since they had long been oppressed, being relieved in all things, they might give grateful thanks to God as petitioners. And because, persisting in their fathers’ transgression, they refused to turn their minds away from idols, He testifies that the nations, together with the remnant who kept the faith, will enjoy the Covenant which He had said would come: so that the faithless Jews might be tortured in a twofold way. For they were burdened for a time by the precepts, and in the future they will pay fitting penalties, because they were found faithful neither in the Old nor in the New Covenant. So He said that He would give a New Covenant, so that the Old, which had been given to the Fathers, would cease. And therefore, whoever serves God in this Covenant does not observe the sabbath, nor new moons, nor circumcision, nor distinctions of foods; but has only the fear of God in faith: because he will not be justified by the Law, but by faith, as the prophet Habakkuk says: “For the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. 2:4); so that he no longer uses many precepts to gain favor with God, but few. Isaiah again, speaking with the same meaning, says: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of them shall be saved. For the Lord shall accomplish and cut short His word in righteousness, because the Lord will make a short word upon the whole earth” (Isa. 10:22–23). For the remnant who will persevere in the faith of the promise, while the others do not believe, He shows the shortened word of the Law: this is the New Covenant which He promised. It would not otherwise be called a Covenant, unless in a similar way this too were confirmed by the witness of blood, just as the Old Covenant, so that both might have one and the same name: but in the Old, many precepts, in the New, however, few, as He promised. So that, since He had said that Abraham would be the father of many nations (Gen. 17:4–5), in the same way the sons might be justified as the father had been justified: so that, once those things ceased which began after the faith of Abraham, those who receive the faith by which that same Abraham was justified might be sons of Abraham, as was said by the Lord. And this is neither strange nor unheard of, that men should be justified without care for the sabbath and circumcision and the rest of the commandments of this sort. For Enoch did not please God by this, that he might be translated; nor was Noah found righteous in the flood by observing this alone; nor was Abraham himself justified after he was circumcised: “Abraham,” it says, “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Heb. 11:5, 7, 8; Rom. 4:3). Then he was circumcised, so that there might be in him a sign that, though he was old, he believed that he would have a son. Therefore it is not circumcision that commends Abraham, but faith. And so, for those who believe, faith is sufficient for justification, that they may be sons of Abraham in faith, not in circumcision, because they have no need of circumcision. For what Abraham believed is not what is believed in their case. But the Jews were therefore ordered to be circumcised, so that they might have the sign of Abraham’s faith, not of their own faith, but so that they might be known as his sons according to the flesh. Yet if they believe, they will be his sons also in justification. For what advantage is it to be called the son of a powerful man if one is powerless, except that it is even more harmful? For it is a disgrace to be the son of a noble and glorious man without honor. Indeed, bodily circumcision is so far from being a merit that God says through the prophet Jeremiah that He will take vengeance on all the circumcised in foreskin, if they are not circumcised in heart (Jer. 4:4). Yet He is not angry with those who are circumcised in heart but uncircumcised in flesh, because no one has ever pleased God without the circumcision of the heart. Whoever, therefore, are circumcised in the flesh signify the lineage of Abraham according to the flesh; but those who are circumcised in heart signify the lineage of God according to faith, because, being circumcised from all worldly error, they confess God as their Father. What then does the circumcision of the flesh profit, if, when faith is lacking in the Jew, he cannot attain to the merit of Abraham? Or what harm is there in foreskin, when no one attains to his righteousness except the one who has followed the faith of Abraham? They therefore glory in the circumcision of the flesh in vain, since they see that it has no merit before God. And since, as has been shown, it is better to have faith than circumcision, the Gentiles are better than the Jews; for the Gentiles have faith, the Jews have circumcision. And whom do you think He recognizes more as sons of Abraham: those who are like him according to the flesh, or those who are like him in faith? But the faith of Abraham bears witness. And therefore he glories not in the flesh but in faith. For this reason he has received as sons those whom he sees to be imitators of his glory. For how can he call those sons from whom he sees a shrinking back from that by which he pleased God and was justified? He will therefore be able to judge them not as his sons, but as his enemies. For they appear to be envious of him, despising the faith through which he was glorified. Nor is it surprising if the Jews are found untrusting, not at all accepting the New Testament, when we know that they were not faithful even in the Old. They were always rebellious and disrespectful against God, and therefore they received such commandments by which their necks, which were unbending, might be pressed down. For they never wished to hope for good things from God, whose such great benefits and such wondrous powers they had come to know. Therefore it is that, among other things, the prophet Ezekiel says: “I lifted up my hand to them in the desert, that they should be scattered among the nations and dispersed in the lands, because they did not perform my ordinances and rejected my commandments.” And in what follows: “I gave them laws that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live in them” (Ezek. 20:23–25). He shows for what reason such great and so harsh commandments were given to them: because they proved ungrateful for such great benefits, and, justice dictating, they were to be pressed by more severe precepts. Therefore He called them “not good,” although they are just: because they did not lead them to justification, but to destruction; and although a punishment rightly inflicted, yet for the one who suffers it, it is not a good. After these things, however, because God is merciful, He promised that He would give the New Testament, in which the shortening of the Law would justify believers, just as Abraham was justified: so that, with new moons and the sabbath and circumcision and the other precepts ceasing, not those that belong to the natural law, that is, murder, adultery, and such things, they might be justified as Abraham was. For, with the faith of Abraham renewed, He willed that all things should cease, so that the time might be such as it was when Abraham believed. But perhaps the Jews say: “If those things that were given by Moses are said to cease through the shortening of the Law, was circumcision given by Moses so that it should cease? And therefore we have the sign of our father, because we are the sons of Abraham, a sign which, for the sake of the testimony of our lineage, ought not to cease.” Circumcision indeed had to be observed in its time, that is, before the New Testament which had been promised was given. But when, by the grace of God, the burdens of the Law were ordered to cease, what need is there of circumcision? Therefore a new Law was given, that is, a spiritual one, so that carnal things might cease, and those who received it might accept its sign: so that just as in the Old Testament they had the sign of Abraham, from whom the Old Testament began, so also in the New they might have the sign of the Savior, who is the institutor of the New Testament. For just as from Abraham they were called Hebrews, so from Christ they are called Christians. Whoever, therefore, are still called Hebrews have not received the New Testament which God promised, bringing to nothing the kindness and mercy of God: for He no longer wished His people to be designated by the name of a man, but agreed to establish them under the name of His Son. With what courage, then, do the Jews say that we do not use our Law but theirs, when David says, “I will give thanks to you among the nations” (Ps. 17:50), and again, “Rejoice, O nations, with his people”? And to the prophet Jeremiah the Lord says, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you; and I appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (Jer. 1:5). Judaism certainly has its own particular signs: for this people is signified either in Jacob, or in Samaria, or in Jerusalem, or in Judea, or in Israel. As for the nations, however, it is clear that He signifies them in a different way than He does the Jews. Therefore Jeremiah is our prophet. For although in all the Prophets God showed that the nations would share in His gift, yet to Jeremiah in particular He says that He has given him to us as a prophet. For he signified that the New Testament would come, which would profit the Gentiles more than the Jews, as now appears clearly. For since the preaching of the New Testament is spread over the whole earth, a faithful Jew is so rarely and with such difficulty found that all the Churches of the New Testament are called “of the nations,” as it was said in the prophet Hosea: “I will call that which is not my people, my people; and her that was not beloved, beloved” (Hosea 2:24; Rom. 9:25). Therefore, the Jews having been rejected, He calls the nations with the same mercy and grace with which He agreed to call Abraham. For Abraham did not come to know the Lord without being called. Therefore, He who agreed to call Abraham likewise agreed to call the nations. Why then do they say, “The Law is ours,” when it is clear that the gift of God is for all who are willing? Let this careless violation cease, since the grace of God is common to all. With what shame do they deny that our Christ was promised in the Law, when they see in Him all the signs which the Law foretold as to come? For both according to the promise made to Abraham all nations are justified by believing in Him (Gen. 22:18); and according to the prophet Isaiah He was born of a Virgin (Isa. 7:14) in Bethlehem from the tribe of Judah, as was promised, from the seed of David (Micah 5:2); and in accordance with what Jeremiah prophesied (Jer. 31:31–32), He proclaimed the New Testament which God then promised would come; and after all the signs of power had been shown, He humbled Himself, according to the words of the Prophets; and having suffered all that had been foretold, He rose on the third day, as it is written in the prophet. And if they inquire about the time of the promise, as it is shown in the prophet Daniel (Dan. 9:24 ff.), they will find it fulfilled in the time when Christ was born and suffered: for from the first year of Darius, king of the Persians, down to the birth and passion of the Lord and the destruction of Jerusalem, which was carried out by Vespasian, chief of the Roman Empire, the seventy weeks were completed, which are four hundred and ninety years, a reckoning made clear through the kingdoms and the successors of the empire. Therefore also it is found calculated by Tertullian in the book which he wrote against the Jews; but, lest this should backfire to his disadvantage, although he calculated correctly, we have passed it over in silence. And who can doubt this number, when now about three hundred years are found in addition to that number? It is therefore shameless, after so many years have been added beyond the time of the coming of the Saviour, to say, “He has not come.” Under the Apostles, or at the time when the Lord was living among men, hatred opposing the truth could still hide itself; so that, although it saw all the signs of the Christ who had been promised in the Savior, it could say that it doubted about the time, to conceal its unbelief. But afterwards, when many years began to exceed the promised number, what shamelessness it is to deny that He has come, whose coming is known to have been fulfilled both by signs and by times! For when something is full and does not overflow, a combative person may say that it is not full; but overflow closes the mouth of the argumentative. So the Jews, in the time of the Saviour, could say, though deceitfully, that the calculation from the time of Darius to the Lord Christ was not correctly made, so that He might not be acknowledged as the one who had been promised. We are mistaken, they might say, in the years and in the months and in the days of the emperors, and we do not make an exact reckoning. But when the times have extended beyond the prescribed number of years of the promised Christ, no excuse can be put forward to deny that He who has come is the Christ, unless, which God forbid, the one who promised is said to have lied. For when the time of the promise has elapsed, and it is denied that the one who was promised has come, what else is charged against the promiser but falsehood? Yet that He who made the promise is truthful, all the signs teach which were foretold in Christ and are known to have been found in Christ. The Jews, however, while they are ashamed to change themselves, do not consider that there will be a judgment to come. For nothing is worse than for someone to deny that a thing is true when he understands that it is not a lie.
Commentary on Isaiah

It follows: The redeemer of Zion shall come, and of those who return from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord. For this the Seventy translated: He who delivers shall come from Zion, and shall turn away impieties from Jacob. If, then, he who turns away the impieties from Jacob will come from Zion, we understand this: that a man was born in Zion, and the Most High founded her, he who turns away the crimes of Jacob. But if the redeemer shall come to Zion, and to those who return from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord, this is the sense: Christ will come, who will redeem Zion with his blood; or, according to the Hebrew idiom, he who is the kinsman of Zion and was begotten of the stock of Israel; for this is what GOEL (גואל), that is, ἀγχιστεὺς, means. And lest we think that all of Zion is redeemed and freed from its crimes, Zion which is bloodied with the blood of the Lord, he added significantly: to those who return from iniquity, if they are willing to do penance, in whom the Lord's prayer may be fulfilled: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34).
Commentary on Isaiah

Paul, explaining this place carefully, writes to the Romans that there is no distinction of Jew and Greek, but the same Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him (Rom 10); and that the nations did not believe in such a way that Israel was wholly driven out. For I too, he says, am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not cast off his people whom he foreknew (Rom 11:1, 2). And a little after, when he had set down the example of Elijah, complaining to the Lord that he alone was left, and hearing from him that the Lord had left for himself seven thousand men who had not bent the knee before Baal (1 Kgs 19), he added: So then at this present time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. And if by grace, it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. What then? What Israel was seeking, this it has obtained; but the election has obtained it, and the rest have been blinded. And they, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in. For God is able, he says, to graft them in again (Rom 11:5ff.): not against nature from the wild olive, as the multitude of the nations was grafted in, but according to nature into the good olive, that is, into their own. And at the end he set down, so as to arrive at the present chapter: For I would not have you ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own eyes: that blindness has befallen Israel in part, until the fullness of the nations should come in, and so all Israel should be saved, as it is written: He who delivers shall come from Zion, and shall turn away impieties from Jacob; and this is my testament to them, when I take away their sins (Rom 11:25ff.). We have pursued these things at greater length so that we may understand that whatever promises we have read, and are going to speak of, concerning Zion and Jerusalem, are said not generally to all the Jews, but specially to those of Israel who were chosen in the Apostles and through the Apostles.
Commentary on Isaiah

Theirs, then, is the redemption in Zion, and theirs the kinsman, who from Jacob have received him; and to them he promises, saying: This is my covenant with them, or pact, as all the others translated, or testament, as the Seventy put it. What the covenant, pact and testament is, the following verse shows: My spirit, he says, which is in you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, from now and for ever. This is said either to Isaiah, as it seems to me, or to the Lord, as very many think. With reference to Isaiah, then, the order is connected thus: This is the everlasting pact of the Gospel: that my spirit which is in you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, by which you foretell things to come, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from that of your sons and grandsons and your seed, so that every generation in succession is indicated: namely, that the grace of the Prophets comes upon the Apostles, and through those of Israel who are to believe through the Apostles. What he adds, from now and for ever, agrees with that testimony: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away (Matt 24:35).

f: AGAINST CELSUS 6:5

And the Logos, exhorting us to come to this light, says, in the prophecies of Isaiah, "Enlighten yourself, enlighten yourself, O Jerusalem, for your light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen on you." Observe now the difference between the fine phrases of Plato respecting the chief good and the declarations of our prophets regarding the light of the blessed; and notice that the truth as it is contained in Plato concerning this subject did not at all help his readers to attain to a pure worship of God, or even himself, who could philosophize so grandly about the chief good, whereas the simple language of the Scriptures led to their honest readers being filled with a divine spirit; and this light is nourished within them by the oil, which as a certain parable is said to have preserved the light of the torches of the five wise virgins.
ORATION CONCERNING SIMEON AND ANNA 13

Hail, thou heaven upon earth, Sion, the city that is for ever faithful unto the Lord.
