LXX: Be enlightened, be enlightened, ÷ Jerusalem ⁚ for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you. Behold, darkness will cover the earth, and thick gloom upon the nations. But upon you the Lord will appear, and his glory will be seen in you. And the nations will walk in your light, and kings in your brightness. What we thought about the restoration of Zion and Jerusalem, and about everything that is promised to her by the prophetic oracle, we said more fully at the end of the preceding book, where we explained what that little verse meant: The redeemer will come to Zion, and to those who return from iniquity in Jacob. Now we must touch briefly on what most people think of this passage, so that, once the error has been seen through, we may more easily take up the truth. The Jews and our half-Jews, who expect a golden and jewelled Jerusalem from heaven, contend that these things will come to pass in the kingdom of a thousand years, when all the nations are to serve Israel, and the camels of Midian and Ephah, coming from Sheba, will bring gold and incense, and all the sheep of Kedar will be gathered, and the rams of Nebaioth will come to be sacrificed upon the altar of the Temple that will have been built. They say too that from the islands, and above all in the ships of Tarshish, her daughters will fly like doves, bringing riches of gold and silver; that the walls of Jerusalem will be built by foreigners, with the kings of the nations set over them; that the gates of the city will always stand open, so that by day and by night the riches of Jerusalem and the victims may be brought in; and that everything that lies desolate will be rebuilt with cypress and pine and cedar cut in Lebanon, above all the Temple of the Lord, in which there will be everlasting gladness; so that she will suck the milk of the nations and eat the riches of kings, and there will be such an abundance of all things that they will have gold for bronze, silver for iron, bronze for wood, iron for stones. Her princes too, they say, will enjoy everlasting peace, and bishops will preside over the peoples in righteousness, and her gates will be carved in relief. And what is greater than these, instead of the sun and the moon the Lord himself will shine with everlasting light; and for one man she will have a thousand very strong men, and for little ones she will possess very mighty nations. So say those who desire earthly pleasures, and seek beauty in wives and a great number of children, whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame (Phil 3); and whoever follows their error confesses himself, under the Christian name, to be like the Jews. Others, however, assert that all these things were promised to the Jews in a carnal sense, if they had received him who says in the Gospel: I am the light of the world (John 8:12), which enlightens every man coming into the world; so that, just as victims were granted to the people of Israel, not because they were good in themselves, but so that they might not be offered to demons, so too the Lord promises these things to the gluttonous Jews, who seek nothing but the pleasures of the body, so that at least for the sake of their carnal desires and an abundance of wealth they might receive the Son of God; and since they did not receive him, the promises too, they say, became void. Thus to the Canaanite woman pleading for her daughter: I did not come, he says, except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). And to his disciples: Do not go away into the way of the nations, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 10:5, 6). For this reason the Apostles too first proclaimed the Lord in the synagogues, and when these did not receive the Gospel they said to them: It was necessary that the word should be preached to you; but since you have not received salvation, behold, we turn to the nations (Acts 13:46). For the light came into the world, and the Jews loved darkness rather. Hence the Lord too, when he had wept over Jerusalem, added: If you also had known the things that make for your peace (Luke 19:42). And since she did not receive it, he went on: But now a day will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, and hem you in, and bring you down to the ground together with your children (ibid., 43). But let us, following the former sense, believe that all of this is said to the Church, which was first gathered from the Jewish people, and which through the Apostles passed on to the nations the light that had risen upon her. To her it is said: Arise, be enlightened, so that she who fell in the unbelievers may rise in the faithful; she who fell in the synagogues may rise in the churches; and, once she has risen, may be enlightened, so that she may have no darkness of error at all. For your light, he says, has come, the light that all the Prophets promised, which you were ever awaiting. And the glory of the Lord, which was once upon the tabernacle and his Temple, has risen upon you; of which it is said: Glorious things have been said of you, city of God (Ps 86 [87]:3).
Commentary on Isaiah

For behold, darkness will cover the earth, that is, those who savor earthly things; and thick gloom the peoples, or, as we read in the Hebrew, the tribes: which refers properly to the Jews, of whom it is written in another psalm: For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel (Ps 121 [122]:4). But upon you the Lord will rise, the sun of righteousness, and his glory will be seen in you, of which it is written: And we saw his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
Commentary on Isaiah

And the nations will walk in your light. We all shall walk in the light of the Apostles, which shines in the world, and the darkness did not comprehend it. And kings, he says, in the brightness of your rising, when you were first born in Christ. This is fulfilled both spiritually and carnally: so that kings whose heart is in the hand of the Lord, and in whose mortal body sin does not reign (Prov 21), may walk in the brightness of the newborn Church, or in him who has risen in the Church, and may bow their necks to the faith of Christ, the true king (Rom 6). And we see this fulfilled daily, when the Roman princes, the error of idolatry and the fury of persecution being removed, pass over to the faith and tranquillity of Christ. There are some who await in a time to come all these things which we relate as partly fulfilled and wholly to be fulfilled from the first coming of the Savior until the consummation of the world, when, as the fullness of the nations comes in, all Israel is to be saved (Rom 11). Their opinion is by no means to be rejected, provided we know that these things are to be fulfilled spiritually and not carnally.
Commentary on Isaiah

Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have gathered and come to you. Your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will suck at your side. LXX: Lift up your eyes round about, and see all your sons gathered. All your sons have come from afar, and your daughters will be carried upon the shoulders. It is said to the Church, Zion, which was first gathered through the Apostles; of whom we also read in the Acts of the Apostles that devout men from the whole world were in Jerusalem, who received the word of God, and in the tongues of their own and of foreign nations either heard others speaking or themselves spoke to the rest (Acts 2). And they are commanded to lift up their eyes round about, which the Lord too commanded the Apostles, saying: Lift up your eyes and see, for the crops are already white for the harvest (John 4:35). For out of Zion, and by no means out of Mount Sinai, the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And she is commanded to lift up her eyes and see her sons gathered, who come from afar. To her it is said in another place too: Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion, proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem: Behold, I come, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord (Zeph 3:17); and: Many nations will come to the Lord, and they will be my people, and I will be their God (Zech 2:11). Now we are the sons who come to the Lord from afar, once strangers to the Testament of God and to his promises, having no hope, and without God in the world. But what does the Apostle say? You who were once far off have now been brought near (Eph 2:13). And what follows, And your daughters will suck at your side, signifies that souls that are sucklings in Christ, and in the infancy of baptism, of whom the apostle Peter too speaks, Like newborn babes, desire the rational milk without guile (1 Pet 2:2), suck the milk of the apostles. To such babes and sucklings Paul also spoke: My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you (Gal 4:19). And in another place: As a nurse cherishing her children, so, longing for you, we desire to impart to you not only the Gospel of Christ but our own souls as well (1 Thess 2:7, 8). But what is said instead of this in the Seventy, your daughters will be carried upon the shoulders, must be considered more carefully. For the sons, who are strong, come from afar by themselves and are gathered to the faith of the Lord. But the daughters, who are weaker and, through the frailty of their sex, have not yet come to the perfect man, are carried on the shoulders of the Apostles, so as to be brought into the bosom of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then you will see and overflow, and your heart will marvel and be enlarged, when the multitude of the sea has been turned to you, and the strength of the nations has come to you. LXX: Then you will see, and you will fear, and you will be astonished in heart: because the riches of the sea, and of the nations, and of the peoples will be transferred to you. When you have lifted up your eyes and beheld your sons and daughters either coming swiftly by themselves or carried on the shoulders of the saints, then you will rejoice, and like rivers you will overflow with sudden waters, and your heart will marvel and be astonished, nay rather will be enlarged, as it hears the Apostle: My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians. And again: Be enlarged, and we too (2 Cor 6:11); lest through narrowness of heart you should be unable to have as your guest Christ, who says in the Gospel: I and the Father will come and will make our dwelling with him (John 14:23). But what is added in the Seventy, and you will fear, is not found in the Hebrew; unless perhaps, after the greatness of the joy, fear crept in, lest she lose so great a good. Or is it not joy to see riches, and the multitude of the sea being transferred and turned to oneself, and the strength of the nations coming to oneself, so that whatever is in the world and on the face of the earth is one's own; and, the faith of the nations being strengthened, to say: I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Jesus Christ (Phil 4:13)?
Commentary on Isaiah

A flood of camels will cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All from Sheba will come, bringing gold and incense, and proclaiming praise to the Lord. All the flock of Kedar will be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth will minister to you; they will be offered upon my altar of propitiation, and I will glorify the house of my majesty. LXX: And herds of camels will come to you, and the camels of Midian and Gephar will cover you: all from Sheba will come, bringing gold and incense, and they will proclaim the salvation of the Lord. All the sheep of Kedar will be gathered to you, the rams of Nabaeoth will come, and they will be offered as propitiatory upon my altar; and the house of my prayer will be glorified. After the riches of the sea and the strength of the nations, herds of camels too, and the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah, are promised to Jerusalem, all of which will come from Sheba carrying gold and incense, and, what is greater than these, proclaiming the salvation of the Lord. All the sheep of Kedar too will be gathered to the Church, and the rams of Nebaioth will come, or, as is written in the Hebrew, will minister, and will be offered, or will offer victims upon the altar of the Lord, so that his house may become renowned. Midian and Ephah are regions beyond Arabia, fertile in camels, and the whole province is called Sheba, whence came also the queen of Sheba, who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, she too bringing gold and incense, carrying much to the peaceable king and receiving greater things from him (1 Kgs 10). Kedar is the region of the Saracens, who in Scripture are called Ishmaelites. And Nebaioth is one of the sons of Ishmael, from whose names the desert is called, which, poor in crops, is full of flocks. Through the familiar names of barbarian nations, then, that are neighbors to Israel, the conversion of the whole world is proclaimed. For in this place Midian means iniquity; Ephah, loosed, or pouring out; Sheba, conversion, or captivity; Kedar, darkness; Nebaioth, prophecies. So herds of camels, loosed from the bonds of iniquity and pouring out their souls to God, will cover Jerusalem with gifts, and all will come from captivity and in their conversion, bringing the gold of faith and the incense of sacrifice. And through these gifts, by no means content with their own salvation, they will advance so far as to proclaim the salvation of God to others as well. That rich man in the Gospel who, like a camel, carried the burdens of riches, and was a camel, would not listen to the Lord's counsels nor be unloaded, so that, the pack cast off, he might fly to heaven on the wings of a dove; therefore he went away sad. And of a camel of this kind the Savior speaks: It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man into the kingdom of heaven (Matt 19:24). He set forth the difficulty of the thing, not its impossibility. Indeed your mother Paula, of holy memory, and your brother Pammachius passed through the eye of a needle, that is, through the strait and narrow way that leads to life, into the kingdom of heaven, leaving behind with its burdens the broad way that leads to Tartarus. Nay, whatever they had they carried into the gifts of the Lord, fulfilling what is written: The ransom of a man's soul is his own riches (Prov 13:8). For the things that are impossible with men are possible with God (Matt 19). Having among their gifts the chief things, gold in understanding and incense of the sweetest odor, and saying: Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight, and: We are the good odor of Christ in every place (2 Cor 2:15), they proclaim daily the salvation of the Lord by the example of their virtue, so that all the sheep of Kedar may be gathered in the Church and pass from the darkness of error to the light. And let the rams of the Prophets, of whom it is sung in the twenty-eighth psalm, Bring to the Lord, sons of God, bring to the Lord the young of rams, come and be offered, or, according to Theodotion, offer themselves as a sacrifice to the Lord, and become propitiatory victims, so that the Church of Christ may be glorified. Of sheep of this kind the Savior spoke to his disciples: Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 10:6). And again: My sheep hear my voice (John 10:27). And more fully in Ezekiel: Behold, I will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd seeks his flock. Thus says the Lord: I will seek the lost, and bring back the straying, and bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak, and guard the strong, and I will feed them with judgment (Ezek 34:11, 12). And so that we might know who the sheep were, he puts it more plainly: And they will know that I am the Lord their God, and they are my people, the house of Israel, says the Lord God; and you are my sheep, and you are all the sheep of my flock, and I am the Lord your God (ibid., 27, 28). If anyone among the nations is rich, then, let him be saved as a camel, not without gifts and offerings, with which he may proclaim the word of the Lord. If anyone is of the simplicity of sheep and of the authority of rams, let him go up, or be offered upon the altar of the Lord by those who have the power, so that his house may be glorified. But what we noted as written in the Hebrew, The rams of Nebaioth will minister to you, and they will offer upon my altar of propitiation, is properly understood of those who, chosen from the nations for the priesthood, are ministers of the Savior. And if anyone is contentious, and contends that these things were promised in a carnal sense, let us answer him: We have no such custom, nor has the Church of God (1 Cor 11:16). And let us say this too: that even if they were promised carnally to the Jews, still they were promised under a condition, namely that if they had received their light, which had been sent to them, then these things also would follow; that is, that through the desire of gold and an abundance of wealth and of carnal things, by whose allurements this nation was always captivated, they might receive the Son of God sent to them; and since they did not receive him, all was taken away, and the inheritance was given back spiritually to those who received him.
Commentary on Matthew

And again I say to you: It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. By this saying it is shown that it is not difficult but impossible. For if, as a camel cannot enter through the eye of a needle, so a rich man cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, none of the rich will be saved. But if we read in Isaiah how the camels of Midian and Ephah come to Jerusalem with gifts and offerings, and how those who were formerly bent and twisted by the perversity of vices enter the gates of Jerusalem, we shall see how these camels too, to which the rich are compared, when they have laid down the heavy burden of sins and the crookedness of the whole body, can enter by the narrow and strait way that leads to life.
ON VIRGINITY 18

Thus, typically, under the leadership of the Law (for Moses was a type of the Law that was coming) Israel passes unwetted over that sea, while the Egyptian who crosses in her track is overwhelmed. Each fares according to the disposition which he carries with him; one walks lightly enough, the other is dragged into the deep water. For virtue is a light and buoyant thing, and all who live in her way "fly like clouds," as Isaiah says, "and as doves with their young ones"; but sin is a heavy affair, "sitting," as another of the prophets says, "upon a talent of lead." If, however, this reading of the history appears to any forced and inapplicable, and the miracle at the Red Sea does not present itself to him as written for our profit, let him listen to the Apostle: "Now all these things happened unto them for types, and they are written for our admonition."
Concerning Virginity 17:108

For the soul has flights, as has been said, "Who are these that fly like clouds and like doves with their young?" You see, the soul has spiritual flights that, in a brief moment, circle the whole globe. For the thoughts of wise people are free and, insofar as they rise up from lower to higher shadows, so much and more they fly without the hindrance of any earthly weight, and they are the more carried along by the beating of spiritual wings onto that ethereal and rarefied place; [the soul] despises all worldly things. It soars above the world in its regard for eternal virtues; for justice is above the world, goodness is above the world, wisdom is above the world, even when it is found in the world, it is above the world nevertheless.
Commentary on Isaiah

Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows? For the islands wait for me, and the ships of the sea in the beginning, that I may bring your sons from afar, their silver and their gold with them, to the name of the Lord your God, and to the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you. LXX: Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves with their young to me? The islands have waited for me, and the ships of Tarshish among the first, to bring your sons from afar, and their silver and gold with them, for the sake of the holy name of the Lord, and because the Holy One of Israel has been glorified. Since the Lord entered Egypt upon a light cloud, and commanded the clouds of the Prophets, to whom the truth of God has come, not to rain showers upon Israel, the Church, first gathered from the people of the Circumcision, marvels that a crowd of nations is flying to her from the whole world, and, having taken the wings of the Holy Spirit, is hastening, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, to their windows, according to Aquila to their floodgates, in order to enter the Church. Or that teachers with their disciples, that is, doves with their young, are flying to the Church from the islands of the nations, which, according to the oracles of the Prophets, will wait for the Lord. The ships of THARSIS (תרשיש) too, that is, of the sea, of which we spoke more fully in the vision of Tyre, will bring the sons of the Church in the beginning of faith, carrying gold and silver. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Rom 10:10). Of this gold and silver it is written in the sixty-seventh psalm: The wings of a dove covered with silver, and her hinder parts in the gleam of gold (Ps 67 [68]:14). And in the seventy-first psalm: The kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts, and the kings of the Arabians and of Sheba will bring presents (Ps 71 [72]:10). All these things are brought to the name of the Lord God and to the Holy One of Israel, who has glorified him.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 21

For death indeed climbs in through the windows and enters houses, in that through the body's sense lust comes and enters the dwelling of the mind. Quite to the contrary is this which we have often cited from Isaiah concerning the righteous: "Who are they who fly like clouds and like doves come to their windows?" The righteous are said to be like clouds since they are raised above earthly contagions, just as doves go to their own windows, since each one does not pay much attention to their exterior senses, and fleshly lust does not catch them when they are far from home.… For the holy person who receiving the senses of his body like servants to help him is in control of them; and the fairest judge sees sins before they come and closes the windows to the plundering death of the body, saying, "I have made a covenant with my eyes, that I should not gaze at a young woman."
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 5

But this sacrifice of good will is never fully paid unless desire for this world is perfectly abandoned. For whatever we covet in it, we without doubt envy our neighbors. For it seems that what another obtains is lacking to us. And because envy always conflicts with good will, as soon as the former seizes the mind, the latter departs. Therefore the holy preachers, that they might perfectly love their neighbors, strove to love nothing in this age, never to desire anything, to possess nothing even without desire. Looking upon them well, Isaiah says: "Who are these that fly as clouds, and as doves to their windows?" For he saw them despise earthly things, draw near to heavenly things in mind, rain down words, flash forth miracles. And those whom holy preaching and sublime life had lifted up from earthly contagions, he calls both flying and clouds. Moreover our windows are our eyes, because through them the soul looks upon what it desires outwardly. But the dove is a simple animal, and free from the malice of gall. Therefore they are as doves to their windows who covet nothing in this world, who look upon all things simply, and are not drawn by the zeal of rapacity in what they see. But on the contrary, the kite and not the dove is at its windows, who pants with desire for plunder at what it considers with its eyes.
Commentary on Isaiah

Or certainly this must be said: that she who was once afflicted and handed over to captivity in the people of the Jews he reconciles to himself in the calling of the nations, so that her gates are always open, and are shut neither by day nor by night, and stand continually open to those who desire to be saved; that is, that entrance to her is not denied to those who wish to believe, whether in joy or in tribulation. And let the strength, or the riches, of the nations be brought in to her, and let their kings minister to her, or be led to her as captives. This you will understand when you see the most eloquent men led to the faith of Christ, and the wisdom of the wise made foolish, and the prudence of the prudent rejected (1 Cor 1), so that the foolishness of God is wiser than men.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the sons of strangers will build your walls, and their kings will minister to you. For in my indignation I struck you, and in my reconciliation I have had mercy on you. And your gates will be open continually; they will not be shut by day or by night, so that the strength of the nations may be brought to you, and their kings be led in. For the nation and the kingdom that will not serve you will perish, and the nations will be laid waste with desolation. LXX: And foreigners will build your walls, and their kings will stand by you. For because of my wrath I struck you, and because of mercy I have loved you. And your gates will be open always; they will not be shut by day or by night, so that they may bring in to you the strength of the nations, and their kings who are to be led in. For the nations and the kings that will not serve you will perish; the nations will be made desolate with desolation. Among the other things with which the Church is enriched and the city of the Savior is built, foreigners too and the sons of strangers build her walls, so that the enemy cannot enter nor faithlessness find a place. Foreigners and strangers properly signify the people of the nations, who truly built up the Church of Christ, so much so that their kings and princes minister to her, or stand by her. This is taken either carnally or spiritually. If carnally, we see the Roman Caesars bow their necks to the yoke of Christ, build churches at public expense, and issue decrees of law against the persecutions of the heathen and the snares of heretics. If spiritually, whoever among them are princes in continence, eloquence and holiness, and subjugate the servitude of the flesh to the rule of the soul, these minister to her and stand by her, or give aid to her whom he often forsakes because of her negligence, or strikes with the rod of persecutors, so that he may again love her for his own mercy's sake.
Commentary on Isaiah

But the nation and their kings who refuse to render the Church a good and profitable service, so as to pass over into apostolic dignity, will perish with the perdition that is prepared for the ungodly; and whatever was in them who refused to have God as their guest will be reduced to desolation.
Commentary on Isaiah

The glory of Lebanon will come to you, the fir and the box and the pine together, to adorn the place of my sanctification; and I will glorify the place of my feet. And the sons of those who humbled you will come to you bowed down, and all who disparaged you will worship the footprints of your feet, and they will call you the city of the Lord, the Zion of the Holy One of Israel. LXX: The glory of Lebanon will come to you, in cypress and pine and cedar together, so that my holy place may be glorified, ÷|÷ and I will glorify the place of my feet ⁚ And the sons of those who humbled you will go to you in fear, ÷ and provoked you ⁚ and all who provoked you will worship the footprints of your feet; and you will be called the city of the Lord, Zion, of the Holy One of Israel. Much is lacking in the Seventy, which I have set down from the Hebrew under asterisks, and what they added I have marked beforehand with an obelus. Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, planted with lofty trees, which the Psalmist describes when he says: I saw the ungodly exalted above measure and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon (Ps 36 [37]:35). And in another place: The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon (Ps 28 [29]:5). And many other things which I pass over for the sake of brevity. From this mountain Hiram king of Tyre once sent timber to Solomon at Joppa, for building the Temple of God (1 Kgs 5). From it too Scripture now promises that the fir and the box and the pine, or, according to the Seventy, the cypress and the pine and the cedar, or, according to Aquila, the fir, thaadaor, and thaassur, or, according to Theodotion, Brais, Thadaar, and Theassur, are to be cut together, so that the temple of Zion may be built (2 Chr 2). If that is so, where will the golden and jewelled Jerusalem be? Where the wife of the Lamb? Where the twelve gates adorned with a variety of gems? Unless perhaps she will have jewelled walls and foundations, and the Temple, which ought to be more richly adorned, will be built of wood! For this reason we are compelled to take everything spiritually: that the fir, the cypress, the pine and the cedar, once lofty trees of Lebanon, have glorified the Temple of God and the place of his feet, and made it renowned. And not to draw out the sense in a long discourse: do not the holy man and most eloquent martyr Cyprian, and Hilary, the confessor of our own time, once lofty trees in the world, seem to you to have built the Church of God?
Commentary on Isaiah

And what follows, And the sons of those who humbled you will come to you bowed down, or returning, and all who had disparaged you will worship the footprints of your feet, we ought to understand of those who are Christians not by will but by necessity, and who bow with fearful minds through dread of offending those who reign. Or certainly that those who were formerly persecutors afterwards believed: such as was the apostle Paul too, who persecuted the Church of God and was afterwards called a vessel of election (Acts 9). When these things have been so fulfilled that the fullness of the nations enters in, then all Israel will be saved. And she will truly be called the city of the Lord, the Zion of the Holy One of Israel, who stands upon the watchtower and has been gathered from both peoples.
Commentary on Isaiah

Because you were forsaken and hated, and there was none who passed through I will make you the pride of the ages, a joy from generation to generation; and you will suck the milk of the nations, and you will be suckled at the breast of kings. And you will know that I am the Lord who saves you, and your redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob. LXX: Because you were forsaken and hated, and there was none who helped, I will make you an everlasting exultation, a joy of generations unto generations. And you will suck the milk of the nations, and you will eat the riches of kings. And you will know that I am the Lord who has saved you, and who has rescued you, the God of Jacob. She who before had been forsaken and hated, when the branches in you were broken off because they had not borne fruit, branches which were broken off for this reason, that there was no one who passed through and offered help there, of whom it is said in the psalms, And those who passed by did not say: The blessing of the Lord be upon you (Ps 128 [129]:8): therefore I will make you an everlasting pride, or an exultation and joy of two generations, other branches from the wild olive of the nations being grafted in place of the former branches, which contrary to the nature of the pattern will bear fruit, not of the former bitterness but of the sweetness which they have drawn from the root.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10:294

And they will be called the city of the Lord, Zion of holy Israel. On account of your being trapped and despised when there was no help, I will give you eternal rejoicing and joy for ages to come. And though you desire the milk of the nations and to consume the riches of kings, so that you might know that I am the Lord who saved you and led you out of Israel, "I will render for you gold instead of brass, and silver instead of steel … and I will give you rulers in peace and your bishops in justice, and injustice will no longer be heard in your land."
Commentary on Isaiah

You will suck too the milk of the nations, and you will be suckled at the breast of kings. What sense this passage has we explained more fully above, when discussing the little verse, Your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will suck at your side. Or, according to the Seventy, you will eat the riches of kings. These riches, according to the Hebrew truth, are the breasts of kings and teachers, by which the infancy of those born in Christ is instructed and nourished. When you have sucked these and have come to solid food, so that you also eat the riches of such kings, then you will know that I am your Savior, who redeemed you with my blood, or the mighty God of Jacob.
1 CLEMENT 42:1-5

The apostles received the gospel for us from the Lord Jesus Christ; Jesus the Christ was sent forth from God. So then Christ is from God and the apostles are from Christ. Both, therefore, came of the will of God in good order. Having therefore received their orders and being fully assured by the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ and full of faith in the Word of God, they went forth with the firm assurance that the Holy Spirit gives, preaching the good news that the kingdom of God was about to come. So, preaching in the country and in the towns, they appointed their firstfruits, when they had tested them by the Spirit, to be bishops and deacons for the future believers. The same thing, according to the nature of its position, is a genus to one, a species to another. And so as not to seem to say anything about the arts of rhetoric and dialectic, I shall give common examples which can instruct the simple reader. My son, who in relation to me is a species and has me as his genus, is a genus to his own son. I shall give another: what is greater to one is smaller to another. A centurion is greater than a common soldier, smaller than a tribune. Five are few compared with ten, many compared with one. So in the restoration of the spiritual Jerusalem, wood will be turned into bronze, and stones will be changed into iron; that is, men once brutish and senseless will be changed into those materials which provide some use to the city. WHY HAVE THE DEEDS AND SAYINGS OF THE LORD BEEN ARRANGED IN WRITING IN FOUR BOOKS BY FOUR AUTHORS? — It was fitting that the acceptable year of the Lord, as the prophet says (Isa. 61:2), should be contained in four books as if in four seasons. For just as the year unfolds in four seasons, in such a way that they need one another, so too the deeds and sayings of the Lord have been set forth in four books, in such a way that each one needs the others; yet together they form perfect fullness. And as to why they were ordered by four writers, this was the reason: because the names of the seasons are different, so also the titles of the Gospels should be different. And if anything in their wording seems contrary, yet in meaning they do not differ, thanks to an interpretation suitably adapted to the matter: just as the seasons, although they clearly differ in name, in climate, and in the course of the stars, yet do not differ in the effects of the things they bring forth.

Or certainly it is to be understood of the Apostles, so that the order is: When masons, shepherds, ploughmen and vinedressers from the nations have been set over the churches, you, of whom it was said, A remnant will be saved (Rom 9:27), and, Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9), will be called priests and ministers of God, such as the sons of David also were, of whom Scripture says: And the sons of David were priests of God (2 Sam 8:18). These will eat the strength of the nations, and in their riches they will be admirable. For the crown of fathers is the glory of their children, and the progress of the people is the feast of the priests (Prov 17). Of riches of this kind Paul wrote to the Corinthians: I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ that in everything you have been made rich in him, in all speech and in all knowledge, even as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you, so that you lack nothing in any grace (1 Cor 1:4ff.). The strength of the nations is the triumph of the Martyrs, and we are proud in their glory, not with that pride which lies in vice, which God resists, that he may give grace to the humble, but with that which is taken for power and glory (Jas 4). Hence Moses too had a horned face (Exod 34), who could say: In you we shall toss our enemies with the horn (Ps 43 [44]:6). And for the pride of glory Aquila translated καὶ ἐν δόξῃ αὐτῶν πορφύρᾳ ἐνδύσεσθαι, that is, you will be clothed in purple, to show the badge of royal splendor.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what follows, Instead of double confusion and instead of shame they will praise their portion, which is not found in the Seventy, I think should be explained thus: Because you had a double confusion, both over the people of the Jews, which had departed from God, and over the nations, which served idols, you will see them, converted to the fear of God, praising their portion: without doubt the Lord, of whom the holy man also spoke: My portion is the Lord (Ps 72 [73]:26). No one can say this except one who has no other portion. Because, then, you had over them a double confusion and the shame of their sin, over which they themselves did not blush, therefore in their land, that is, in the land of the gentle and of the living, they will possess double things, since they will have believed both in the things present and in the things to come. And they will have everlasting gladness. For which we read in the Seventy, thus they will possess the land a second time. And everlasting joy will be upon their head, so that those who had possessed the land within the very narrow borders of Judea afterwards possess the whole world. Of this land the Father speaks to the Savior: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession (Ps 2:8).
Dialogues, Book 4, Chapter 25

About this twin glory it is written, "they will possess double in their own land." This is written concerning the souls of the saints, for single white cloaks are given to them, and it is said that they might have rest a short time until the number of their colleagues and brothers is filled up. So they take now single cloaks, but they will have double cloaks on the day of judgment; for the first is in the way of souls only, but later they will rejoice in the glory of souls and bodies together.
Commentary on Isaiah

This the Lord has granted, who loves the truth of judgment and hates robbery in burnt offering. For which the Seventy translated robbery from iniquity, as though there were some robbery that did not consist of iniquity. What he says, then, is this: God loves the poverty of the righteous more than the gifts of the rich, which come from robberies and iniquity.
Commentary on Isaiah

And I will give their work in truth, and I will strike an everlasting covenant with them. And their seed will be known among the nations, and their offspring in the midst of the peoples. All who see them will recognize them, that these are the seed which the Lord has blessed. LXX: And I will give their labor to the righteous, and I will set an eternal testament with them. And their seed will be known among the nations, and their descendants in the midst of the peoples. Everyone who sees them will recognize them, that these are the seed blessed by God. God, who loves righteousness and judgment and detests violent burnt offerings (for whatever comes from robbery he reckons as the hire of a harlot and the price of a dog), will himself give the labor of those who will possess the land a second time, and whom he will have crowned with a double gladness, to the righteous, or, as is better in the Hebrew, in truth: so that it is no longer, as in the Law, the shadow of the truth, but the truth itself. And he will strike an everlasting covenant, not such as he had given to Moses, which has passed away, but the covenant of the Gospel, of which Christ speaks: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Matt 24:35).
The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 3, Chapter 21

But it is one thing to show mercy for sins, another to sin for the sake of showing mercy, which cannot really be called mercy since it does not issue in sweet fruit, since it is embittered through the influence of a diseased root. For here the Lord rebukes such sacrifices through the prophet, saying, "I, the Lord, love justice and hate robbery with whole burnt offerings." … Such people also often withdraw from the poor what they give to God. But the Lord shows how strongly he disowns and censures such conduct.
Commentary on Isaiah

And then the apostolic seed will be known among the nations, and all future generations will receive the sowing of God's doctrine; by no means saying that in which the people of the circumcision formerly erred, saying: For what else does God seek but seed? Everyone who sees them will recognize at first sight that they are the seed which the Lord has blessed. For who would not recognize the people of God from their manner of life, their gentleness, continence, hospitality and all their virtues? And who, on the contrary, would not detest the bloody hands of Israel, against whom the Prophet prays, saying: Fill their faces with shame, O Lord (Ps 82 [83]:17)?
Commentary on Isaiah

Rejoicing I will rejoice in the Lord, and there has exulted my soul in my God: for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, and with the vesture of righteousness he has encompassed me, as a bridegroom adorned with a crown, and as a bride decked with her jewels. For as the earth brings forth its shoot, and as a garden makes its seed spring up, so the Lord God will make righteousness and praise spring up before all the nations. LXX: With joy they will be glad in the Lord; let my soul exult in the Lord. For he has clothed me with the garment of salvation, and has put about me the tunic of gladness. As a bridegroom with a mitre, and as a bride he has adorned me with a woman's finery, and as the earth putting forth its flower, and as a garden makes its seeds spring up, so the Lord God brings forth righteousness and praise in the sight of all the nations. The beginning of the passage according to the Seventy, who said, With joy they will be glad in the Lord, is joined to the end of the preceding passage. But according to the Hebrews it is the opening of another section, in which the Church is brought in answering the words of Christ: Rejoicing I will rejoice in the Lord, and my soul will exult in my God: by no means in the fathers, as the Jews gloried, saying, We are the seed of Abraham, and have never been slaves to anyone (John 8:33), but in God, as Scripture says: Now the multitude of the believers had one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32). And she gives the reasons for her gladness: For he has clothed me with the garment of salvation, and with the vesture, or tunic, of righteousness and gladness, which in Hebrew is called MAIL (מעיל), he has adorned and encompassed me. For as many of us as have been baptized in Christ put on Christ, and have the tunic of righteousness, who has been made for us holiness, righteousness and redemption (Gal 1). And she sets forth a likeness of two companies in the Church, the perfect and the beginners (1 Cor 1). The perfect she compares to the beauty of the bridegroom; the beginners she likens to the adornment of the bride. Paul was perfect, who, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and to be crowned, or, as Aquila translated, ἱερατευμένος στεφάνῳ, which in our language is bearing a crown as a priest, said by the authority of Christ speaking in him: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness (2 Tim 4:7). And in another place: As many of us, then, as are perfect, let us be thus minded (Phil 3:15). But he was a beginner in comparison with fullness, when he spoke in the person of beginners: When I was a little child, I spoke as a little child, I understood as a little child, I thought as a little child (1 Cor 13:11). And again: We see in part and we know in part, until that which is perfect comes (ibid., 9). And therefore he is likened to the adornment of the bride, who is adorned with a woman's finery, or, as the others translated, with vessels, or with her jewels.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.61:10-11

Generously he lays his hands on them and in order to crown with many fine gifts those petitioning he says, "Everyone who sees them will recognize that they are a seed blessed by God" and adds, "And they will rejoice in the Lord." And he immediately gives them joy. Here the person of the church is introduced full of joy as it sounds forth, "May my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me in a cloak of salvation and a tunic of rejoicing." The tunic of rejoicing means our Lord Jesus Christ. … They who have him like a garment gain not only salvation but also happiness and many joys. The Savior says, "The thief only comes to steal, but I have come that they may have life and have it abundantly." … Christ is, therefore, the tunic that is from heaven and from above, which if anyone takes he or she will be crowned with all beauty (spiritually understood) and with the distinction of good work—like a groom wearing a mitre or as a bride clothed in all beauty. For those in Christ, fortified for the spiritual mastering, are well-equipped and ready for every aspect of virtue. They are like brides on account of their fruitfulness, with the many-splendored beauty that comes from the brilliance of virtues. Thus spoke one of the holy prophets, highlighting those who made straight the well-led life, "For the fear of you, Lord, we have conceived in the womb and labored and brought forth the spirit of salvation that you have given throughout the world." Thus, the saints are compared with a bridegroom and bride on account of their fortitude and their fertility.… It shows that Christ shines out justice and gladness among the nations, just like flowers garland the earth.… For as the small and growing seed becomes a flower, just so was our Lord Jesus Christ proclaimed before the nations when it says also in the Song of Songs, "I am flower of the field, a lily of the valleys."
Commentary on Isaiah

And she sets forth examples of another comparison, of which the first refers to the bridegroom, the next to the bride. As the earth brings forth its shoot and is watered by the rains of heaven, and as a garden makes its seed spring up, which longs for the waters of springs and rivers, so, he says, the Lord will make righteousness and gladness spring up before all the nations: by no means before Israel, so as to strike down the haughtiness of the Jews, but before all the nations, which are gathered in the Church.
Retractions on Acts 8:4

Therefore, those who had been scattered returned, preaching the word of God. Instead of "the dispersed," the Greek text has "disseminated," that is, scattered like seed, for they were those about whom Isaiah said, "their offspring in the midst of the peoples" and about whom the Lord in the parable of the Gospel said, "the good seed is those sons of the kingdom." For this seed was disseminated throughout many regions, so that the harvest of faith that started in Jerusalem filled first Judea and Samaria and then the whole world. About these same ones, dispersed or rather disseminated through the next generations, it is said that they spoke the word not only to Jews but also to Greeks, and the noblest foundations of the new church in Antioch were planted through these.

n: Rest, as long as God grants me life, or till I behold the Saviour; or Cyrus, the figure of Christ. (Calmet) --- True preachers will not be silent on account of any threats, but will labour for the Church, 2 Timothy ii. (Worthington)

One. No profane historian mentions what Cyrus did for the Jews; but all the world knows how much Christ has favoured his Church. (Calmet) --- Name. Thou shalt be no longer the rebellious Jerusalem, but the spouse and chosen people, the Church of Christ. (St. Ignatius of Antioch, ad Magnesians) (St. Jerome)
Hand. Chaldean, "before." Hebrew, "by the protection."

Forsaken. Yet the synagogue was again rejected, at the death of Christ. The promises naturally relate to his Church. (Calmet) --- Inhabited. Protestants retain the Hebrew words Chephtsi-bah, "my delight in her," and Beulah, (marginal note) "married." (Haydock)

Dwell. Hebrew, "marry." They shall be attached to their country. --- Thee. He shall love thee as a bridegroom does one whom he has lately married. Christ never abandons his virgin spouse. (Calmet) --- Isaias speaks of some state of the Jews which has not yet taken place. (Houbigant)

Watchmen; priests and prophets, (Matthew ii. 1., and Psalm cxxxiii. 2.; Calmet) or angels. (St. Jerome; St. Bernard) --- The synagogue has been long destitute of guides, but the Catholic Church has an uninterrupted succession of watchful pastors. --- Mindful whose duty it is to remind him of his promises, and to recite the Church office. (Calmet) --- Hebrew mazcirim, monitors, 2 Kings viii. 16. (Haydock) --- In these faithful watchman the Church is always visible. (Worthington)

Hand; inviolably, Deuteronomy xxxii. 40. The Persians deemed this oath most sacred. (Calmet) --- Darius, just expiring, said to Polycrates, "By thee I give this right hand to Alexander," (Plut.[Plutarch?]) that he may revenge my death. --- Wine. The Church cannot be deprived of her faith or of her God.
People, that they may return to Judea, and be converted to Christ. (Calmet)
Work the redemption of mankind. (Haydock) --- Though Cyrus was a figure of Christ, he was as much beneath him as earth is below heaven, Zacharias ix. 9. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

For Zion's sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest, until her righteous one goes forth as brightness, and her savior is kindled as a lamp. And the nations will see your righteous one, and all kings your renowned one, and a new name will be called for you, which the mouth of the Lord has named. And you will be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a diadem of the kingdom in the hand of your God. LXX: For Zion's sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not leave off, until her righteousness goes forth as light, and her salvation burns as a lamp. And the nations will see your righteousness, and all kings your glory, and he will call you by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord will name. And you will be a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord, and a diadem of the kingdom in the hand of your God. The Lord and Savior had said, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me (Luke 4:18), up to the place where it is written, All who see them will recognize them, that these are the seed which the Lord has blessed (Isa 61:1). After this promise the Church answered, Rejoicing I will rejoice in the Lord, she who in the third of the Psalms of the Steps, in the person of the repentant people, sang joyfully: I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: we shall go into the house of the Lord (Ps 121 [122]:1). Now the person of the prophet is brought in, saying: For Zion's sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest. By day and by night, he says, I will not close my mouth, nor will my prayer ever be silent; but I will cry out so long, and join prayers to prayers, until he who was promised comes and enlightens the whole world with his brightness. Who it is whom he seeks, whose coming he longs for, he puts more plainly: Until her righteous one goes forth as brightness, and her savior is kindled as a lamp. Or, according to the Seventy: Until her righteousness goes forth as light, and her salvation burns as a lamp: the light which said in the Gospel, I am the light of the world (John 8:12); which, when it has been kindled in Zion and in Jerusalem, will by no means shine in Judea alone, but it will be said to her: The light that is in you has been kindled; the light that went forth from the Father has begun to burn within your borders, and it will enlighten all the nations (Matt 6).
Commentary on Isaiah

And all kings will see your renowned one, O Jerusalem and Zion: he who was begotten of your stock, who, lifted up in you on the gibbet, drew all men to himself; so that the nations see his righteousness, by which the Creator of all has had mercy on the nations, and kings his glory, by which he was glorified on the cross and subjected all kingdoms to his rule. Indeed she will no longer be called Jerusalem and Zion, but she will receive a new name, which the Lord will have given her, saying to the apostle Peter: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it (Matt 16:18). This title he derived from the name of the Lord, so that she is called the Lord's. And her people will no longer be called by the old name, Israel, but by a new one, that is, Christian.
Commentary on Isaiah

And she will be as a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord, and as a diadem of the kingdom in the hand of her God, when the throng of believers has crowned her, and the diadem of empire, which the Martyrs have adorned with the variety of their gems, is in the hand of God, that he may crown his Son with their victories. Hence the apostle Paul too said to the saints: My joy and my crown.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.62:3-5

"You will be a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God." For each holy soul, and the Church as a whole, that is, the communities of the saints, must be compared to a crown composed of many flowers, or to a royal diadem, shining with Indian stones, and having manifold excellence: for the heroic deeds of the saints are very many, and the manner of their boasts is not one, but many and various. And indeed the divine David introduces the Church of Christ clothed in gold-fringed garments, variegated, but the phrase "In the hand of the Lord," he says, that is, under the shadow of my hand I will cover you: and Christ himself somewhere concerning his own flock, that is, of the flock of those who have believed in him, says, that "No one will snatch them out of my Father's hand."
Commentary on Isaiah

You will no longer be called Forsaken, and your land will no more be called Desolate; but you will be called My-will-is-in-her, and your land Inhabited, for the Lord has been well pleased in you, and your land will be inhabited. LXX: And you will no longer be called Forsaken, and your land will not be called Deserted any more. For you will be called My will, and your land Inhabited. Instead of Zion and Jerusalem you will be called the Church and the Lord's; instead of Jews they will be called Christians. Nor will you be content with this end of names; but you who before were called forsaken, which in Hebrew is AZUBA (עזובה), will be called EPESI-BA (חפצי־בה), which means my will is in her; and your land, which before was called SEMEMA (שממה), desolate or deserted, will afterwards be called BULA (בעולה), which Aquila translated ἐσχημένη, Symmachus and Theodotion συνωκισμένη, the Seventy οἰκουμένη, all of which signify inhabited and possessed. It is a custom of the Hebrews always to give names to things from what befalls them: as Abram, who was first called high father, when he heard the promise, And in your seed all the nations will be blessed (Gen 12:3), was named father of many nations, that is, Abraham. And above, a name is given to the Lord Savior: Quickly take the spoils, swiftly plunder (Isa 8:1). The sons of Zebedee too, one of whom could utter the voice of thunder (Mark 3), In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1), were called BANEREEM (בני רעם), which means sons of thunder. But what follows, For the Lord has been well pleased in you, and your land will be inhabited, has been passed over by the Seventy; and it gives the reasons why she is called EPHSI (חפצי) and why she is called BULA (בעולה): because the Lord has been well pleased in Zion, and has made habitable her land, which before had been deserted through the error of the Jews. Or we may refer this same thing to the Church, which, possessed before by idols, had been deserted by God.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the young man will dwell with the virgin, and your sons will dwell in you. And the bridegroom will rejoice over the bride; your God will rejoice over you. LXX: And as a young man dwelling with a virgin, so will your sons dwell. And it will be that as a bridegroom is glad over a bride, so the Lord will be glad over you. The Apostle too says: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church (Eph 5:25). And when in another place he had set down the example, For this reason a man will leave his father and mother, and will cleave to his wife, and the two will be in one flesh, he added: This is a great mystery; but I speak in Christ and in the Church (Eph 5:31, 32). If, then, because of the shortness of the time, which is straitened, husbands ought so to have their wives as though they had them not, how much more holy will the union between the bridegroom and the bride be? This is the bridegroom of whom it is sung in the eighteenth psalm: And he as a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber (Ps 18 [19]:6). And this is the bride who is written of quite often in the Song of Songs, who has neither wrinkle nor spot (Song 4); whom Paul longs to present as a chaste virgin to one husband, so that she may be holy in body and spirit (1 Cor 2). Of her also, under the title of the beloved, the forty-fourth psalm sings: The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety (verse 10). As, then, the bridegroom rejoices in the bride, and the young man with the virgin, examples in which there is a holy union, so the Lord will be glad in her whose names have been changed.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.62:3-5

"As a young man marries a virgin." This is said to the church about the time in the beginning when it was constituted from the Jewish tribes. For the godly disciples were Jewish according to their human origin, but they stood out from the others and took the lead since they had apostolic status. Yet they retained a great love and respect for their religion, so that there seemed to be great affection toward it as a man ought to feel toward a young virgin bride when he lies with her.…
"The Lord will rejoice over you." … For the only-begotten Word of God came down from heaven to make the church fertile, which he presented to himself as a pure virgin, without spot or stain, wholly blameless. She received from him the seeds of the evangelical citizenship, became pregnant and gave birth, not with blood … but rather as one shaped to the beauty of the truth.
Commentary on Isaiah

Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set watchmen; all the day and all the night they will never be silent. You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no silence, until he establishes, and until he makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth. LXX: And upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set watchmen, all the day and all the night, who will never be silent, remembering the Lord: for there is none like you if he corrects, and he will make Jerusalem a joy upon the earth. The Prophet had said, For Zion's sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest, and the rest, up to the place where the passage has now ended: The bridegroom will rejoice over the bride; your God will rejoice over you. And he had promised that he would pray by day and by night that the Savior and Righteous One who had been promised might come and, like a lamp, light up the whole world. After this is brought in the person of God speaking to Jerusalem, that is, to the Church of the firstborn, and to her that was built in the Apostles and through the Apostles: Upon your walls I have set watchmen, whom we can take to be either the angels, or the Apostles and all her princes and teachers. They guard the walls of the Church, so that our adversary the devil, who as a roaring lion goes about and seeks how he may enter (1 Pet 5), may not find an occasion for laying waste the Lord's flock. These watchmen ought not to be silent by day or by night, neither in glad times nor in sad, but ought always to entreat the Lord's mercy, so that his flock and the walls of Jerusalem may be guarded and fortified by his help. Hence the word is directed to these same watchmen and teachers: O you who remember the Lord, and weary his mercy with your prayers day and night, take care that prayer is never silent in your mouth.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.62:6-9

Jerusalem … there is nothing like you; for there is nothing like you among us. Nevertheless, because whatever he has surpasses the human by the excess of glory, God outstrips us by the glory of his divinity in his being good and compassionate.…If you could correct yourself, Jerusalem, that is, if you could change to spiritual worship, if you could … take notice of the things written by Moses, if you would receive God's grace through faith and make his praise known through the earth, then you would make known the shining glory that is in Christ. This is the glory by which the Lord has sworn, since he has no one better to swear by. He has sworn "by his right arm," in that those who of old afflicted you with great injustice would no longer get in your way.
Commentary on Isaiah

Give him no silence, understand: the Lord; but be always troublesome, in season, out of season, and imitate the woman who importuned the hard judge. For if he laid aside the fierceness of his mind because of constant entreaty, how much more will the heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him? And you ought to ask for as long as it takes until Jerusalem, which fell in the Jews and is become an example and a curse, is turned into the praise of the whole world. And I wonder what the Seventy meant, instead of what is in the Hebrew, give him no silence, until he establishes and makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth, by saying what does not cohere in sense with what precedes: For there is none like you, if he corrects, and makes Jerusalem a joy upon the earth. Unless perhaps we fit it together with artful speech, so that it is said to the watchmen of the Church that there will be none like those who by their preaching have brought it about that Jerusalem is corrected and becomes the joy of the whole earth.
Commentary on Isaiah

The Lord has sworn by his right hand and by the arm of his strength: If I give your wheat any more as food to your enemies, and if the sons of strangers drink your wine, for which you have labored! For those who gather it will eat it and praise the Lord, and those who bring it in will drink it in my holy courts. LXX: The Lord has sworn by his right hand and by the strength of his arm: If I give my wheat any more to be food for your enemies, and if the sons of strangers drink any more your wine for which you have labored! But those who have gathered will eat it and praise the Lord, and those who have gathered will drink it in my holy courts. Almighty God, who had said to the Church, Upon your walls I have set watchmen, who will never be silent, and whom I bid never to cease praying until they obtain what they pray for, now swears by his right hand and the arm of his strength. Of this we have often said that it is our Lord and Savior, who according to the Apostle is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1). And he swears that the wheat and wine of Jerusalem will by no means go to be food for enemies, nor will foreigners enjoy her labor; but whoever have sown in tears will reap in joy, and those who have harvested, and, the chaff cast away, have gathered the pure grain into the barns, will themselves eat the labors of their hands, and extol the Lord with everlasting praise, and drink the wine in his holy courts. By these we understand either the many mansions with the Father, if we take it of the future blessedness in the kingdom of heaven, or certainly the churches spread throughout the whole world, in which we are planted, and afterwards shall flourish in the house of the Lord. And when he says, I will by no means give your wheat any more to your enemies, and foreigners will not drink your wine for which you have labored, he shows that the labor of the Jews and all their works were formerly possessed by demons, when they wavered between God and idols, when Elijah said to them: How long do you limp on both feet? If the Lord is God, follow him (1 Kgs 18:21). And according to the typical history which is narrated in the book of Judges, the Midianites came and laid waste its fruits as far as Gaza, so that the food of men was turned into the fodder of brute beasts (Judg 6). Now this is the wheat and this the wine which they will not eat except praising the Lord, and will not drink except in his holy courts; of which the Lord said in his passion: Amen, amen, I say to you, I will not drink of the fruit of this vine until I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father (Mark 14:25). These things are fulfilled in part in the Church, when the Lord says to his disciples: Drink, my friends, and be inebriated, brethren, for wine gladdens the heart of man (Ps 103 [104]). And it is drunk in full light and at midday by Joseph with his brothers (Gen 43). And it will be fulfilled more fully when the earth is inebriated with the blessings of the Lord. The wheat too, from which the heavenly bread is made, is that of which the Lord speaks: My flesh is truly food. And again of the wine: And my blood is truly drink (John 6).
Commentary on Isaiah

And lest the Jews should think this was said of themselves, there is joined to it: Lift up a signal to the nations, and to the peoples of the Gentiles, so that it is not the narrow confines of the one land of Judea that are called to salvation, but the message is made heard at the ends of the earth, so that the whole world may hear of the passion of the Creator of all.
Commentary on Isaiah

Pass through, pass through the gates, prepare the way for the people, make the road level, and pick out the stones; lift up a signal to the peoples. Behold, the Lord has made it heard at the ends of the earth: say to the daughter of Zion, Behold, your Savior comes; behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him. And they will call them a holy people, redeemed by the Lord. But you will be called a city sought out, and not forsaken. LXX: Go through my gates, and make a way for my people, and throw the stones off the way. Lift up a signal to the nations; for behold, the Lord has made it heard to the end of the earth. Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your Savior comes, having his reward with him, and his work before his face; and he will call it a holy people, redeemed by the Lord. But you will be called a city sought after, and not forsaken. He commanded the watchmen of the walls of Jerusalem, whom he had commanded before not to be silent and never to cease praying, to pass through the gates of Jerusalem and make a way for the people. This the half-Jews contend will come to pass in the last time, when, after the fullness of the nations, Israel is to be saved and return to the Lord. Others think it is to be fulfilled in the kingdom of heaven, when there will be true gladness, and each will receive according to his merit, and they will by no means see the Lord in humility, but will perceive him in the guise of a judge, when he comes upon the clouds with a multitude of angels to render to each according to his work. But we, following the explanation we have begun, can understand these things of the first coming as well, so as to say that the Apostles and apostolic men are commanded to go in and pass through the gates against which hell does not prevail, and to remove every hindrance from the way, so that the people may enter the Church of the Savior without any stumbling block. Hence John too cried in the wilderness: I am the voice of one crying in the desert, as Isaiah said: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight; every valley will be filled, and every mountain and hill will be brought low (John 1:23; cf. Isa 40:3, 4). And the same sense is now expressed in other words. The churchman chooses the stones, who softens all hardness from the heart of believers; of whom the same Baptist said: God is able from these stones to raise up sons to Abraham (Matt 3:9). Or, according to the Seventy, he throws the stones off the way who separates the unbelieving from the believers.
Commentary on Isaiah

Say, he says, to the daughter of Zion. She is called the daughter of Zion either because she first arose from the Jews, she of whom it says in the Song of Songs, The sons of my mother have fought against me (Song 1:5); or certainly she is called daughter because she received from God the name of adoption. For as many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God (John 1). And what is it that the masters and teachers are bidden to announce to the daughter of Zion? Behold, your Savior comes, who in the Hebrew is called Jesus. Hence Gabriel too, to Joseph: And you will call, he says, his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt 1:21). This Savior is the judge of all believers, to render to each according to his works: to the righteous rewards, to sinners everlasting punishments (Matt 16).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.62:11-12

This forecasts the coming of the Savior and our redemption by his coming. It also foretells the granting of riches to those who believe in him.… Concerning that which is new, that is, the church, it may be fittingly said that it is the daughter of Zion.… For whom does he order to proclaim good news to Zion? Those holy spiritual guides, of course, who took on the leadership role in the church and whose job it was to open the gates and to remove the stones from their midst. And what were they to announce? "That the Savior has come bringing his own reward and his work before his face." Two points are made, that which relates to his godhead and that which is a reward for us. Through both the Savior's glory becomes apparent.
Commentary on Isaiah

And he will call, he says, them, the Lord and Savior himself. Or, according to the Hebrew, they will call them, the Apostles and apostolic men, a holy people, and redeemed by the Lord, who have been redeemed by the blood of Christ. The city itself too will by no means be called forsaken, as she had been called before, whether among the Jews because of their trafficking, or among the nations because of their idolatry, but sought after, as it is said in Hebrew DRUSA (דרושת); so that, according to the growth and variety of their virtues, they may always receive new names.

n: Edom. Edom and Bosra (a strong city of Edom) are here taken in a mystical sense for the enemies of Christ and his Church. (Challoner) --- St. Jerome with reason finds it difficult to explain it of Christ, as it regards the Machabees. (Houbigant) --- The first six verses are applied to our Saviour's ascension, which excites the admiration of angels, Psalm xxiii. 7. Judas, the Machabee, the glorious figure of Christ, is introduced speaking in this and the following chapter. He conquered Idumea, (1 Machabees v. 3., and 2 Machabees x. 10.) and fought to save the people, 1 Machabees ix. 21. (Calmet) --- The highest order of angels asks this question, admiring the beauty of Christ, though imbrued in blood after his victory. (St. Dionysius, Hierar. vii.) (Worthington)
Press. Christ suffered, (St. Cyril) and punished his enemies, Apocalypse xiv. 19. Judas received God's sword from Jeremias, (2 Machabees xv. 15.) and liberated his people.
Me. I depended on the goodness of my cause, and on God's aid, chap. lix. 15. (Calmet)
Drunk with the wine of my fury, Psalm lxxiv. 9., and Ezechiel xxiii. 31. (Haydock)
I, Isaias; or rather the hero mentions what induced him to rise up, 1 Machabees xvi. 10. (Calmet) --- The Jews confess God's mercies. (St. Jerome)
Deny, or prove degenerate. (Calmet) --- God approves the conduct of the Machabees. (Haydock)
Presence, in high authority, Exodus xxxiii. 20. (Calmet) --- The angel guardian of the Church. Particular guardians also see God's face, Matthew xviii. (Worthington)
One; Moses, Numbers xiv. 29., and xx. 3, 12.
Flock. Psalm lxxvi. 21. --- One. Moses inspired by God. (Calmet)
Not, the road was so plain, Wisdom xix. 7. (Haydock)

Back. This is spoken by the prophet in the person of the Jews, at the time when for their sins they were given up to their enemies. (Challoner) --- Judas uses the same language at Maspha, 1 Machabees iii. 50. (Calmet)

Abraham, &c. That is, Abraham will not now acknowledge us for his children, by reason of our degeneracy; but thou, O Lord, art our true father and our redeemer, and no other can be called our parent in comparison with thee. (Challoner) --- Abraham is not able to save us. (Calmet) --- The patriarchs may justly disregard us, as degenerate children; yet we hope in God's mercies. Thus St. Jerome, &c., explain the passage, which does not favour the errors of Vigilantius and of Luther, who maintain that the saints departed do not know what passes in this world. St. Augustine (Cura xv.) shews the contrary, from the example of Lazarus, Luke xvi. They know each other, though they had not lived together, (St. Gregory, Dial. iv. 33.) and behold in the light of God what regards their clients. (St. Augustine, City of God xxii. 29.) We cannot decide how the martyrs do help those whom it is certain they assist. (St. Augustine, cura xvi., and contra Faust. xx. 21.; St. Jerome, contra Vigil.; St. Gregory, 3 ep. 30., and 7 ep. 126., &c.) (Worthington)

Hardened, &c. The meaning is, that God, in punishment of their great and manifold crimes, and their long abuse of his mercy and grace, had withdrawn his graces from them, and so given them up to error and hardness of heart. (Challoner) --- They had abused his patience, to sin the more. (Theodoret) --- The Jews are accustomed to attribute all to God, though they agree with us in reality God might prevent any sin. (Calmet) --- But he chooses to leave man to the free exercise of his liberty. He hardens (Haydock) "not by infusing malice, but by not shewing mercy; and those to whom he shews it not, are undeserving." (St. Augustine, ep. ad Sixt. cxciv. 14.) --- God is never the author of error. Man takes occasion from his indulgence to become obdurate. (St. Jerome) (Worthington)

Nothing; holding them in the greatest contempt. Epiphanes thought he should make them easily change their religion. His persecution lasted only three years and a half. --- Sanctuary. 1 Machabees i. 23, 49, 57., and iii. 45.
Name. We seem to have no distinction, temple, &c. (Calmet) --- Protestants, "We are thine. Thou never bearest rule over them. They were," &c. (Haydock)

f: AGAINST MARCION 4.40

He likewise, when mentioning the cup and making the New Testament to be sealed "in his blood," affirms the reality of Christ's body. For no blood can belong to a body that is not a body of flesh. If any sort of body were presented to our view, which is not one of flesh, not being fleshly, it would not possess blood. In order, however, that you might discover how anciently wine is used as a figure for blood, turn to Isaiah, who asks, "Who is this that comes from Edom, from Bosor with garments dyed in red, so glorious in his apparel, in the greatness of his might? Why are your garments red, and your clothing as his who comes from the treading of the full winepress?" The prophetic Spirit contemplates the Lord as if he were already on his way to his passion, clad in his fleshly nature; and as he was to suffer therein, he represents the bleeding condition of his flesh under the metaphor of garments dyed in red, as if reddened in the treading and crushing process of the winepress, from which the laborers descend reddened with the wine juice, like men stained in blood.
HOMILIES ON JUDGES 7

Blessed is that soul which, by the gore of blood poured out in martyrdom, casts down the airy throngs of demons that meet it. Blessed is he of whom, as he goes to heaven, the angels speak that prophetic word: "Who is this that comes up from Bozrah?"—that is, who ascends from the flesh to heaven. "Who is this that comes up from Bozrah, the redness of his garments?"—by the "redness of his garments" signifying the gore of blood. Blessed, then, are the souls that so follow Christ as Christ went before them. And therefore, because they so follow, they arrive even at the very altar of God, where the Lord Jesus Christ Himself is, the "high priest of the good things to come," "to whom is glory and power unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
On the Mysteries 7:36

The angels, too, were in doubt when Christ arose; the powers of heaven were in doubt when they saw that flesh was ascending into heaven. Then they said, "Who is this King of glory?" And yet some said, "Lift up your heads, O gates! And be lifted up, O ancient doors! That the King of glory may come in." In Isaiah, too, we find that the powers of heaven doubted.
Commentary on Isaiah

Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe, marching in the greatness of his strength. LXX: Who is this who comes from Edom, with tawny garments from Bosor? So beautiful in his robe, violence with strength. This whole passage, from the place where according to the Seventy it is said, Be enlightened, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you (Isa 60:1), up to the present passage, where it is said, Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?, many of our people refer to the end of the world, in which they contend these things are to be fulfilled, whether carnally or spiritually (for the opinion of most is divided). But we, since we read above in this same section too, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor, which the Lord and Savior, having read the volume of Isaiah in the synagogue of the Jews, showed to be fulfilled in himself, saying, Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your ears (Luke 4:21); and since it is now said of the same one that after his passion he ascended to the Father bloodied, we are compelled by necessity to take everything that is said of the first coming of the Savior. For it cannot be, as most of our people strive to make it, that things joined together in the works should be divided in time. Nor do we deny that it is a task of the greatest toil to join all these things together, and so to show that they are to be fulfilled spiritually at the consummation as to teach that they have already been fulfilled in Christ both according to the flesh and according to the spirit.
