Since, then, the Savior has come to the daughter of Zion, whose reward is with him and his work before him; and the righteous one has gone forth as brightness, and the Savior has been kindled as a lamp; and the bridegroom has rejoiced over his bride the Church, nay rather her God has exulted over her, who is himself both bridegroom and Lord: therefore, according to the assumption of the flesh and the passion of the cross, it is said to him: That your foot may be dipped in blood (Ps 67 [68]:24). And under the name of Judah it is prophesied in Genesis: Judah, your brothers will praise you; your hands will be on the necks of your enemies (Gen 49:8ff.), the sons of your father will worship you. Judah is a lion's whelp; to the prey, my son, you have gone up; resting, you have couched as a lion, and as a lioness: who will rouse him (Gen 49:8, 9)? And again: Binding his foal to the vineyard, and his she-ass, O my son, to the vine, he will wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape (ibid., 11). This is he whom the angelic powers, seeing him ascend bloodied to the Father, command the other angels, and hear from them: Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the king of glory will come in. Who is this king of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle (Ps 23 [24]:7, 8). And again: The Lord of hosts, he is the king of glory (ibid., 10). We have set this down beforehand to show that the present passage too agrees with the other testimonies. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs too: My kinsman is ruddy and white (Song 5:10): ruddy in the passion, white in the resurrection. The angels, then, terrified by the strangeness of the thing (for the mystery of the passion and resurrection of Christ, according to the apostle Paul (1 Cor 2), had been unknown to all past generations), ask: Who is this who comes bloodied from the land of Edom? For EDOM (אדם) is expressed in our language as both earthly and bloody. With dyed garments from Bozrah? Many, falling into a pious error, think this is to be understood of the Lord's flesh, that is, BASAR (בשר); but if this word signified flesh, it would be written with the letter SIN in the middle, whereas now it is written with SADE, and means strong and fortified. This we take either of Jerusalem (Ps 59 [60]:11), which formerly was surrounded with very strong walls, in which the Lord suffered; or of hell, of which it is written in the fifty-ninth and in the hundred and seventh psalm: Who will lead me into the fortified city (Ps 107 [108]:11)? in which the souls of the dead are shut up, and which is surrounded with very strong guards. It must be known also that according to the history BOSRA (בצרה) is not in Edom but in Moab. There follows: So beautiful in his robe, marching in the greatness of his strength. Of him the forty-fourth psalm too sings: Beautiful in comeliness above the sons of men. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty. In your comeliness and your beauty set out, proceed prosperously, and reign (Ps 44 [45]:3-5). For which the Seventy translated, violence with strength. What sense this has, let the prudent reader inquire.

I who speak righteousness, and am a champion to save. LXX: I who speak righteousness, and the judgment of salvation. The Lord answered the angels who asked: Do you ask who I am, who ascend bloodied to the heavens, and that the blood with which I am sprinkled has given me not unsightliness but beauty? I am he to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5). Of him the Psalmist too said: O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son (Ps 71 [72]:1). I who speak righteousness, so as to repay evil to the evil and good to the good; who came to fight against the adverse powers, and to preach remission to the captives, and to free the bound from prison, so that the adversaries may feel punishment and the captives liberty.
Commentary on Obadiah

Furthermore, because Idumea means both earthly and, on account of the color red, can also be understood as bloody, for this reason the Savior, carrying back to the Father the victory over the world, when the angels were crying out: Open your gates, O princes, and the king of glory shall enter in. And in Isaiah, astonished, they were asking: Who is this who comes up from Edom, with garments tawny from Bozrah, so beautiful in a white robe? And one spoke to him face to face: Why is your clothing red, and your garments like those of men who tread in the winepress? He himself speaks in triumph, displaying the palms of his cross: I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there is no man with me.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.63:1-7

For he appeared to the powers above not only in the form in which he came for us, that is, as a human, but also showing the signs of his passion. Thus, we say that after his resurrection from the dead the marks of the nails and the other things of his wounds were marked on the holy flesh.… So that the angels asking each other might say, "Who is this?" He considers and replies to them, "I speak justice and the judgment of salvation." He calls "justice" the divine and good news-bearing message or every just word that the Lord speaks. And the judgment of salvation refers to the judgment we receive. He indicated the world also to Satan, who was accusing it, and he saved those burdened by terrible greed. And he expelled the rebel and foreign usurper from among them, saying, "Now is the judgment of this world."
Commentary on Isaiah

Why then is your clothing red, and your garments like those of men treading the winepress? LXX: Why are your garments red, and your clothing like that of men treading the winepress, full and trodden down? Where it now says red, the Hebrew reads EDOM (אדום). So above too, where Edom is written, it is not the name of a place but a word for blood. And again the angels ask and say: We have learned that you are he who speaks righteousness, and that the salvation of all has been placed in your judgment. Now we wish to know why your garments are as if dyed with new wine; or what cause there was for you to stain with blood the tunic that was woven from the top and cannot be torn, and that had from the virgin's womb such whiteness as no fuller on earth could make? For mercy befits you more than cruelty, whiteness more than gore. To them the Lord answered, not with one little verse as before, but with many words, so as to teach everything to those who did not know, lest they be compelled to ask again.
Epistle LXII:7

And does not also the Holy Spirit, speaking in Isaiah, testify the same thing concerning the passion of the Lord, saying, "Why are your vestments red and your garments as from treading the wine press full and well-trodden?" For can water make vestments red, or is it water that is trodden by the feet in the winepress or forced out by the press? The mention of wine is placed there, indeed, that in the wine the blood of the Lord may be known and that which was afterward manifested in the chalice of the Lord might be foretold by the prophets who announced it. The treading and pressing of the winepress are also spoken of, since wine cannot be prepared for drinking in any other way unless the cluster of grapes is first trodden and pressed. Thus, we could not drink the blood of Christ unless Christ had first been trodden on and pressed, and unless he had first drunk the chalice of which he should also give believers to drink.
Catechetical Lecture 13:27
Who is that who for shame is clothed in scarlet? For Bosra among the Hebrews has such a meaning.
Commentary on Isaiah

I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there is no man with me. I have trodden them in my fury, and trampled them in my wrath; and their blood has been sprinkled upon my garments, and I have polluted all my clothing For the day of vengeance is in my heart; the year of my redemption has come. I looked round, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to give aid. And my own arm saved for me, and my indignation itself helped me. And I trampled the peoples in my fury, and made them drunk in my indignation, and brought down their strength to the earth. The Seventy, instead of what we have said, I have trodden the winepress alone, translated full and trodden down, which is rather to be read with the preceding passage than taken as the beginning of the following one. The rest they translated thus: And of the nations there is no man with me; and I trampled them in my fury, and broke them like earth, and brought down their blood to the earth, and I have defiled all my garments. For the day of retribution has come upon them, and the year of redemption is at hand. I looked, and there was no helper; I considered, and there was none to give aid; and my arm rescued them, and my fury came on, and I trampled them in my wrath, and brought down their blood to the earth. For the winepress, which in Hebrew is called GETH (גת), Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, PHURA (פורה). But Symmachus is better in this place, and we have followed him. For the word PHURA is ambiguous, and generally signifies both winepress and flask. Something must be said, then, about the winepress: that according to the custom of holy Scripture it is sometimes put for the vengeance and punishment of sinners, sometimes for the gathering of new fruits. It is put for penalties and torments when Jeremiah, lamenting the overthrow of Jerusalem in Lamentations, says: The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah; therefore I weep (Lam 1:15, 16). In a good sense the eighth and the eighty-third psalms are inscribed 'for the winepresses'. Of these we shall speak in their own places, if life goes with us, the Lord granting it. This winepress, in which both punishments for the evil and rewards for the good are trodden out by the Savior, he alone trod, and he had no helper. For neither angel nor archangel, Thrones, Dominions, nor any of the heavenly powers assumed a human body, and suffered for us, and trampled and crushed the adverse powers, but only he who speaks in the psalm: Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed (Ps 11 [12]:1); so much so that even the most confident apostle Peter, most firm in the truth of faith, fled terrified with fear, nay even denied the Lord (Matt 27). And what follows, And their blood has been sprinkled upon my garments, and I have polluted all my clothing, must by no means be understood as though we believed that demons and the adverse powers have blood; but everything is to be taken tropologically, when the most merciful God, in order to instruct his people and free them from the bonds of captivity, is compelled to strike the enemies.
SERMON 372:2

Each quality, though, that is both beauty and strength, had been seen and understood by Isaiah, when he said, "Who is this who is arriving from Edom, the crimson of his garments from Bozrah, so handsome in the robe of his garment with strength?" So this prophet, who called him both handsome and strong, knew him as bridegroom and giant.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the day of vengeance, he says, is in my heart; the year of my redemption has come. Of this we read above too (cf. Isa 61), in a good sense, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution to our God; and now it is taken both in a bad and in a good sense. In a bad sense: For the day of vengeance is in my heart. In a good sense: The year of my redemption has come; so that at the time when the adversaries are punished, the people of God might be set free, nay rather redeemed by the precious blood of the Lamb, who in the Apocalypse of John is said to have been slain. Of this day of retribution Moses too prophesied by the Holy Spirit: And he will render vengeance to his enemies, and will repay those who hate him. I looked round, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to give aid (Deut 32:41).
Commentary on Isaiah

He had also said in the psalm: And I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none, and for one who would comfort me, and I found none (Ps 68 [69]:21). For he, though he was in the form of God, did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself (Phil 2), taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross; and therefore he gave him a name above every name, so that he might save for himself by his right hand those who believe in him, and his indignation, which was against the adversaries, might set the people of God free. Or he rescued the believers by his arm, and no longer put off his fury; and he brought down their blood to the earth, either that of the demons, τροπικῶς, or certainly the blood of the Jews; for which the other translators rendered contention; who strove with all zeal that they might let the bound people go.
Commentary on Isaiah

I will remember the mercies of the Lord, the praise of the Lord for all that the Lord has rendered to us, and for the multitude of good things to the house of Israel, which he has bestowed on them according to his indulgence and according to the multitude of his mercies. LXX: I have remembered the mercy of the Lord; I will remember the mighty works of the Lord in all that he has rendered to us: the Lord, a good judge to the house of Israel, will repay us according to his mercy and according to the multitude of his righteousness. Now that the passage on the coming of the Savior has been completed, the first coming, as we judge, the second, as most suppose, in which is understood the voice of one judging, nay rather fighting and slaughtering the adversaries of himself and of his people, and in which he is described as bloodied and victorious, another περικοπή begins, in which the Prophet speaks in the person of the people, recounting God's benefits toward it and the hardness of its own heart, on account of which Jerusalem was given over to burning and Israel to captivity. This the Jews refer to the Babylonian times. But we have shown by order and by reason that it is said of the present time, in which they serve the Romans, and Israel having been shut out, the crowd of the nations has taken its place. Let us run, then, through each member of the discourse, and set them forth briefly, so that the exposition may not be rambling. Pressed by the weight of evils, I have hope in nothing else but in the mercy of God, who shows mercy to thousands of those who love him, and extends his mercy to those who know him. From this it is shown that the mercy of the Lord comes to the aid of those who love and know God. For it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom 9). And unless the Lord builds the house and guards the city, he who builds and guards it watches in vain (Ps 126 [127]). For he himself will grant strength, so that we may do valiantly and be able to say: My strength and my help, and my refuge in the day of my evils (Jer 16). These evils in the present place we ought to take not for vices and sins but for distresses. And as for what follows according to the Seventy, I will remember the mighty works of the Lord in all that he has repaid me, for which the Hebrew contains the praises of the Lord, let us understand signs and miracles, for which 'mighty works' is often put, as there: My glory I will not give to another, nor my mighty works to graven images (Isa 42:8). And elsewhere: They will proclaim his mighty works in the islands, that is, either to the nations of the whole world, or to the churches, which are founded on a firm mass, and are struck rather than overthrown. Sometimes virtue is by no means taken for strength and miracles, but for good conduct, as in that saying of the Apostles, of Peter: Supply virtue in your knowledge (2 Pet 1:5); and of Paul: If there is any virtue, and if any praise (Phil 4:8). In accordance with which it is said in another place too: Better is barrenness with virtue. The first understanding of virtue befits God, the second men. And instead of what we have translated, For all that the Lord has rendered to us, which can be taken both in a good and in a bad sense, Symmachus set it down more plainly as a repayment of good things, saying: For all things in which he has done good to us, and for the multitude of goodness which he has shown toward the house of Israel. For which the Seventy translated: The Lord, a good judge to the house of Israel, has repaid us according to his mercy and according to the multitude of his righteousness. No one can say this except one who understands that he justly bears what he suffers. Thus in the seventy-second psalm, whose opening is, How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart, the prophet speaks in the person of those who are troubled by the judgments of God: But my feet were almost moved, my steps had well nigh slipped, seeing the peace of sinners, and the rest, up to the end of the psalm. Hence the apostle Paul, who had known the Lord as a good and righteous judge, speaks with confidence: There is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the righteous judge will render to me; and not to me only, but also to all who love the coming of our Lord and Savior (2 Tim 4:8). Nor is there any difference, as the heretics would have it, between good and righteous, for the same Apostle writes: So the law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (Rom 7:12), so that goodness is understood as the genus and righteousness as the species. Wherefore he writes to the Romans: For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous man; for perhaps for a good man someone would dare to die (Rom 5:7).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.63:7-10

"For the Lord is a good judge to the house of Israel." For he is not harsh but benevolent or good. For the task of a harsh judge takes the way of interrogating those sinners like ones standing accused. The good judge has mercy on them as weak ones. Since the judge is good, he will act according to his mercy, that is, he will temper his anger and will work in mercy in making the complaint. For there is so much justice in him that he will prosecute justice to the letter. Therefore, it is fitting that he will not let Israel go unpunished, but rather he will mingle his wrath with kindness, as I said. For a remnant will be saved.…Now he will save them himself, finding nothing worthwhile in them, but only because he loved them and cared for them. This is a strong visible sign of his unequaled philanthropy and the calmness of divinity. For he saved them from the house of slavery, carried them and raised them up. This is what he was talking about at the beginning of Isaiah, "I have borne and raised sons."
Commentary on Isaiah

And he said: Surely they are my people, sons who do not deny; and he became their Savior. In all their tribulation he was not troubled, and the Angel of his face saved them; in his love and in his indulgence he himself redeemed them, and he bore them and lifted them up all the days of the age. But they provoked him to anger and afflicted the spirit of his Holy One and he was turned to be their enemy, and he himself fought them down. LXX: And he said: Is it not my people? Sons will by no means reject. And he became their salvation out of all their tribulation; not an envoy nor an angel, but he himself saved them, because he loved them and spared them; he himself redeemed them, and took them up, and exalted them all the days of the age. But they did not believe, and they embittered his Holy Spirit; he was turned to be their enemy, he himself fought against them. Where we have translated, In all their tribulation he was not troubled, the word which in Hebrew is LO, and is an adverb of negation, for not, can also be read as he himself, so that the sense is: In all their tribulation he himself was troubled, that is, God; so that he himself bore not only our sins but also our tribulations. For he bears our infirmities and grieves for us. Further, the Seventy put down something else which is not found in the Hebrew, not an envoy nor an angel, but he himself saved them, of which we shall speak in its place. So God, who is a righteous judge to the house of Israel, and who tempers the severity of righteousness with the mercy of one who judges, said: I have begotten sons and exalted them, and they have spurned me. Yet because they are my people, and have once been named sons, they will not perish for ever; if they cease to spurn and deny me, they will find a Savior, because in all their tribulation he himself was troubled. Or, he was not troubled, so that he forsook them for a little while, and compelled them, stripped of his help, to pray. Or certainly, he by no means troubled them, but on the contrary, when others persecuted them, he was their helper, and sent his angel to free them from danger. Or, according to the Seventy, he did not wish to save his people through angels and prophets and other holy men, but he himself came down to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, to carry back the sick sheep on his shoulders, and to find the drachma that had been lost, and to run joyfully to meet the prodigal son as he returned. For this reason the bride says in the Song of Songs: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: not through the Patriarchs, Moses and the Prophets, but let him assume my body, let him dwell in my flesh, let the Word become flesh, and so let him kiss me, dwelling in me, that he may be Emmanuel. Not as an envoy, then, nor as an angel, but he himself will save those who have received salvation, not by the merit of their works but by the love of God. For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.
Commentary on Isaiah

But if the prudent reader should answer in silent thought, Why have many not been saved, if he himself saved them, and loved and spared his sons, and redeemed them with his blood, and took them up and exalted them once assumed?, a clear reason is given: But they did not believe, and they embittered his Holy Spirit, or the Spirit of his Holy One, which in Hebrew is CADESO (קדש). God, then, willed to save those who desired it, and he called them to salvation, so that their will might have its reward; but they would not believe. Otherwise it is written of John too: There was a man sent from God, whose name was John; he came to bear witness to the light, that all might believe through him (John 1:6). Nor is he at once at fault if many would not believe; but the will of the one who came was this, that all should believe and be saved. And if whoever has exasperated and afflicted the Holy Spirit, or the Spirit of his Holy One, that is, of Christ, exasperates God, it is because the Holy Spirit is of the same nature with the Father and the Son. Wherefore the Apostle commands: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you have been sealed (Eph 4:30). This Holy Spirit withdraws from a body subject to sins, and wisdom does not enter a perverse soul (Wis 1). Hence David too, conscious of his sins, prayed that he might not lose the Holy Spirit, saying: And do not take your Holy Spirit from me (Ps 50 [51]:13). And so that we may know that everyone who exasperates the Holy Spirit offends God, and from a friend becomes an enemy and a foe, the apostle Peter speaks more expressively in the Acts of the Apostles: Why have you agreed to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to men but to God (Acts 5:9). This is the Holy Spirit of whom the Lord said in the Gospel: If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to be with you for ever, the Spirit of truth (John 14:15, 16). Of him we find also in the Wisdom which is written under the name of Solomon: For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from foolish thoughts (Wis 1:5).
Commentary on Isaiah

And he remembered the days of the age, of Moses, of his people. Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock? Where is he who put in its midst the Spirit of his Holy One? Who led Moses by the right hand with the arm of his majesty; who divided the waters before them, to make for himself an everlasting name; who led them through the depths like a horse in the desert that does not stumble. Like a beast going down into the plain, the Spirit of the Lord was its leader; so you led your people, to make for yourself a name of glory. LXX: And he remembered the ancient days, he who brought up from the land the shepherd of the sheep. Where is he who put the Holy Spirit in them? Who led Moses by the right hand, the arm of his glory. So he led his people through the mighty water in his sight, to make for himself an everlasting name. He led them through the deep like a horse through the wilderness, and they did not labor. And like cattle through the plain the Spirit came down from the Lord, and was their leader: so you led your people, to make for yourself a name of glory. The Lord, who from a protector became the adversary of the people of the Jews, who provoked his Holy Spirit to anger, and who fought them down, himself remembered the ancient days, when Moses prayed for them in the wilderness, saying: Either forgive them this offense, or if you do not, blot me out of the book which you have written (Exod 32:31, 32). Isaiah, then, remembering the ancient history, says: Where is that Moses who brought them up out of the Red Sea? Where is the shepherd of the sheep? Where is he who labored with the other shepherds of the Lord's flock? Who obtained the Spirit of God by his prayer and entreaties, and put it in the Lord's flock? Or certainly it is to be understood thus: Where is that mercy of the Lord with which he once had pity on his people, so as to grant them the grace of the Holy Spirit too; who led Moses his servant to the right-hand side, not to the left, with the arm of his majesty; who divided the waters before them, to make for himself an everlasting name, so that his power might be told even to the present day?
Commentary on Isaiah

For he led his people through the boundless depths of the waters like a horse through the wilderness, and like cattle over the plain, and the Spirit of the Lord was its leader, that is, of the Lord's flock (Exod 14). By Spirit here we ought to understand the angel who was the leader of the people of Israel, according to what is written: Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire (Ps 103 [104]:4). And in the Epistle to the Hebrews: These are ministering spirits, sent forth to serve for the sake of those who are to possess salvation (Heb 1:14). Let us consider whether what is written in the Acts of the Apostles, The Spirit of the Lord caught away Philip, and the eunuch saw him no more (Acts 8:39), ought to be taken of an angel. There are some who maintain that the angel did these things in the Holy Spirit. We run through what is plain so as to dwell on what is more obscure.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5. 63:11-14

Where is he who put in them the Holy Spirit, that is, he who established the divine and saving Spirit in them? For the Spirit descended from the Lord and guided them, saying, "David divinely uttered, 'Send forth your word and heal us.' " For the Lord is the Spirit; he works through the Spirit that is of the same nature. Where then is he? For they forgot him and did not seek him, when they clearly should have remembered him and loved him. Where is he who led Moses by the right hand? Moses was great, famous and lofty in dignity. And this is shown in that it says [Moses] led them, working through [the Spirit] who is the right hand of God.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.63:11-14

It seems that Isaiah is making mention here of the resurrection of Christ, the Savior of us all. "He who has gone up" is said in place of "he who has risen"—from the earth—the chief shepherd of all, not just that he was rising up from the dead, but in the sense that he was clearly distinct among human beings. For he became like one of us, undergoing birth from a woman according to the flesh—he who was the only-begotten Word of the Father.
Commentary on Isaiah

Look down from heaven, and see from your holy dwelling and that of your glory. Where is your zeal and your strength? The multitude of your bowels and of your mercies toward me have held themselves back. For you are our father; and Abraham has not known us, and Israel has been ignorant of us. You, O Lord, are our father, our redeemer from of old is your name. LXX: Turn from heaven, and see from your holy house and that of your glory: where is your zeal and your strength? Where is the multitude of your mercies and of your compassions, with which you bore with us? For you are our father, because Abraham has not known us, and Israel has not known us. But you, O Lord our father, deliver us: from the beginning your name is upon us. You who granted such great things to the people as the preceding discourse has related, so that you even deemed us worthy of the fellowship of your Spirit, now too look down from heaven and see our works, if indeed they are worthy of you. Why do you turn away your face from us? Now heaven is called the holy dwelling and the house of his glory (Ps 43 [44]), according to that saying: Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet (Isa 66:1); and in another place: He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them; and: To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven (Ps 122 [123]:1). Not that almighty God, who holds heaven in his palm and the earth in his fist, is shut in by any place, but that the things which are holier are called his place and dwelling. Thus Solomon, who built the house of God, says in prayer to him: The heavens of heavens and the earth do not suffice you (Sir 16:18). And in the Lord's Prayer it is said: Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth (Matt 6:10). Wherever, then, the will of God is done, that is his dwelling and the house of God. As for what follows, Where is your zeal and your strength?, let us discuss it by that testimony in which God, through Ezekiel, speaks to Jerusalem, who had followed her lovers: Now I will not be angry with you, and my zeal has departed from you (Ezek 16:42). And the sense is: Because we have sinned and you have begun to hate us, your zeal has departed from us, the zeal which does not depart when he speaks through Zechariah: I have been zealous for Zion and Jerusalem with great zeal (Zech 1:14). Hence he says too in what follows: And I will be angry over the nations that have gathered against her round about. When zeal departs, the strength of God departs too, and the affection of a father's bowels is overcome, while the incredible mercy of God is conquered by the greatness of our sins, so that he who could not bear to see me oppressed holds himself back from helping me.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.63:15-17

Here onwards the prophet prays for every nation, and in the person of the Israelites he presents his supplication. He prays that God will withhold his wrath from them and cease rebuking them and in a forgiving manner subdue Israel's desertion; for there was no one on earth for them other than the true God, one having a glorious home in heaven, their father. Although God is said to dwell in heaven, this should not be thought of him in physical terms. For we say that God is not in a place or to be circumscribed; he is simple, and without a body he fills all things.
''Catechetical Lectures, Lecture 7''

For Thou art our Father, though Abraham be ignorant of us, and Sarah travailed not with us, need we inquire further on this point? And if the Psalmist says, Let them be troubled from His countenance, the Father of the fatherless, and Judge of the widows, is it not manifest to all, that when God is called the Father of orphans who have lately lost their own fathers, He is so named not as begetting them of Himself, but as caring for them and shielding them. But whereas God, as we have said, is in an improper sense the Father of men, of Christ alone He is the Father by nature, not by adoption: and the Father of men in time, but of Christ before all time, as He saith, And now, O Father, glorify Thou Me with Thine own self, with the glory which I had with Thee before the world was.
Commentary on Isaiah

For you, he says, are our father, you who are the creator of all. Abraham does not know us, and Israel is ignorant of us, because we have offended you, nor do they recognize as sons those whom they perceive not to be loved by their God. A sudden question arises: why did he set down Abraham and Israel, that is, Jacob, and leave the name of Isaac unspoken (Gen 32)? To this we shall answer that, when the beginning and the end are set down, the middle too is named. Or thus: Abraham was called to faith from the nations, and according to the character of his former and his subsequent condition received a change of name. Jacob too reached it only by much toil, to be called Israel. Hence too Abraham had three wives, and Jacob four; but Isaac kept his ancient name from beginning to end, and, signifying the chastity of the Church, was content with one wife. Those, then, who pray for a change from sinners to a better state take on the likeness of those to whom joy succeeded after sorrow. And this is all that they ask: that, since he is their father and has deigned to give them this name, he may not forget his sons, lest through them the name of God be blasphemed among the nations.
Commentary on Isaiah

Why have you made us stray, O Lord, from your ways? You have hardened our heart, so that we did not fear you. Return for the sake of your servants, the tribes of your inheritance. As if for nothing they have possessed your holy people; our enemies have trodden down your sanctification. We have become as in the beginning, when you did not rule over us, nor was your name called upon us. LXX: Why have you led us astray, O Lord, from your holy way? You have hardened our hearts, so that we did not fear you. Return for the sake of your servants, for the sake of the tribes of your inheritance, that we may possess a little of your holy mountain; our adversaries have trodden down your sanctuary; we have become as from the beginning, when you did not rule over us, nor was your name called upon us. The Epistle which Paul writes to the Corinthians, though it is written to the people of one city, according to the variety of its inhabitants, that is, of saints and sinners, now praises them, now corrects them, now teaches, now rebukes; it calls them to continence; it does not refuse marriage; it draws them back from idolatry; it instructs them about the resurrection; it stretches out a hand to second marriage, lest it give place to fornication. We have said this so that we may understand that the present passage too, which is woven entirely out of the prayer of the people entreating God, belongs either to the righteous or to sinners, and that they now praise the Lord, now raise a question with the Lord and refer their own fault to God. Hence after the rest they say this too: Why have you made us stray, O Lord, from your ways, or led us astray from your way? You have hardened our heart so that we did not fear you? Not that God is the cause of error and of hardness, but that his patience, as he waits for our salvation and does not correct those who do wrong, seems to be a cause of error and hardness. Hence, when he is vehemently angry with some, he withholds his hand from striking and says: I will not punish your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your brides when they have committed adultery (Hos 4:14). For he scourges every son whom he receives, and he strikes in order to amend (Heb 12). Thus of those who have by no means lost the name of sons, but are drawn back to repentance through punishment, he says: I will visit their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with scourges; but my mercy I will not take from them (Ps 88 [89]:33). For there is a sorrow that leads to life, and there is a sorrow that leads to death. Hence the sinner too says in the psalm: You have made our paths turn aside from your way, and have humbled us in the place of affliction (Ps 43 [44]:19). And for forty years the people wander in the desert, so that they may not find their former way nor return to the Egyptians (Num 32). In Hosea too the paths of Jerusalem are hedged in and closed with thorns, so that she may not follow her lovers, and, compelled by necessity, may return to her former husband (Hos 2). And God is said to have hardened the heart of Pharaoh, so that he would not let his people go, and so that he might be afflicted with ten plagues (Exod 4). This question Paul discussed most carefully to the Romans (Rom 9), and we have touched on it in a certain work.
Commentary on Isaiah

As for what is set down above, Why have you made us stray (Isa 63:17)?, in what sense it is to be taken Jeremiah teaches most fully: You have led me astray, O Lord, and I was led astray; you took hold of me, and you prevailed (Jer 20:7). For while you promise me mercy, and like a merciful father you conceal your severity, and like a skilful physician you hide the sharpest knife so as not to frighten the sick man before you heal him, you have made me careless. For this reason God says of Jerusalem too: Behold, I will lead her astray, and I will make her like a desert, and set her like a land without water, and I will speak to her heart; and I will give her possessions from there, and the valley of Achor to open understanding (Hos 2:14, 15). Let us consider the order of each thing: he leads her astray, and makes her deserted and without water, so that she may suffer thirst for the virtues. After she has said, My soul has thirsted for you, how many ways my flesh for you (Ps 62 [63]:2), then he will speak to her heart and console her as she mourns. And he will give her a possession from there, that is, from the repentance and sorrow which works salvation. And the humility of her troubled heart (for this is what the valley of Achor means) opens her understanding, so that she may not be ignorant of her Creator.
Commentary on Isaiah

Return, he says, O Lord, or turn us back, for the sake of your servants, Abraham and Israel, who have not known us, or whom we believe to be among the people. For as if for nothing, and without any toil, our adversaries have possessed your holy people. Or, turn us back so that, according to the Seventy, we may possess a little of your holy mountain, since we cannot possess the whole of your mountain; so that when we have had a part we may come to its fullness and contemplate the glory of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1); of which it is said in this same prophet: In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be manifest (Isa 2:2).
Commentary on Isaiah
Our enemies, he says, have trodden down your sanctuary. There is no doubt that he means the Temple, which the victorious Romans trod down.
Commentary on Isaiah

And we have become as in the beginning, before we were called in Abraham, and while we were in Egypt, having no God, nor kings, nor princes, nor Prophets, nor the Law of the commandments of God (Hos 3); all of which was fulfilled after the passion of the Lord, and is being fulfilled today. For since they said, His blood be upon us and upon our children (Matt 27:25), an everlasting curse remains, and God does not rule over them, nor is his name called upon them, since they are by no means called the people of God.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.63:18-19

The church is often called "the holy mountain" in the sacred Scriptures, and those from Israel are only a small part of it. For if they had demonstrated faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the company of the faith would have sprung from them for the most part and the Gentiles would have been added in to complete the number. But because of the serious disobedience of the Jews, the people of the church were consequently largely drawn from the nations, and these provided the majority; the former people were few in number (for a remnant shall be saved), so only in small measure will they be called on to the holy mountain, that is, into the church.

n: Presence, as at Sinai, Exodus xix. 16., and Judges v. 4. Judas [the Machabee] continues to pray. (Calmet) --- The faithful sigh for Christ's coming. (Haydock) --- All good people desired it most fervently. (Worthington)
They. Septuagint, "As wax melts before the fire, so also fire will burn the adversaries, and thy," &c. (Haydock) --- Burn. Sparks of fire seemed to proceed from it.
Bear. Exodus xx. 18. Hebrew, "expect." Judas [the Machabee] appeared victorious, when the nation was prostrate.

Thee. Never was deliverance more unexpected or miraculous. St. Paul quotes this passage, to shew the wisdom manifested in the incarnation, 1 Corinthians ii. 9. It is commonly applied to the glory of heaven.

Thee. The little band of Judas was sincerely attached to the Lord, 2 Machabees i. 3. --- Sinned. This excited thy anger. Yet thou wilt shew mercy. Sin is often put for punishment. (Calmet) --- Vau means also, "for, and, yet." Protestants, "for we have sinned." But we follow St. Jerome and the Vulgate. (Worthington)

Unclean: leper. (Grotius) (Leviticus xiii. 45.) --- Justices. That is, the works by which we pretended to make ourselves just. This is spoken particularly of the sacrifices, sacraments, and ceremonies of the Jews, after the death of Christ, and the promulgation of the new law. (Challoner) --- The justice which is under the law is stated uncleanness, when compared with evangelical purity, Philippians iii. 8. --- "If any one after the gospel....would observe the ceremonies of the law, let him hear the people confessing that all that justice is compared to a most filthy rag." (St. Jerome) --- The good works which are done by grace, and not by man alone, cannot be said to be of this description. They constitute the internal glory of man, and God will one day crown these his gifts. Of ourselves indeed we can do nothing, and the works of the Mosaic law will not avail, as St. Paul inculcates; but those works, point out the saint, which are preformed by charity with faith in Christ. This justice is not imputed only, but real; and shews where true faith exists, according to St. James. Thus the apostles explain each other. (Haydock) --- Woman. Septuagint, "of one sitting down;" like Rachel, Genesis xxxi. 35. Symmachus, "lying-in." Aquila, "of proofs." Grotius, "like a plaster on a sore, which is thrown away." Such were Alcimus, &c. (Calmet) --- To practise (Haydock) the Jewish rites would now be sinful. (Menochius)
Of thee; to remove thy indignation, like Moses, Jeremias, (vii. 15.) &c. See Ezechiel xiii. 5.
Desolate, under Antiochus Epiphanes, 1 Machabees i. 31., and iv. 38. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

O that you would rend the heavens and come down! At your presence the mountains would flow down. As the burning of fire they would melt away; the waters would burn with fire, so that your name might be made known to your enemies; at your presence the nations would be troubled. When you do wonders, we shall not endure them; you came down, and at your presence the mountains flowed down. LXX: If you open heaven, trembling will seize the mountains because of you; and they will melt as wax melts before the fire, and fire will burn up the adversaries; and your name will be manifest among the adversaries; at your presence the nations will be troubled. When you do glorious things, trembling will seize the mountains because of you. Since our enemies have trodden down your sanctuary, and we have become as in the beginning, when your name was not called upon us, therefore we entreat and say: O that you would rend the heavens and come down, and that you who are always promised would at some time fulfill your promises. This was said at the time when the Savior had not yet come, nor had yet assumed from the virgin's womb, out of our nature and substance, the man whom he would save; so that, as we have borne the image of the earthly, we may bear the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 15). If you did this, they say, and the heavens, or heaven, were opened, at the coming of your majesty the mountains would flow down, or trembling would seize the mountains, and they would be consumed as wax is consumed before the fire. To Ezekiel too the heavens were opened, and he saw a great vision (Ezek 1). And Moses as well, in the blessings of Deuteronomy, prays: May the Lord open to you his good treasure, the heaven, to give you blessing (Deut 28). And in the Gospel (Matt 3) John the Baptist is related to have seen the heavens opened, and the Holy Spirit coming down upon the Lord in the form of a dove. The mountains which at the coming of the Lord, of whom it is written, God is a consuming fire (Deut 4:24), will be consumed and melt like wax, are the adverse powers and all who raise themselves up against the knowledge of God. Of them it is sung in the ninety-sixth psalm too: He saw, and the earth was shaken. The mountains melted like wax at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of the whole earth (Ps 96 [97]:4, 5). For if you came down and fulfilled your promises, the waters of the sea would melt away (according to Symmachus), and that fire would consume all their saltness. Of this it is written in another psalm too: As smoke vanishes, so let them vanish; as wax is consumed before the fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God (Ps 67 [68]:2). And this is to be noted, that when the waters of the sea have been consumed by the divine fire, then the name of the Lord Savior will be made known to his enemies; of whom it is said in the sixty-seventh psalm: The tongue of your dogs, from the enemies, by him; so that him whom they had not perceived through his benefits they may come to know through the overthrow of their city and their own captivity. And at his presence the nations will be troubled, or, as is said more expressively in the Hebrew, will be moved: so that those which before were immovable may come to salvation. And when he has done wonders, and shown in the Gospel the signs which he once showed in Egypt and in the wilderness, they will confess that they cannot bear the glory of his coming, or that trembling has seized the mountains. And beautifully, according to the Hebrew, as though those who above had entreated, O that you would rend the heavens and come down! At your presence the mountains would flow down, had been heard, they afterwards add: You came down: you, the Word, were made flesh and dwelt among us, truly Emmanuel, which means God with us. And therefore at your presence all the mountains flowed down, of which we spoke above. The Hebrews expound this passage thus: The fire will burn up the wicked just as the waters boil with the heat of fire; for by AMASIM (חמסים) they wish to be understood not consumption and melting, as the others translated, but the wicked.
ON THE TRINITY 5:33

But it may be argued that the Apostle was not inspired by the Spirit of prophecy when he borrowed these prophetic words; that he was only interpreting at random the words of another man, and though, no doubt, everything the Apostle says of himself comes to him by revelation from Christ, yet his knowledge of the words of Isaiah is only derived from the book. I answer that in the beginning of that utterance in which it is said that the servants of the true God shall bless Him and swear by Him, we read this adoration by the prophet: "From everlasting we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen God, except Thee, and Thy works which Thou wilt do for them that await Thy mercy." Isaiah says that he has seen no God but Him. For he did actually see the glory of God, the mystery of Whose taking flesh from the Virgin he foretold. And if you, in your heresy, do not know that it was God the Only-begotten Whom the prophet saw in that glory, listen to the Evangelist: "These things said Esaias, when he saw His glory, and spake of Him." The Apostle, the Evangelist, the Prophet combine to silence your objections. Isaiah did see God; even though it is written, "No one hath seen God at any time, save the Only-begotten Son Who is in the bosom of the Father; He hath declared Him," it was God Whom the prophet saw. He gazed upon the Divine glory, and men were filled with envy at such honour vouchsafed to his prophetic greatness. For this was the reason why the Jews passed sentence of death upon him.
Commentary on Isaiah

From of old they have not heard, nor perceived with their ears; the eye has not seen, O God, besides you, what you have prepared for those who wait for you. You have met him who rejoices and does righteousness in your ways; they will remember you. LXX: From of old we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a God besides you, and your works, which you will do for those who wait for mercy; for he meets those who do righteousness, and they will remember your ways. A paraphrase of this testimony the apostle Paul, as a Hebrew of the Hebrews, takes from the authentic books in the Epistle which he writes to the Corinthians, not rendering word for word, which he altogether disdains to do, but expressing the truth of the sense, which he uses to support what he wished (1 Cor 2). Let the ravings of the apocrypha, then, fall silent, which on the pretext of this testimony are thrust upon the churches of Christ. Of them it can truly be said that the devil sits in ambush with the rich in the apocrypha, to kill the innocent. And again: He lies in wait in the hidden place like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor (Ps 9 [10]:8). For the Ascension of Isaiah and the Apocalypse of Elijah contain this testimony. And on this pretext, and through many things of this kind, silly women of the Spains, and above all of Lusitania, laden with sins, led away by various desires, always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth (2 Tim 3), were deceived into taking up the monstrosities of Basilides, of Balsamus and Thesaurus, of Barbelo too and Leusibora, and of the remaining names. Of these the apostolic man Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons and martyr, writes most carefully, explaining the origins of many heresies, and above all of the Gnostics, who through Mark the Egyptian deceived noble women, first of the Gauls about the Rhône, then of the Spains, mixing pleasure with fables and claiming for their ignorance the name of knowledge (Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 1). What the people says in the present passage is this: that they have never come to know, either by ears or by eyes, what God prepares for his saints in the future; that he meets those who do righteousness and remember his ways. Further, according to the Seventy, they say that they have never known any other God besides him who is truly God, nor seen such and so great works of another, which he will do for those who wait for his mercy and do righteousness and remember his ways. And how is it written, No one has ever seen God (John 1:18), and again, No one sees my face and lives (Exod 33:20)? God, then, is by no means set forth in words, nor is he visible to the eyes; but he is seen by those of whom it is written: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:5.64:4-5

The divine is invisible in nature. "For no one has ever seen God," as it is written. But God can be seen by the eyes of faith from those things that happen without explanation and beyond speech. For the invisible things, since the foundation of the world, are clearly understood by the things that are made, that is, his heavenly power and godhead. For he is often recognized through those in whom he works the good and makes a sign of the serenity dwelling in him, marvelously saving those deprived of all hope, and he extends a saving hand from the ground to those lying on the earth. In like manner, they who make this prayer speak, "From the foundation of the world we have not heard nor have we seen such a God, except now for you and you alone. For you give mercy to those who wait for you and put their hope in you, refining and making them to fit together, those who work for your justice and who are mindful of your paths, that is, all who carry out the things you want. For we say that his commandments are the ways of the Lord."
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, you are angry, and we have sinned; in them we have always been, and we shall be saved. And we have become as one unclean all of us, all our righteousnesses as the cloth of a menstruous woman. And we have all fallen like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, have carried us away. LXX: Behold, you are angry, and we have all sinned; therefore we have gone astray, and we have all become as unclean, all our righteousness as the cloth of a woman who sits apart; and we have fallen away like leaves because of our iniquities; as the wind will carry us away. The order is inverted. It is not because you are angry that we have sinned, but because we have sinned that you are angry. And because we have sinned, you are angry with us, O Lord; therefore we have gone astray and left the right way. Or, according to the Hebrew: we who have always been in sins shall be saved only by your mercy, we who of ourselves are unclean; and whatever righteousness we seem to have is compared to the cloth of a woman who sits apart, or of a menstruous woman. For this Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, EDDIM (עדים), which Symmachus translated κυουσῶν, that is, of women in childbirth; Aquila μαρτυριῶν, that is, of testimonies: when in the first marital union the blood proves a bride a virgin. And we have fallen away, he says, like leaves from the trees, which because of our iniquities are scattered by the blasts of the winds. Here it must be considered that the righteousness which is in the Law is called uncleanness in comparison with the purity of the Gospel. For what was formerly glorified has not been glorified, because of the surpassing glory. Hence the apostle Paul too, who had fulfilled everything according to the righteousness which is in the Law, says that he counted all things as loss, that he might gain Christ (Phil 3), and because of the surpassing knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose sake he reckons all things as dung, that he may gain Christ and be found in him, not having his own righteousness, which is from the Law, but the righteousness which is from God through the faith of Christ. For there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness (Eccl 7), if after the truth of the Gospel he wishes to practice the shadows of the Law, and not to pursue justly what is just. Hence, according to the most wise Solomon, every man seems righteous to himself when he lives in the Law; to whom the Lord says in the Gospel: You are those who justify yourselves before men (Luke 16:15). Fleeing this, Paul says: I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not justified by this (1 Cor 4:4). But out of sin, the righteousness of God, of which the same Solomon speaks: Understand true righteousness. There is, then, another righteousness which has no truth, and this is the true righteousness, of which again it is said in the Gospel: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt 5:6); which many prophets and righteous men desired to see, and did not see (John 8). But Abraham saw this righteousness and was glad, by no means following the letter that kills, but the spirit that gives life. Nor is it surprising to say this of men, when even the stars, compared with the righteousness of God, are not clean, and he has found out something perverse in his angels (Job 4:18; 15:15). If anyone, then, after the Gospel of Christ and the coming of the Son of God, observes the ceremonies of the Law, our tutor, let him hear the people confessing that all that righteousness is compared to a most filthy cloth; to which Esther too compares her diadem, which was the badge of royal power, and which she wore by no means willingly but of necessity: You know my necessity, that I detest the sign of my pride, which is upon my head in the days of my display; I abhor it like a menstruous cloth, and I do not wear it in the days of my quiet (Esth 14:16).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:6.64:6-7

Some translators try to alter the meaning of this passage.… For it is not, they say, that the divine anger was the cause of their misdeeds, but that because they misbehaved, God was angry. For they are afraid lest God's anger be thought of as the effector of sins. I think it ought to be said that there is no condemning the divine anger, if those receiving it were insufficiently motivated to flee the attack of sin. As long as the Savior is pleased in us, let us flee sin and forcefully leave the filth of vices and with increase be crowned in spiritual success.… For God is the Lord of powers.… Just as the kind clemency from above shows us how to be strong and brave for the resistance of evil, by the same reason when we fall under divine wrath, it is necessary that we bow in servile fashion.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 9.38

It is hence that Isaiah laments bitterly, saying, And we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities like the wind have taken us away. And there is none that calleth upon Thy Name, that stirreth up himself to take hold of Thee. Now any of the righteous may sometimes be able to resist the visitations of a present judgment, by the merits of a derived innocency, but they have no power by their own goodness to rid mankind of the woes of the death to come. Therefore let the holy man bethink himself whereunto the human race has run out, let him cast his eye on the woes of eternal death, which it is plain that human righteousness can never withstand, let him see how frowardly man has offended, let him see how severely the wrath of the Creator is directed against man, and let him call for the Mediator between God and man, God and Man in one, forasmuch as he beholds Him destined to come long after. ... For the Redeemer of Mankind, who was made the Mediator between God and Man through the flesh, because that He alone appeared righteous among men, and yet, even though without sin, was notwithstanding brought to the punishment of sin, did both convict man, that he might not sin, and withstand God, that He might not smite; He gave examples of innocency that He took upon Him the punishment due to wickedness.
Commentary on Isaiah

There is none who calls upon your name, who rises up and takes hold of you. You have hidden your face from us, and have dashed us down in the hand of our iniquity. LXX: And there is none who calls upon your name, and who, remembering, lays hold of you. For you have turned away your face from us, and have handed us over because of our iniquities. Because we have fallen away like leaves from the trees, which the wind scatters when they are dried up, therefore no one has been found who would call upon your name, and, rising from the ruin of his iniquities, would lay hold of you or take hold of you, and say with the bride: I have found him whom my soul sought; I will hold him and will not let him go (Song 3:4). The wind is put in the Scriptures in three ways: either for the greatness of temptations, or for perversity of doctrine, or simply for the wind by which the clouds are gathered and the air is driven together into clouds. Of temptations there is that saying of the Gospel: The rivers came, the winds blew, and beat upon that house, and they could not overthrow it, for it had been founded upon rock with a firm mass (Matt 7:27). Of perversity of doctrine: That we may not be carried about by every wind of doctrine in the wickedness of men (Eph 4:14). Of the wind simply: And they could not sail, for the wind was against them (Mark 6:48): not that this too cannot be understood tropologically, but that it only provides a likeness for the present sense. For when the Lord turns his face away from us, we are dashed down in the hand of our iniquity, or we are handed over to temptations because of our sins. From this we learn that iniquity too has hands, and so have all sins, which desire to hold us tightly bound. Hence too death and life are in the hand of the tongue (Prov 18); and the holy man prays: Let not the foot of pride come to me (Ps 35 [36]:12). But we, since the Lord has turned his face away from us, knowing what is written, Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved (Joel 2:32), let us call upon his name and say: I have made my sin known to you, and I have not covered my iniquity. I said, I will declare my iniquity against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my heart (Ps 31 [32]:5). And at once we shall have the Lord answering: I have blotted out your iniquities like a mist, and your sins like a cloud (Isa 44:22); and we shall say: Show your face, and we shall be saved (Ps 79 [80]:4), so that we may by no means be slaves of sin, but your servants. For everyone who commits sin is its slave (John 8).
Commentary on Isaiah

And now, O Lord, you are our father, and we are clay; and you are our fashioner, and we are all the works of your hands. Do not be angry, O Lord, exceedingly, and do not remember iniquity any longer. Behold, look: we are all your people. The city of your Holy One has become a desert; Zion has become a desert, Jerusalem desolate. The house of our sanctification and of our glory, where our fathers praised you, has been made a burning of fire, and all our desirable things have been turned into ruin. Will you hold yourself back over these things, O Lord, will you be silent, and afflict us exceedingly? LXX: And now, O Lord, you are our father; but we are clay, we are all the works of your hands. Do not be angry with us, O Lord, too much, and do not remember our sins in time. And now look, for we are all your people; the city of your Holy One has become a desert, Zion; Jerusalem as a wilderness, for a curse; the house of our sanctuary and glory, which our fathers blessed, has been burned with fire, and all our glorious things have fallen. And over all these things you have held back, O Lord, and you have been silent, and have humbled us exceedingly. If we consider our merits, we must despair. But if we consider your mercy, you who scourge every son whom you receive, we dare to pour out prayers (Heb 12). For you are our father, who deigned to say: Israel is my firstborn son (Exod 4:22). And although we are clay, and the works of your hands, and you are our fashioner, and the vessel cannot answer the potter as to why it was made thus or thus, yet, knowing that we are sons, we dare to say: Do not be angry, O Lord, exceedingly. We do not forbid wrath, nor do we seek any further your patience, through which we have stored up for ourselves wrath on the day of wrath. But this we ask: that you be not angry with us exceedingly, that in the time of vengeance and punishment you do not remember our iniquity, but rather look upon your people, which was once called your people.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:6.64:8-9

They entreat God insistently concerning his removal from friendship with them. Since they had come to this situation through their many sins, they wove their prayers with great skill. For since they are unable to mollify the one who could save them with their own works and blameless lives, they now take another route. They ask him as the creator of his own work to be reasonable and sparing with those who were brought into being and life by him.… "We are not unaware that we have offended you; we confess that we showed ourselves to deserve judgment and acted savagely towards the Son."
Commentary on Isaiah

And have mercy on the city of your sanctuary, in which your name has been called upon. This city is called Zion and Jerusalem, which the rush of the river makes glad, and in which there was once the watchtower of the virtues and the vision of peace (Ps 43 [44]). Your house too, that is, the Temple of our sanctification and glory, in which our fathers praised you, has fallen into ruins and ashes, and has been destroyed by devastating fire; so that no victims are offered in it, no Passover is celebrated, nothing is done of the ceremonies which you commanded to be done; but all our desirable things have been turned into ruins. Since, then, this is how things stand, will you, O Lord, hold back your mercy over these things, and be silent toward the adversaries who blaspheme, and afflict and humble us, not in the usual manner but exceedingly? All this the Jews think was fulfilled in the times of the Assyrians and the Babylonians. But we, in accordance with what follows in the person of the Savior, I appeared to those who did not ask for me; I was found by those who did not seek me (Isa 65:1), refer everything to the time of the Roman victory, which Josephus, the writer of the Jewish history, sets forth in seven volumes, to which he gave the title The Capture of the Jews, that is, περὶ ἁλώσεως. And it is superfluous to discuss in words what lies open to the eyes, since all their desirable things have been turned into ruins, and the Temple, celebrated throughout the whole world, has become the dunghill of the new city, which was called by its founder Aelia, and has passed into a dwelling-place of owls; and in vain they say daily in their synagogues: Over all these things, O Lord, you will hold back, and you will afflict us and humble us exceedingly.
Commentary on Isaiah

We can refer these things to the Church, or to the soul of a holy man, which can rightly be called a watchtower and vision of peace when the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit have dwelt in it. But if, through our fault or that of the people, such a Zion has been forsaken by the Lord, it will at once lie open to the burning of the fiery arrows of the devil; for all who commit adultery, their hearts are like an oven. And when the coolness of chastity has been driven out, the flame of lust will rage in the temple of God, so that whatever in us was formerly glorious and renowned may collapse, be destroyed and perish. And then is fulfilled what is said in the Psalms: They have burned your sanctuary with fire; they have profaned on the earth the tabernacle of your name. This he alone can quench out of whose belly flow rivers of living water.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 5:6.64:10-12

The defendants speak of the damage in the soul and that they have been caught in their sins; they are like leaves blown about by every wind and, scattered all over, now remember the external misfortunes that came on them. And the destruction of Jerusalem is deplored along with the temple's burning. For after the Savior's crucifixion, these things were fulfilled.

n: Me. God answers the preceding prayer, and announces the rejection of the synagogue, alluding to the armies which prevailed in the days of the Machabees. --- Not. St. Paul explains this of the conversion of the Gentiles, Romans x. 20. (Calmet) --- It cannot regard the Jews, who are spoken of in the next verse. (Worthington)
Gardens, to the impure Venus and Adonis. --- Bricks, to the Manes. (Calmet) --- Tegula porrectis satis est velata coronis Et sparsæ fruges parvaque mica salis. (Ovid, Fast. x.)
Idols: to have dreams, (Strabo xvi.) and commit impurities. --- Broth of swine's flesh, which was prohibited, Leviticus xi. 7.
Unclean. Thus acted the hypocritical Pharisees. --- Smoke. A just punishment of those who had sought the smoke of human applause.
Bosom: good measure, Luke vi. 38. Rewards and punishments will be eternal.
Hills. Some offered sacrifices to God, others to idols; both unlawfully. (Calmet)
Whole. The good grain is preserved amid the general corruption. (Haydock) --- A few of the Jews were chosen to believe in Christ.
Mountains of Judea, (Deuteronomy iii. 25.) which the captives shall recover, as a figure of those who shall embrace the Christian faith.
Plains. Hebrew Sharon, in the land of Basan. --- Achor, near Jericho, called after Achan, (Calmet) who perhaps was more correctly styled Achor, Josue vii. 26., and Osee ii. 15. (Haydock)

Fortune. Hebrew, "Gad," the sun, Genesis xxx. 11. --- Upon it. Symmachus, "without me." Septuagint, "to fortune." Hebrew, "to Meni," the moon, or Queen of heaven, Jeremias vii. 18., and xliv. 17. (Calmet)
Chosen. Free-will is clearly expressed, as rewards are, ver. 13. (Worthington)
Servants; Christians, (Calmet) particularly the elect. (Haydock) --- When the Romans approached Jerusalem, the Christians retired to Pella, and had plenty. (Houbigant)

Execration. They can wish to be preserved from nothing worse. --- Name. The faithful shall be no longer called Jews. (Calmet) --- They shall be hated, while the name of Christian shall point out God's servants. (Worthington)

Amen, or "of truth." False gods shall be neglected. They shall not swear by them, as formerly, Sophonias i. 5. --- Christ usually adopted the asseveration, Amen, Amen, to enforce his truths. (Haydock)

New earth, in eternity, (Clarius) or here indeed, (2 Peter iii. 3., &c.; Houbigant) having purified the former by the general conflagration, which many assert will take place at the end of 6,000 years. (St. Jerome; St. Augustine, &c.) At the return of the captives, the country flourished again under the Machabees; (ver. 18.; Grotius) or rather the gospel changes the face of the earth, chap. lxvi. 22. (Calmet) (Forerius) --- After the resurrection the qualities, and not the substance, of the world, will be changed. (Worthington)

Fill up. To die soon was deemed a misfortune, Psalm liv. 24., and Exodus xx. 12. Virtue is the measure of the Christian's life, and God will reward those who labour even late, Matthew xx. 13. --- Accursed. This age will not be spared. Both just and wicked shall be immortal in eternity. (Theodoret)
A tree. Septuagint, "of the tree of life," Jeremias xviii. 8. (Calmet) --- Continuance. Hebrew, "My elect shall long enjoy the works," &c. (Haydock) --- They shall not build for others to enjoy.
In. Hebrew, "for trouble." Chaldean, "death." Septuagint, "malediction." The children shall not be cut off; and baptism shall secure their salvation.

Straw. People of the most perverse tempers shall become mild by the influence of the gospel, and shall dwell together in perfect concord. (Calmet) --- Food, according to the sentence, Genesis iii. 14. (Menochius) --- The devil's power is abridged, chap. xi. 6. (Calmet) --- The proudest Gentiles are converted, and adopt the mild manners of Christians, in fasting and mortification. (Worthington)

f: Dialogue with Trypho, Chapter CXIX

And after that Righteous One was put to death, we flourished as another people, and shot forth as new and prosperous corn; as the prophets said, "And many nations shall betake themselves to the Lord in that day for a people: and they shall dwell in the midst of all the earth." But we are not only a people, but also a holy people, as we have shown already. "And they shall call them the holy people, redeemed by the Lord." Therefore we are not a people to be despised, nor a barbarous race, nor such as the Carian and Phrygian nations; but God has even chosen us and He has become manifest to those who asked not after Him. "Behold, I am God," He says, "to the nation which called not on My name." For this is that nation which God of old promised to Abraham, when He declared that He would make him a father of many nations; not meaning, however, the Arabians, or Egyptians, or Idumaeans, since Ishmael became the father of a mighty nation, and so did Esau; and there is now a great multitude of Ammonites. Noah, moreover, was the father of Abraham, and in fact of all men; and others were the progenitors of others. What larger measure of grace, then, did Christ bestow on Abraham? This, namely, that He called him with His voice by the like calling, telling him to quit the land wherein he dwelt. And He has called all of us by that voice, and we have left already the way of living in which we used to spend our days, passing our time in evil after the fashions of the other inhabitants of the earth; and along with Abraham we shall inherit the holy land, when we shall receive the inheritance for an endless eternity, being children of Abraham through the like faith. For as he believed the voice of God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness, in like manner we having believed God's voice spoken by the apostles of Christ, and promulgated to us by the prophets, have renounced even to death all the things of the world. Accordingly, He promises to him a nation of similar faith, God-fearing, righteous, and delighting the Father; but it is not you, "in whom is no faith."
On the Incarnation of the Word 38:2

Who then, one might say to the Jews, is he that was made manifest? For if it is the prophet, let them say just when he was hid, afterward to appear again. And what manner of prophet is this, who was not only openly made manifest from obscurity but also stretched out his hands on the cross? None surely of the righteous, save the Word of God only, who, incorporeal by nature, appeared for our sakes in the body and suffered for all.
Commentary on Isaiah

They sought me who before did not ask for me: they found, who did not seek me. I said: Behold me, behold me, to a nation that did not call upon my name. LXX: I appeared to those not seeking me: I was found by those who did not ask for me. I said: Behold me, in a nation that did not call upon my name. To the prayer of the people mingled with complaints, in which it had said: Why have you made us err, O Lord, from your way: you have hardened our hearts, so that we did not fear you (Isa 63:17)? there answers, as the Jews would have it, God the Father; as we hold, the Lord and Savior: So far am I from being harsh and cruel, I who prefer the repentance of the sinner to his death, and do not repel repentant sons, provided they have kept the dignity of their name, that I wish to save even strangers (Ezek 33). For those who did not seek me, and could not say: We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the Law, and the prophets, Jesus (John 1:45), to these very ones I appeared; of whom the Prophet also testified elsewhere: Those to whom nothing was announced concerning him will hear, and those who have not heard will understand (Isa 52:15). But you, who meditate on the law of God day and night, boast in vain of a repentance whose works you do not do. Hence the Evangelists and apostles, always wishing to strengthen the coming of the Lord with testimonies of the Old Testament, said: That what was spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled (Matt 1:22). The centurion was not seeking the Lord, and he heard from the Lord: Not even in Israel have I found such faith (Luke 7:9; Matt 8:10). The Syrophoenician woman did not know the utterances of the Prophets, and she is praised by the voice of the Lord: O woman, great is your faith. The nobleman (John 4), who in Greek is called βασιλικὸς, and whom, from the royal court, we can more correctly render palatine, found healing not only for his son but for his whole house. And what is said according to the Hebrew: They sought me who before did not ask, refers to the same sense: that those who formerly had no knowledge of God afterwards seek the Lord and come to know him by revelation; he who was also revealed to Paul while he was persecuting the Church of believers (Acts 9). And he says to the apostle Peter: Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, for flesh and blood have not revealed it to you, but my Father who is in heaven (Matt 16:17). Him Moses too was seeking when he said to God: If I have found favor with you, show yourself to me openly, that I may see you (Exod 33:13). Looking for the reproach of Christ as greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, while he longed for the recompense of things to come, he contemplated in his mind the invisible God as if he saw him. Of whom it is also read in the Psalms: The hope of all the ends of the earth, and in the sea far off (Ps 64 [65]:6). And in Genesis: He himself shall be the expectation of the nations (Gen 49:10). And what follows: I said: Behold, I am: to a nation that did not call upon my name (Exod 3:14), agrees with that sense: He who is has sent me to you. Who, though he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal to God, etc. (Phil 2); but, calling forth the nations of the whole world, he made one nation of his name, that of the Christians.
Commentary on Isaiah

I have spread out my hands all the day to an unbelieving people, who walk in a way not good, after their own thoughts. LXX: I have spread out my hands all the day to an unbelieving and contradicting people, who have not walked in the good way, but after their sins. This which was said above: I appeared to those who did not ask for me: I was found by those who did not seek me, the apostle Paul, writing to the Romans, when he had expounded it of the person of the nations, added: But to Israel he says: I have spread out my hands to an unbelieving and contradicting people (Rom 10:21); a people which, when it was overcome by the benefits of the Lord and saw signs beyond what a man can do, said: This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of the demons (Luke 11:15). And again: You are a Samaritan and have a demon (John 8:48). And again: though you are a man, you make yourself God (John 10:33). And elsewhere: This man is not from God, for he does not keep the sabbath (John 9:16). And many other things, which it would take long to string together. Finally, when he on the cross stretched out his hands to the unbelieving people and said: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do (Luke 23:34), they on the other side said: Ah! you who destroy the Temple and in three days build it up: let him come down now from the cross, and we believe him. He saved others, himself he cannot save (Matt 27:40). Of him Simeon too, holding the little child in his arms, prophesied: Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the rising of many, and for a sign that will be spoken against (Luke 2:34). At Rome the Jews say to Paul: Concerning this sect it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against (Acts 28:22). We can also take the spread-out hands of the generosity of the giver, in that he denied them nothing when they asked, but at once restored health to the leper who asked (Matt 8), and the man blind from birth received eyes (John 9), and thousands of the people, hungry in the desert, besides children and women, were satisfied (Matt 14). The spread-out hands also signify the mercy of a parent eager to receive his children into his bosom. But they, on the contrary, walked in a way not good, and followed their own thoughts. To them the Lord speaks through the Prophet: Turn your foot away from the rough way (Prov 4:27). For they had loved strangers, and like a harlot had said: I will go after my lovers (Hos 2:5). And leaving the good way, which says in the Gospel: I am the way (John 14:6), they walked on the broad and spacious way that leads to death, and followed their own thoughts; and the Prophet, shunning these, entreats the Lord: From my hidden faults cleanse me, O Lord, and from those of others spare your servant. If they have not ruled over me, then I shall be spotless (Ps 18 [19]:13, 14). And the Apostle teaches that those who did not have the knowledge of God are handed over to a reprobate mind and to evil works, to do the things that are not fitting (Rom 1). But let us say with the voice of the Psalmist: Lead me in the right way (Ps 138 [139]:24).
Commentary on Isaiah
