Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my seat, and earth the footstool of my feet. What is this house that you will build for me, and what is this place of my rest? All these things my hand has made, and all these things have come to be, says the Lord. LXX likewise. Lest we should understand the holy mountain as Zion and be covered with the Jewish error, who think that Jerusalem is to be built up and that all the things the Lord promises are to be fulfilled there carnally, he takes this suspicion away from us, and sets down the testimony which Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, used against the contentiousness of the Jews (Acts 7). Solomon built him a house, without doubt for God; but the Most High does not dwell in things made with hands, as the Prophet says: Heaven is my throne: but earth is the footstool of my feet. And Paul in the same volume: God, who made the world and those who are in it, by no means dwells in temples made with hands (Acts 17:24). For if, like one sitting on a throne and reigning, heaven is his throne and earth the footstool of his feet, how shall he be shut up in a small place who fills all things, and in whom all things are? Hence Moses too: Do not say, he says, in your heart, He is far off: for God is in heaven above and upon the earth beneath: and there is no other God besides him (Deut 4:39). And the Psalmist: Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I go up into heaven, you are there: if I go down to hell, you are present (Ps 138 [139]:7). With him Jeremiah too agrees, speaking in the person of God: I am a God at hand, and not a God from afar. Can anyone hide in secret places, and I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth (Jer 23:23, 24)? For in him we all are and move (Acts 17). And he says this to refute the Jewish error, who think that the invisible, incorporeal and incomprehensible God can be shut up in the temple of Jerusalem. This indeed Solomon himself, the builder of the Temple, confesses at length in his prayer to the Lord (1 Kgs 8). And lest we think that the greatness of God is to be measured even by heaven and earth, we read of him in another place: Who holds heaven in his palm, and the earth in his fist (Isa 40:12). By these things God is shown to be both outside and within, both poured into and poured around, since he is not shut in by the throne that surrounds him, and he shuts in with his fist and his palm. He is the creator not only of heaven and earth, but also of the invisible Angels and Archangels, Dominions, Powers, and of all men, of whom the Apostle speaks (Col 1): all of which the hand of God has worked. Of this hand both Job and the Psalmist make mention: Your hand has made me and fashioned me (Job 10:18; Ps 118 [119]:73). For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. Of whom John says again: He was in the world, he says, and the world was made through him (John 1). For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created (Ps 32 [33]). And this is what the Scripture of Genesis shows in mystical speech: God said, and God made (Gen 1). For by the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth. And there is no place of the Lord's rest except the one which the Prophet adds next.

"Heaven is my throne, while the earth is my footstool." … Haven't you also read that other text, "Who measured the heaven with the palm of his hand?" … Whoever sat in the palm of his own hand?…Does the same heaven become wide when he is sitting in it and narrow when he is measuring it? Or is God the same size in his seat as he is in his palm? If that is the case, God did not make us in his own likeness, because we have palms that are much narrower than the part of the body we sit with. But if he is as broad in the palm as he is broad in the beam, then he made very unequal parts for us. No, that is not where the likeness lies. Such an idol should be ashamed of itself in a Christian mind.
So then, take "heaven" as standing for all the saints, since earth too stands for all who are on the earth, "Let all the earth worship you."

For the prophet says in the person of the Father, "My Hand made all these things," meaning by "Hand," in his dark saying, the power of the Only-begotten. Now the Apostle says that all things are of the Father, and that all things are by the Son, and the prophetic spirit in a way agrees with the Apostolic teaching, which itself also is given through the Spirit. For in the one passage, the prophet, when he says that all things are the work of the Hand of Him Who is over all, sets forth the nature of those things which have come into being in its relation to Him Who made them, while He Who made them is God over all, Who has the Hand, and by It makes all things. And again, in the other passage, the Apostle makes the same division of entities, making all things depend upon their productive cause, yet not reckoning in the number of "all things" that which produces them: so that we are hereby taught the difference of nature between the created and the uncreated, and it is shown that, in its own nature, that which makes is one thing and that which is produced is another.

But to whom shall I look, except to the poor little one and the contrite of spirit, and the one who trembles at my words? He who sacrifices an ox is as one who kills a man. He who slaughters a sheep is as one who brains a dog. He who offers an oblation is as one who offers swine's blood. He who remembers frankincense is as one who blesses an idol. LXX: And upon whom shall I look, except the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at my words? ÷ But the wicked man ⁚ who sacrifices a calf is as one who strikes down a man. He who sacrifices from the flock is as one who kills a dog. He who offers fine flour is as one who offers swine's blood. He who gives frankincense for a memorial is as a blasphemer. Once the altar and the earthly Temple, which the hand of man had built, have been taken away, the victims of the Jews too are rightly taken away, lest perhaps they should say: We are not so foolish as to think that God can be shut up in a place; but in a place set apart for sacrificing, we sacrifice to God the victims which are prescribed by the law. The inhabitant of heaven, then, or rather the Creator of all, who denies that he has a temple on earth, gladly takes up as his temple the man who is humble and quiet and trembles at his words, according to that saying of the Apostle: But you are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you. If anyone violates the temple of God, God will violate him. For the temple of God is holy, which you are (1 Cor 3:16, 17). Whoever, then, is humble and quiet and trembles at the words of God, him the Lord looks upon; and of him may be understood what is prophesied under the name of the earth: The earth trembled and was quiet, when God arose to judgment (Ps 75 [76]:9, 10). For its inhabitants, for whom the earth is named μετωνυμικῶς, considering the judgment of God, keep quiet from evil works; and sitting at home, rest in an eternal sabbath, so as not to stir themselves to the servile work of sin, as the builders of the tower once moved their feet from the East and left the rising of the true light. Nor did they hear what is said to Cain: You have sinned, be quiet (Gen 4). But according to the Proverbs of Solomon: He who hears God shall dwell confidently, and shall rest without fear from every evil (Prov 1:33). This is the humble and poor little one, contrite of spirit and trembling at the words of the Lord, of whom it is written in the Gospel: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt 5:3). And elsewhere: Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor (Ps 40 [41]:1). And again: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor (Isa 61:1).

All these things they have chosen in their ways, and in their abominations their soul has delighted. Therefore I too will choose their mockeries, and what they feared I will bring upon them. For I called, and there was none to answer: I spoke, and they did not hear: and they did evil in my eyes: and what I did not will, they chose. LXX: And they themselves have chosen their ways, and their soul has willed their abominations: and I will choose their mockeries, and repay them their sins. For I called them, and they did not hearken: I spoke, and they did not hear. And they did evil in my sight, and what I did not will they chose. To sacrifice an ox, to slaughter a ram, to offer sacrifice, to burn frankincense, which God regards as murder and the offering of a dog, and swine's blood and blasphemy, they themselves chose; and that they should worship such things was of their own choice; according to what he says through Ezekiel: I gave them statutes not good, and precepts not good (Ezek 20:25). And in their own ways, he says, they walked, not in the way of the Lord. And their soul has willed their abominations, so that they were lovers of themselves rather than lovers of God. For this reason, since they chose their own ways, and not him who says: I am the way (John 14:6), the Lord too chose their mockeries, or their mockers, who in Hebrew are called THALULE (תעללי), that is, ἐμπαῖκται, so as to set over them very wicked princes, and bring upon them likewise all their evils, or what they feared. And he gives the reasons why they were handed over to the Scribes and Pharisees, their mockers, of whom the first psalm sings according to the Hebrews: And he has not sat in the chair of the mockers: whom the Seventy call the pestilent: such as were the sons of Eli, sons of pestilence, for which in the Hebrew BELIAL (בליעל) is written, that is, of the devil. For, he says, I called, and there was none to answer: I spoke, and they did not hear: and they did evil in my eyes: and what I did not will, they chose. These verses he sets down a second time in the present place, and also above, where it is said: I will number you for the sword, and you shall all fall in the slaughter: for I called, and you did not answer (Isa 65:12), and the rest likewise.
